title: ITO-free perovskite solar cells using laser-patterned graphene oxide electrodes reach 10.5% efficiency indoors
content:
ITO-free perovskite solar cells using laser-patterned graphene oxide electrodes reach 10.5% efficiency indoors
Researchers at Hellenic Mediterranean University (HMU), the HMU Research Center's Institute of Emerging Technologies (i-EMERGE), the Foundation for Research and Technology's Institute of Electronic Structure and Laser (FORTH-IESL), and the University of Crete report the first perovskite solar cells built with a spray-coated, laser-reduced
graphene oxide
(LrGO) layer in place of indium tin oxide (ITO) as the transparent conductive electrode.
ITO remains the standard transparent electrode for perovskite solar cells, but it's expensive, brittle, and resource-limited, and most prior graphene-based alternatives relied on CVD-grown graphene that then needs to be transferred onto glass, adding cost and complexity. Here, the team instead spray-coated graphene oxide directly onto glass and used an ultrashort-pulse infrared laser to reduce and pattern it into a conductive electrode, reaching about 400 Ω per square sheet resistance at 38% transmittance.
The resulting ITO-free, inverted perovskite solar cells reached a 4.78% power conversion efficiency (PCE) under standard 1-sun illumination. Under indoor warm-light conditions (1000 lux), representative of powering low-energy indoor electronics, the same devices reached 10.49% PCE, since the LrGO electrode's absorption losses are concentrated at shorter wavelengths and therefore matter less under indoor lighting. Optical simulations identified parasitic absorption within the LrGO layer itself, rather than the perovskite, as the main factor limiting performance.
The same LrGO process was also used to laser-scribe micro-supercapacitors directly onto the graphene oxide film, reaching 4.3 mF/cm² areal capacitance. The researchers suggest this could eventually allow an ITO-free perovskite solar cell and a micro-supercapacitor to be interconnected on the same glass substrate, enabling self-powered indoor devices that both generate and store their own energy.

title: German startup offers AI platform to accelerate battery storage engineering - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
German startup Morreon has developed an AI-based platform to streamline engineering, design optimization, tendering, and project scheduling for battery storage and other energy infrastructure projects. The system automates data processing and layout planning while maintaining human oversight, with further integration of cost calculations and construction management planned.
Emiliano Bellini
06 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Batteries
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
German engineering startup Morreon GmbH is developing an AI-based operating system designed to accelerate the planning and execution of complex energy infrastructure projects. The platform, called Anchor, combines document processing, engineering design, cost management, tendering, and project scheduling in a single environment.
The company targets battery energy storage systems (BESS), substations, electric truck charging infrastructure, and data centers, where fragmented documentation, repeated design changes, and coordination between engineering disciplines can significantly extend development timelines.
The first stage of the platform focuses on converting unstructured project information into a standardized engineering brief. Anchor processes inputs including PDFs, CAD files, spreadsheets, emails, site documentation, and meeting transcripts. The system classifies information according to its reliability and scope before organizing it within a version-controlled data structure tailored to the relevant infrastructure asset.
“Every extracted value carries full traceability, complete with a confidence level and a direct citation back to the source passage,” said Morreon CEO and founder Alex Zwilling told
pv magazine
, noting that, rather than automatically resolving conflicting inputs, the system flags contradictions for human review. Missing information is converted into prioritized questions assigned to the relevant engineering disciplines.
“To ensure absolute engineering integrity, the system never silently overwrites data; instead, contradictions trigger intelligent proposals for human review, and knowledge gaps transform into prioritized, discipline-tagged questions,” Zwilling explained, adding that engineers must explicitly approve assumptions before they become part of the verified project dataset. According to the company, this creates a consistent information base that can be reused throughout subsequent planning stages.
Automated layouts and design alternatives
Once the engineering brief has been established, Anchor supports the development and comparison of alternative infrastructure layouts. The software maps project information onto dimensionally accurate site plans, allowing engineers to position equipment such as battery containers, transformers, and power conversion systems according to their actual physical dimensions.
“Instead of managing static, disconnected blueprints, architects and engineers can dynamically reposition equipment on the plan, watching power pathways automatically re-route in real time from the grid connection through transformers and power conversion units,” Zwilling said.
Cable lengths and equipment positions are tracked as numerical quantities rather than merely represented as drawing elements. The platform can also generate initial layout arrangements, giving engineers a starting point for evaluating equipment placement and spatial constraints. “This allows teams to compare multiple configurations within seconds, permanently anchoring positions in metric data as baseline documents evolve,” Zwilling added.
Linking design decisions to project costs
Morreon is also working to establish a closer connection between engineering layouts and project budgets. Instead of treating infrastructure components as static elements in drawings, Anchor represents battery blocks, transformers, and cable runs as structured quantities. Changes to a layout therefore update measurable parameters, including cable lengths, equipment requirements, and spatial footprints.
For cost calculations, Morreon uses pricing information from actual supplier quotations and itemized tenders rather than generic benchmark databases. Currently, engineers can assess design modifications against supplier bids, supported by an impact-mapping function that identifies which documents and cost items require updating. A fully automated link between design quantities and tender prices remains under development.
“Morreon’s roadmap directly links those granular tender prices to the design dataset’s quantities,” said Zwilling, highlighting that the planned functionality would allow developers to assess the financial implications of adding equipment or modifying infrastructure layouts during early-stage planning.
The platform also integrates tender preparation, bid evaluation, and project scheduling. Using the verified engineering dataset, Anchor can assemble requests for quotations (RFQs), including technical specifications, procurement scopes, and supplier information. Supplier quotations submitted as PDFs are extracted and organized into structured comparison tables, allowing project teams to evaluate competing bids without manually transferring individual line items into spreadsheets.
“From this single source of truth, the system assembles formal RFQs, incorporating technical specs, scopes, and target suppliers, while automatically ingesting supplier offer PDFs directly into a structured bid comparison matrix,” Zwilling explained.
The same project data supports scheduling and can be exported to tools such as Microsoft Excel and MS Project. Confidentiality controls are designed to prevent commercially sensitive supplier information from crossing unauthorized boundaries. The integrated workflow currently covers the pre-construction process, from initial project intake and engineering through tendering, contract award, and scheduling.
Morreon plans to extend the data flow into purchase orders, delivery tracking, construction supervision, and commissioning. “The ultimate goal is a continuous, error-free thread from initial design through commissioning, ensuring what is planned, ordered, and built always align seamlessly without a single re-typed spreadsheet,” Zwilling said.
Engineers retain final responsibility
Despite the increased level of automation, Morreon emphasizes that professional engineers remain responsible for critical technical and regulatory decisions. Extracted engineering values must be reviewed, assumptions require explicit approval, and unresolved questions cannot be automatically filled with generated information. Tender actions and final project deliverables are also subject to human authorization.
“At Morreon, artificial intelligence acts as a powerful catalyst and draft generator, but the final professional authority and accountability remain strictly in human hands,” Zwilling said.
The company distinguishes between tasks according to the potential consequences of errors. Lower-risk administrative processes can be automated more extensively, while structural design, architectural layouts, and other safety-critical decisions remain subject to stricter human supervision.
Morreon is also building a knowledge base from historical project decisions, enabling the platform to identify recurring configurations and highlight situations requiring additional engineering attention. Source-level traceability, version control, and data storage within EU jurisdictions form part of its approach to compliance. The company is also
bauvorlageberechtigt
in Germany, meaning it is authorized to submit building permit applications directly.

title: Heliene launches all-black solar module for residential rooftops - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The North American module manufacturer has introduced its 108HC M10 SL All-Black residential solar panel, offering power outputs up to 410 W and 21.0% efficiency built on a 108 half-cut cell architecture.
Ryan Kennedy
06 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
The 108HC M10 SL All-Black solar module
Solar module manufacturer Heliene, Inc. has announced the release of its
108HC M10 SL All-Black solar module
, engineered specifically for residential rooftop applications.
The new framed glass-backsheet panel features 108 half-cut monocrystalline PERC cells based on the M10 wafer format, delivering peak power ratings ranging from 380 W to 410 W with a maximum module efficiency of 21.0%.
The module utilizes split junction box technology to minimize cell-to-module losses and improve thermal management. Constructed with 3.2 mm low-iron, high-transmission solar glass featuring an anti-reflective coating, the panel is built into a 35 mm double-webbed anodized aluminum alloy frame.
The panel measures 1,722 mm by 1,134 mm by 35 mm and weighs 21.5 kg. Electrical performance under standard test conditions ranges from 19.46% to 21.00% efficiency, with a maximum system voltage rating of 1,000 V and a 30 A maximum series fuse rating. For mechanical durability, the module is rated for a 5,400 Pa front load and 2,400 Pa back load, while offering hail resistance capable of withstanding impacts up to 55 mm.
The IP-68 rated junction box houses three bypass diodes and comes equipped with standard 1.2-meter symmetrical 12 AWG cables featuring Stäubli MC4 connectors.
The module is certified under UL 61215, UL 61730, and CSA C22.2 standards, with a Type 1 fire rating. Heliene backs the 108HC M10 SL All-Black with a 25-year product warranty and a 25-year linear performance guarantee covering a maximum first-year power degradation of 2.0% followed by an annual degradation rate of 0.5%, guaranteeing at least 86% of original nameplate output at year 25.

title: Indian startup claims over 1,500 cycles for sodium-ion cell with Prussian white cathode - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Indian startup Macsen Energy claims its Prussian white-based sodium-ion battery cell has exceeded 1,500 charge-discharge cycles in laboratory testing, retaining 90% of its initial capacity after 1,000 cycles. The company also plans to build a cathode material production facility and battery cell pilot line, with construction set to begin in 2027.
Emiliano Bellini
06 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Batteries
Energy Storage
Prussian white is a sodium-rich cathode material used in sodium-ion batteries.
India-based Macsen Energy Private Limited has announced that a sodium-ion battery cell using its proprietary Prussian white cathode material exceeded 1,500 charge-discharge cycles in laboratory testing. The company did not disclose whether the results had been independently verified by a third party.
“Crossing 1,500 cycles with sustained capacity and high coulombic efficiency, and retaining 90% of the cell’s initial capacity at 1,000 cycles, is an important result for our team,” said Achal Agrawal, CEO of Macsen Group, who is also involved in the research project. “This result comes from cycling an actual sodium-ion cell in our battery research lab. It validates the promise of our cell technology for long-life energy storage and supports the potential of our Prussian White cathode material to deliver sustained performance over repeated cycles.”
Prussian white is a sodium-rich, iron-based compound used as a cathode material in sodium-ion batteries. Its open crystal structure enables the reversible insertion and extraction of sodium ions during charging and discharging. The material offers potential advantages, including low production costs, abundant raw materials, fast charging and long cycle life. Its high sodium content can also support higher initial capacity and energy density.
“Prussian White may appear straightforward to synthesize, but producing a material that approaches its theoretical capacity and maintains strong electrochemical performance over repeated charge-discharge cycles is a much more demanding task,” Agrawal said. “We see it as an engineered battery material, and our work spans chemical synthesis, material characterization, cell fabrication and testing.”
According to its website, Macsen Energy’s primary cell-development approach combines a Prussian white cathode with a hard carbon anode, although it is also investigating alternative anode materials and anode-free configurations. The company lists an operating voltage range of 2.2 V to 4.0 V and an average discharge voltage of approximately 2.5 V to 3.6 V for its cathode material.
The company claims its production process addresses key manufacturing challenges, including moisture sensitivity, oxygen exposure and scalability, while yielding a highly crystalline, fully sodiated material with low water content and improved air stability. It reports a specific capacity exceeding 150 mAh/g, coulombic efficiency of approximately 99.9% and capacity retention of at least 90% after 1,000 charge-discharge cycles. It attributes the material’s performance to its open crystal structure, which enables rapid, reversible sodium-ion movement with minimal structural changes.
Macsen Energy has allocated 10,000 m2 of land for a facility to scale up Prussian blue analogue cathode material production to tonne-scale capacity. Construction is scheduled to begin in 2027, although the company has not disclosed the location. The site will also house a sodium-ion battery pilot line to further develop Prussian white-based cells, including electrode preparation, cell assembly, validation and performance testing under near-commercial manufacturing conditions.
The company has also initiated research and development into hard carbon synthesis to advance its full-cell technology.

title: Japan proposes four categories for priority commercial solar support - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Japan wants to prioritize future subsidies for new commercial solar projects it considers compatible with local communities, as ground-mounted plants lose feed-in tariff (FIT) and feed-in premium (FIP) support from April 2027.
Brian Publicover
06 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Japan’s Agency for Natural Resources and Energy (ANRE) has proposed keeping feed-in support for commercial solar on land owned by national or local governments, in projects approved under municipal decarbonization plans, on solar carports, and in infrastructure such as airports, roads, railways, and ports.
ANRE presented the proposal in late September to a government renewable energy panel that reports to the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI).
New ground-mounted commercial solar will
lose FIT and FIP support from April 1, 2027
, under rules Japan promulgated at the end of the 2025 fiscal year. The cut follows a
package of measures on large-scale solar plants
approved by Cabinet ministers in December 2025 and recommendations from the Procurement Price Calculation Committee in February. Rooftop solar already receives preferential treatment, and the agency is now selecting which other commercial categories should keep support.
The agency assessed 10 candidate categories put forward by ministries, local governments, and industry groups including the Japan Photovoltaic Energy Association (JPEA). It applied three tests covering importance for future deployment, compatibility with local communities, and suitability for the FIT and FIP schemes. The deployment test draws on potential estimates and Japan’s Seventh Strategic Energy Plan, while the scheme test requires a category that can be defined objectively through documents and is expected to export power to the grid.
To pass the community test, a project must either involve no new land development or major change in land use, or be overseen by national or local government for its full operating life, with the power to correct problems.
Conditions attached
Public land qualifies only when the government leases it out or runs the project itself. Land sold to developers would not qualify, because oversight could lapse. Ponds owned by neighborhood associations are excluded, as they do not pass through approval by a mayor or local assembly.
Projects inside municipal renewable promotion zones qualify only if they hold an approved regional decarbonization promotion project plan under the Act on Promotion of Global Warming Countermeasures. Location in a zone alone is not enough. Projects with approved facility plans under Japan’s law on renewable energy in agricultural, forestry, and fishing areas would be treated the same way.
For solar carports, the agency asked the subcommittee whether support could encourage construction of new standalone parking lots, such as monthly or coin-operated lots. Infrastructure covers airports, roads, railways, and ports. Urban parks are excluded because ground-mounted panels are not expected there.
Excluded categories
The agency proposed no priority support for industrial parks and commercial sites, saying the categories lack a uniform definition and offer no guarantee that existing land use would continue. It also excluded former golf courses, former ski resorts, and abandoned farmland, citing the tree felling, topsoil removal, and grading that projects on such land can involve. Projects defined by supplying local utilities, municipalities, or emergency power during disasters were also excluded, because those benefits cannot be verified objectively and do not by themselves prevent safety, landscape, or environmental problems.
The agency deferred a decision on agrivoltaics. The Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries is preparing
rules defining “desirable” agrivoltaic projects
, including shading below 30%, ground clearance of at least 3 meters, and support spacing of at least 4 meters. The agency proposed giving priority to implementing those rules and continuing to consider agrivoltaics in the next fiscal year.
The 30% shading cap has drawn criticism. In August, the Japan Renewable Energy Foundation (JREF)
called on the agriculture ministry to review the threshold
, citing farms that kept more than 80% of their yields at shading rates above 30%. Japan had approved 6,137 agrivoltaic sites covering 1,361.6 hectares of farmland by the end of fiscal 2023, according to the ministry.
The proposals still require detailed design. Certification criteria, the split between FIT and FIP, auction rules, and support prices and periods will go to the subcommittee and the Procurement Price Calculation Committee between October and January, according to a schedule the agency set out in June. Public comment on the revised ordinances is planned for February and March 2027, with the changes taking effect on April 1, 2027.
Agency estimates put FIT- and FIP-supported capacity at 54.6 GW for ground-mounted commercial solar and 6.1 GW for commercial rooftop, derived by applying the ground-mounted and rooftop split for projects certified since 2017 to total commercial capacity, alongside 17.3 GW for residential systems. A study cited by the agency, led by the Institute of Energy Economics, Japan, puts remaining potential at 137.2 GW for commercial rooftops and 20 GW to 107 GW for ground-mounted sites.

title: Poland unveils new home storage subsidy  - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Poland’s latest subsidy scheme will offer existing prosumers support to purchase and install home storage units. The PLN 1 billion ($258 million) funding call opens for applications on October 20.
Patrick Jowett
06 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Residential
Poland’s Minister of Climate and Environment Paulina Hennig-Kloska
Poland’s Ministry of Climate and Environment has announced a $257.9 million (PLN 1 billion) subsidy scheme for home battery and heat storage, aimed at increasing self-consumption from residential solar and other renewable energy installations.
The program is open to individuals with grid-connected home solar or other small renewable electricity systems. It will subsidize batteries with at least 10 kWh of capacity and heat storage tanks holding at least 100 liters. Batteries must provide at least 2 kWh of storage per kWp of the accompanying solar installation.
The scheme will cover the costs of purchasing and installing home storage systems. Battery grants will cover up to 30% of eligible costs, capped at approximately $206 (PLN 800) per kWh. Prosumers in the net-billing system can receive up to approximately $4,126 (PLN 16,000), while those in the net-metering system can receive up to approximately $2,063 (PLN 8,000).
Applicants can receive up to 30% of eligible costs for EU-manufactured heat storage systems, capped at approximately $258 (PLN 1,000). An additional bonus of up to approximately $516 (PLN 2,000) is available for an EU-manufactured battery or a necessary replacement EU-manufactured hybrid inverter. Total support is capped at approximately $4,900 (PLN 19,000) per electricity supply point.
The scheme is financed through the Modernization Fund. Applications will open on October 20 and close on October 1, 2027, or when funds are exhausted.
Poland’s Minister of Climate and Environment, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, said equipping residential solar installations with energy storage is a ministerial priority.
“The program has two main goals: increasing the efficiency of renewable energy use and strengthening energy security,” she added.
According to the ministry, the number of home energy storage systems in Poland rose from more than 10,000 in the first quarter of 2024 to around 150,000 in June 2026, supported by subsidies and market growth.
The ministry is targeting more than 200,000 home storage systems by the end of 2027.
Sławomir Ćwik, deputy minister of climate and environment, said eligible battery installations must include an energy management system and backup power capability.
“This allows households to maintain power even during grid outages,” Ćwik said.
An initial phase of support financed through Poland’s National Recovery Plan allocated approximately $28.9 million (PLN 112 million) to support the installation of more than 5,000 home battery systems, according to the ministry.
Poland’s Agency for Restructuring and Modernization of Agriculture recently announced a
renewable energy subsidy scheme
aimed at farmers. It opened for applications on October 5.
Following Australia
In Australia, the
Federal government similarly offered a 30% subsidy on home installations of residential batteries
, without a monetary or kWh cap, or need for existing solar installation, though some restrictions were added to cap the total installation sizing.
The scheme has been budgeted to approximately AU$7.2 billion (US$4.68 billion or PLN 18.15 billion), and has seen more than 500,000 households add storage, or some 13 to 14 GWh of behind-the-meter storage capacity.

title: Spacebound silicon - pv magazine Global
content: With excursions into space becoming more frequent, and the reasons behind them more commercial, the industry is exploring ways to generate electricity in space at lower cost and larger scale. And these requirements make ‘terrestrial’ silicon PV technology difficult to ignore. US-based company Source Energy combines commercial silicon cells with a range of module technologies that “makes them suitable for a space environment,” explained Walter Magiera, VP Sales & Marketing at Source. The company has supplied modules to several spacecraft manufacturers, including Impulse Space’s LEO Express 1 that launched in November 2023. It is now working to automate and scale up production at its base in Longmont, Colorado. Among the technologies it has implemented is the shingle-matrix stringer developed by Germany’s M10 Solar Technologies and Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems (ISE). Fraunhofer ISE’s Najwa Abdel Latif noted that this technology, where cells are cut into strips and laid out in offset pattern, is particularly well suited to space applications thanks to its “resilience to localized physical damage from impacts by small objects in space, flexibility in layout, and tolerance to extreme temperature differences.” The cell strips are interconnected and bonded using an adhesive, encapsulated between thin glass layers. The resulting product is a compact solar module measuring 321mm x 209mm and weighing 64 grams. Prototypes developed by Source and Fraunhofer ISE reached an average output of 15.6 W and 18.8% efficiency, measured based on outer space irradiance conditions (AM 0). Magiera expects the production line in Colorado to be running at 10 MW annual capacity by the end of this year, increasing to 30 MW by mid-2027. And he notes if customer demand is sufficient, the line can reach a maximum capacity of 100 MW per year. He estimated that at its current scale, the company can deliver modules between $5 and $8/W, depending on volume and other factors. And the company is targeting to get this down to under $3/W, which Magiera expects it to achieve through scale and increasing automation of processes. “We see that as a competitive price. Others in the market are endeavouring to get to $5 or less. It’s all going to come down to manufacturing efficiency and supply chain costs,” said Magiera. He further noted that while silicon modules and arrays are Source Energy’s current products, Heterojunction and copper indium gallium selenide (CIGS) thin film are both in development and offer distinct advantages for space deployment.  SOURCE is also tracking tandem perovskites, though the technology will need a mature supply chain before it’s viable for space applications, similar to the trajectory perovskites are following in terrestrial PV. Manufacturing at standard configurations is also key to keeping the costs down and ensuring “off the shelf” availability for customers, as well as assurances that come with extensive testing and qualification of the standard devices. Magiera also stated that it designs its arrays to fit within SpaceX rocket fairing dimensions, the current standard for the majority of launches, and offers those arrays in standard widths to achieve standard power classes and configurations. The same approach extends to other launch vehicles, current and emerging, so arrays adapt to a customer’s platform and power needs rather than being locked to one. The product lineup does offer some flexibility on the configuration, and Magiera also confirmed that Source would accept orders for “bespoke” designs at the right volume. Harsh environment The modules are put through a barrage of tests to ensure they can stand up to the radiation, rapid temperature shifts and other harsh conditions outside of Earth’s atmosphere. Magiera explained that Source has put its standard module designs through 1,500 cycles: -110 C to 90 C + and 40,000 thermal cycles from -70 C to 80 C, as well as proton and electron radiation exposure, designed to be representative of seven years in lower Earth orbit (LEO). “There’s a whole suite of testing that we do to get us to meet the rigours of space,” said Magiera. Fraunhofer ISE testing confirms that Source’s PV modules and arrays can be expected to deliver 76% of their initial output after seven years in space. The research institute also noted that the modules were exposed separately to each stress mechanism, and the result calculated by multiplying the percentage of performance retained after each test. ISE also noted in its results that backing up the results with in-situ testing of modules in space is not currently feasible. However, Magiera said that customers who have already launched SOURCE’s modules have voluntarily shared performance data, and the modules are performing as expected. Developing market Most of the inquiries Source Energy receives today come from customers looking to power satellite telecommunication constellations, as well as various types of Earth observation, and the defence industry. Magiera says the company has also received inquiries regarding data centers in space, but notes a widely held view that launch costs need to fall significantly from their current level of around $7000/kg for that market to take off. Some other applications in space will still need the higher power and long track record of III-V, and be willing to pay a premium for that. But the number of applications for PV in space is growing beyond what the supply chain for those materials, and silicon PV is proving a viable solution for a growing number of companies and missions that need to get to orbit quickly and cost-effectively. title: Spain and Portugal record Europe’s highest number of hours with negative electricity prices in Q2 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Spain and Portugal recorded the highest number of hours with negative electricity prices in Europe in the second quarter of 2026, according to Montel’s European Power Market Outlook Q3 2026 report. The period was marked by record solar power generation, a heatwave in late June and significant electricity price volatility.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
06 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Utility-scale
European solar power generation exceeded the previous record by nearly 20%, supported by prolonged periods of high pressure and abundant sunshine. The increase in output led to recurring electricity surpluses around midday, pushing intraday prices to record negative levels in several markets.
The distribution of negative-price periods also shifted compared with the previous year. Spain recorded the highest number of hours with negative electricity prices, at 596, followed by Portugal with 462, France with 370 and Greece with 317. By contrast, Nordic markets experienced fewer such periods. The report attributes these differences to variations in solar capacity growth and electricity demand patterns across Europe.
In Spain, daily and weekly electricity prices repeatedly exceeded €100 ($112.3)/MWh during the late-June heatwave, following a period of high renewable power generation and negative midday prices. In Germany, electricity prices surged above €600/MWh during evening peak hours.
These developments highlighted contrasting market conditions. While high solar output created electricity surpluses during certain hours, rising demand during periods of extreme heat pushed prices higher during peak consumption periods. According to Montel, these fluctuations exposed the limitations of flexibility resources available to European electricity markets.
In late April, prices in some European markets approached the technical floor of €-500/MWh, which was subsequently lowered to €-600/MWh.
Flexible resources shift away from day-ahead markets
The report also identifies a gradual withdrawal of certain flexible resources from day-ahead electricity markets. In response to recurring negative prices, some flexible thermal power plants, storage operators and industrial consumers opted against submitting bids at negative price levels in day-ahead auctions, instead reserving their capacity for intraday or balancing markets.
According to Montel, this shift could move more system-balancing activity into intraday markets, potentially increasing price volatility. It could also increase the value of flexible resources capable of responding rapidly to fluctuations in electricity generation and demand.
The report highlights grid reinforcement, more granular bidding zones, and faster curtailment and redispatch mechanisms as key measures for managing cross-border electricity flows and local grid congestion.
The extreme price fluctuations observed in the second quarter illustrate the growing challenges facing European electricity markets as solar capacity expands. Periods of surplus generation and negative prices increasingly coincide with sharp price spikes during high-demand hours, underscoring the need for greater system flexibility.

title: Thailand tightens solar panel safety standards - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Thailand will now require crystalline silicon solar panels to meet national safety standards in its latest effort to improve the quality and safety of solar installations.
Patrick Jowett
06 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
Residential
Lalida Periswiwatana
The Cabinet of Thailand has approved a draft ministerial regulation requiring crystalline silicon solar panels to comply with the Thai Industrial Standard (TIS), the country’s official national standards organisation.
The TIS enforces product quality and safety rules designed to prevent risks of electric shock, leakage, heat buildup and fire, according to a government press release.
The draft regulation, brought forward by Thailand’s Ministry of Industry, will also require manufacturers or importers of solar panels to obtain a license in accordance with the country’s Industrial Product Standards Act, which regulates national standardisation product quality and safety. It also stipulates distributors can only sell licensed products that meet the TIS, in a bid to prevent the production or import of substandard solar panels.
The regulation is set to come into effect the day following its publication in Thailand’s Royal Gazette.
Government ministers have stated the new standards will not add steps, costs, or delay to the import of solar panels.
The Thai Industrial Standards Institute (TISI) has confirmed that if imported solar products meet International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) standards, the IEC test results can be submitted to the institute for registration under the TIS without requiring further product inspection or testing. The process takes no more than five days, TISI says.
TISI adds that it is preparing to issue 279 import licenses for solar panels that meet IEC standards this month.
The Ministry of Industry says it plans to gradually review relevant standards covering other solar energy system components, such as inverters, cables, and batteries, before presenting them to the Cabinet “in due course, in order to progressively upgrade the safety standards of solar systems.”
The new regulation is the latest in a series of efforts in Thailand to improve the safety of solar panel installations.
In May, the country’s Office of the Consumer Protection Board
opened an investigation
into substandard solar system installations following growing reports of faulty PV equipment, including signs of melting and burning.
In August, authorities began to
officially register
certified solar installations and PV equipment. The registration forms part of preparations to expand rooftop solar installations in Thailand. The government is currently preparing a two-phase THB 200 billion ($6 billion) energy transition program, with the first phase targeting rooftop solar deployment covering up to 500,000 households.
In the latest update, Lalida Periswiwatana, Deputy Spokesperson for the Prime Minister’s Office, said that while the government is promoting greater public access to solar energy, “the expansion of solar rooftop systems must be coupled with safety measures.”
“The panels installed by the public must be of high quality and meet standards so that people can confidently and safely generate their own electricity, reducing their energy costs,” Periswiwatana added.
Thailand’s cumulative solar capacity reached 6,842 MW at the end of 2025, according to figures from the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), compared to 3,388 MW at the end of 2024.

title: What’s driving Europe’s battery boom? Insights from EUPD Research’s Business Climate Survey and Storage Report - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Europe’s battery storage market is projected to nearly double from 34 GWh in 2025 to 65 GWh in 2026, driven primarily by utility-scale projects and growing renewable energy integration.
Meanwhile, intensifying competition in residential and commercial storage is pushing manufacturers toward integrated energy solutions, strategic partnerships, and advanced energy management technologies.
EUPD Research
06 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Europe’s battery storage market is entering a new phase as utility-scale projects become the industry’s main growth engine, creating fresh opportunities for manufacturers while reshaping competition across residential and commercial markets. According to EUPD Research’s new calculations, Europe’s (
EU + UK + Switzerland + Norway + Ukraine)
annual battery storage installations are projected to increase from 34 gigawatt-hours (GWh) in 2025 to 65 GWh in 2026, marking one of the region’s fastest periods of market expansion.
The shift reflects more than stronger battery demand. Higher electricity prices, tighter energy markets, expanding renewable generation and supportive policy measures are changing storage from a complementary technology into an increasingly important part of Europe’s electricity system. Rather than serving only as a backup solution for homes and businesses, batteries are becoming a critical tool for balancing power systems as solar and wind account for a larger share of electricity generation.
Recent findings from EUPD Research’s Business Climate Survey, indicate buoyant demand sentiment across major European markets. The survey gathered responses from a broad base of installation companies, providing a representative view of current market sentiment.
Figure 1: Solar & Storage Demand Across Major European Markets
Utility-Scale Projects Drive the Next Wave of Growth
The strongest momentum is emerging in large-scale battery projects connected directly to the grid. EUPD Research expects the utility segment alone to install a record of around 44 GWh of storage in 2026, making it the largest contributor to Europe’s overall market growth.
Countries with rapidly expanding renewable fleets are leading that transition as grid operators increasingly rely on batteries to shift electricity across different hours of the day, improve system flexibility and support network stability. While electricity prices have eased from the extraordinary peaks seen during Europe’s energy crisis, they remain high enough in many markets to strengthen the business case for storage investments.
Policy is reinforcing that trend. European electricity market reforms, funding mechanisms, permitting improvements and national storage support measures are creating a more favorable environment for deployment, particularly for larger projects that help integrate growing volumes of renewable electricity. At the same time, changing incentive structures in several countries are encouraging households and businesses to maximize self-consumption, making batteries more attractive as export payments for rooftop solar decline or net-metering schemes begin to phase out.
Bigger Projects Reshape the Competitive Landscape
The expansion of utility-scale storage is changing how manufacturers participate in Europe’s battery storage market. As projects become larger and more complex, engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) companies are becoming increasingly specialized, creating a more structured project ecosystem than the fragmented market that characterized earlier stages of deployment.
Insights from the newly released
EUPD PV and Storage C&I EPCMonitor
indicate that local contractors continue serving smaller installations, while national leaders, regional players and pan-European firms are taking on progressively larger battery projects across multiple countries. That differentiation is creating multiple routes to market for manufacturers, allowing suppliers to build longer-term partnerships with contractors that specialize in infrastructure-scale delivery instead of relying primarily on equipment sales.
Project size is increasingly defining competitive positioning. Companies focused on smaller systems continue serving distributed markets, while firms capable of delivering larger projects are becoming more important as utilities, developers and industrial customers pursue higher-capacity installations. The result is a market where partnerships and delivery capabilities are becoming as important as battery technology itself.
Figure 2: Annual Installed EES Capacity | Company Type | 2025
Residential Storage Enters a More Competitive Phase
While utility-scale deployment is accelerating, distributed storage is entering a more mature stage rather than slowing. Europe’s residential market is becoming increasingly sophisticated as manufacturers expand beyond standalone batteries into broader home-energy ecosystems that combine rooftop solar, electric vehicle charging, heat pumps, energy management software and grid-flexibility services.
Several market forces continue supporting residential adoption. High retail electricity prices, declining battery costs, tax incentives, value-added tax (VAT) exemptions and growing interest in energy independence remain important drivers across Europe. However, the market also faces persistent challenges, including uneven smart-meter deployment, financing constraints, labor shortages and the gradual reduction of some subsidy programs in certain countries.
Despite those headwinds, EUPD Research expects Europe to install roughly 15 GWh of new residential battery capacity during 2026, with Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Austria and the United Kingdom remaining among the strongest-performing markets.
According to EUPD Research’s latest
EES Report Europe
, the competitive landscape is evolving just as quickly as deployment. Residential supplier rankings have already shifted between 2025 and the first half of 2026, illustrating how rapidly manufacturers are competing for market share as customer preferences change. Germany’s residential storage market is becoming increasingly fragmented, as share gradually shifts away from the leading suppliers. The top suppliers’ combined share declined between 2025 and H1 2026, while mid-sized brands and smaller brands expanded their presence. These trends point to a market where competition is intensifying and leadership positions are becoming less secure.
Figure 3: Germany’s Residential Storage Supplier Landscape: 2025 Vs H1 2026
Instead of competing only on battery hardware, manufacturers are increasingly differentiating themselves through integrated energy solutions, software capabilities and broader customer offerings that create additional value after installation.
Storage Becomes Core Energy Infrastructure
Europe’s battery market is increasingly developing along two complementary paths rather than replacing one segment with another. Utility-scale batteries are becoming essential infrastructure for balancing renewable electricity and supporting grid operations, while distributed storage is expanding its role within homes and businesses through integrated energy-management systems.
For manufacturers, this creates a dual opportunity. Larger grid-connected projects provide access to infrastructure-scale investment, while distributed markets offer opportunities to deepen customer relationships through broader energy solutions and connected technologies. As Europe moves toward a projected 65 GWh storage market in 2026, batteries are becoming less of a standalone clean-energy product and more of a core component of the region’s evolving electricity system.
The next phase of this market will be shaped not only by how many batteries are installed, but also by how effectively storage becomes embedded across both the power grid and the wider energy ecosystem. Partnerships and delivery capabilities will become increasingly important, particularly in the commercial and industrial segment, where solar, storage and energy management are converging into a single business case.
This is where industry collaboration becomes critical. European Sustainability Week 2026, taking place from 23 to 25 November at the historic Petersberg near Bonn, brings together manufacturers, EPCs, utilities, investors and industrial energy buyers to explore these developments. As Europe’s C&I event for sustainable industries, with a clear focus on renewable energy, solar and storage, it provides a platform for the exchange of market insights and practical solutions. At the Environmental Forum on 24 November, EUPD Research will share the latest market insights, while industry leaders will discuss how storage can become core infrastructure for European businesses.
Last year, more than 600 decision-makers from over 23 countries took part. Registration is open at

He has extensive international experience in sales, marketing, customer engagement, and strategic event management within the renewable energy and cleantech industries. His work focuses on building customer-centric growth strategies, strengthening global partnerships, and supporting market development across the solar, energy storage, and sustainability sectors. title: Wireless bipolar electrodes raise zinc-air battery power by 80% - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers in Spain and Argentina have developed a zinc-air battery architecture that increases power output by up to 80% by reducing internal resistance without changing the device’s core chemistry.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
06 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Batteries
Energy Storage
Researchers at the Institute of Materials Science of Barcelona (ICMAB-CSIC), working with the Catalan Institute of Nanoscience and Nanotechnology (ICN2) and the National University of La Plata in Argentina, have developed a zinc-air battery architecture that increases power output by up to 80% without changing its core chemistry.
The work, “
Unlocking high power in membraneless Zn-air batteries: A paradigm shift via wireless bipolar electrochemistry
,” was published in August in
Energy Storage Materials
. It challenges the conventional approach of avoiding conductive materials in the electrolyte to prevent short circuits. In the new architecture, conductive elements remain disconnected from the external circuit, while their polarization under an electric field reduces internal resistance rather than causing a short circuit.
The architecture introduces small conductive elements inside the battery that are not connected by wires to either the main electrodes or the external circuit. These elements act as wireless bipolar electrodes and modify the distribution of charge within the device.
The principle relies on the electric field that develops between the two electrodes while the battery is operating. When an electrically isolated conductive element is introduced into the electrolyte, the field polarizes it, causing one end to become positively charged and the other negatively charged. The element thereby creates additional pathways for charge transport without establishing a direct electrical connection between the electrodes.
The effect is particularly relevant to zinc-air batteries, in which the electrochemical reaction involving oxygen limits the rate of operation. Zinc has a favorable oxidation reaction and the system uses aqueous chemistry, while the oxygen reaction is slower and can limit the power the device can deliver.
The wireless bipolar electrodes facilitate charge transport through the electrolyte and reduce losses associated with internal resistance. According to the study, the modification can increase power output by up to 80%.
The system does not require changes to the battery’s main electrochemical materials, instead modifying its internal architecture. This could address a key limitation of zinc-air batteries through an additional physical mechanism alongside the active chemistry.
The authors suggest that the concept could be extended to other energy storage technologies.

title: Forecasting domestic U.S. module production to the end of 2027 - pv magazine Global
content:
Following an incredible two days at
Solar Manufacturing USA 2026
in Austin, Texas on 22-23 September, all the intel gathered regarding the U.S.-specific production and capex plans of more than 60 manufacturers has now been digested and analysed.
Overlapping with the official release of the new Solar Manufacturing USA Quarterly report, during this week, one aspect of the report’s key findings will be presented and discussed every day on
pv magazine
Kicking off this special Austin-debrief series of articles, Part 1 looks at domestic U.S. production volumes to the end of 2027.
Forecasting production bottom-up is the bedrock of market research
The Austin event was pivotal on many fronts, with the 400+ attendees likely each having a unique subset of reasons why the event was needed and how it could help shape what comes next with domestic U.S. solar manufacturing.
One of my hopes is that the event could put an end to the past few years of U.S. solar market observers adding up announced capacity numbers or placing pins in maps every time someone is cited with an aspirational factory investment desire.
Adding announced capacities in the solar industry is naïve, unhelpful and misleading. Ditto, collating random investment figures only detracts from the real picture.
The Solar Manufacturing USA Quarterly report tracks and forecasts (to the end of 2030) the domestic solar manufacturing capex and production volumes for 40-plus companies (and set to grow in 2027), making up more than 99% of value-chain production to the end of 2027 at least.
Production and capex at the company level is split into specific manufacturing sites, expansion phases, technology, effective ramped capacity, capacity conversion rates (aka utilization), production outputs – all at the quarterly level. Capex is further segmented into contributions each quarter at the site/expansion level across buildings/infrastructure, production equipment and upgrades/maintenance contributions.
Forecasting production bottom-up is the bedrock of market research
Forecasting module production to the end of 2030 at the company level is one of the most important outputs from the new report. More than simply the total production volumes by quarter, and year, one can then look company-by-company and estimate the total volumes available for new third-party module procurement in the 4-year window 2027-2030.
U.S. module buyers are less interested in total volumes; rather, which companies will have module availability for projects in this period.
Each manufacturing company has its own set of criteria here. First Solar, for example, has the longest pipeline of committed domestic output. Others, such as Illuminate and Canadian Solar, have in-house commitments to downstream project activities. Then we have companies that are focusing more on rooftop or small commercial shipments only and by default are not in the running for 100-500 MW project business.
Finally, many of the companies are new to the manufacturing space – some even being altogether new companies with no track-record of commercial operations.
Therefore, it is truly a mixed bag of module availability if you are looking for secure supply of high-volume domestic-produced modules in, for example, the 2028-2030 period. Having knowledge at the company level outweighs the overall market metrics for production, far less the meaningless capacity-counting analyses that have plagued the U.S. sector since the IRA was introduced at the end of 2022.
Forecasting module production volumes over the next 12-18 months also has its own set of challenges, except for a few exceptions that are running factories today with strong backlog commitments.
Imported cell volumes, at least according to the monthly United States International Trade Commission (UTITC) numbers, are looking decidedly on the low side of recent, as per the HTC codes accumulated. This may get corrected over time. Therefore, the overall 2026 volumes – leading up to December in particular – are still to be known, even if stockpiling becomes an issue and can be proven at the company/importer level.
Good luck to those tasked with this challenge. Even if 232 had not come into force during 2026, there was inevitably going to be a significant second-half import uptick considering the new ramped capacity being rolled out across a wide range of existing and new market entrants. Each now must prove their cell import uptick (relative to historic volumes) is a consequence of having more effective module capacity, or being a new entrant altogether, and not simply to stockpile cells ahead of the MIP coming into effect. Goodness knows how much time and effort is going to be spent on this side issue in the first few months of 2027.
One of my takes from Austin last week was the business-as-usual approach from many c-Si module producers for 2027 – namely to keep buying cells from overseas, albeit at 20-something cents and hopefully sell modules at 40-something levels. And try make the books work as best as possible.
What choice do these companies have? New cell factories take 12-24 months to come online in the United States, and even if a suitable location/shell-building can be found, upfront costs ahead of production are not small change.
Tomorrow’s Austin-debrief article will show the new analysis for cell production to the end of 2027. Suffice to say now that 2027 – the first year post-232 – could easily end up being a record year for c-Si solar cell imports. What does that say about U.S. trade policy in helping domestic manufacturing, some five years on from the Inflation Reduction Act being introduced?
Let’s leave for now with the module production forecast for 2027. The headline numbers may be record-module production metrics, but the reality is still a fragmented landscape desperately trying to release capital into new factories and have some form of certainty that profitability and long-term growth can be provided.
I have shown the forecast in module production to Q4 2027, back to Q1 2025, in the figure below. The upside reflects a production-led scenario, assuming sufficient cell volumes are indeed imported during 2027. Conversely, the downside forecast would kick in if the market is constrained either from project offtake volumes being lower than production targets or from a push-back on buying cells under MIP conditions.

title: Mixed self-assembled monolayer enables 18.88% efficiency in 5.2 cm² inverted perovskite solar cell - pv magazine Global
content:
Researchers at the
Indian Institute of Technology Bombay
have fabricated a large-area inverted perovskite solar cell based on a mixed self-assembled monolayer (SAM) that improves perovskite film quality, enhances charge transport, reduces interfacial recombination losses, and increases device efficiency and stability.
SAMs have emerged as key components in high-efficiency perovskite solar cells, particularly in inverted architectures, where they serve as ultrathin hole-selective contacts that improve charge extraction and reduce interfacial recombination losses. Previous research has shown that SAMs can also
enhance device stability and mechanical reliability
, while optimizing energy-level alignment between the perovskite absorber and the underlying electrode. More recently, scientists have developed
co-assembled SAM strategies
to improve surface coverage, suppress defects, and promote better perovskite crystallization. Further advances in
SAM molecular engineering
have enabled efficiencies approaching 27%, highlighting their potential for developing efficient, stable, and scalable perovskite solar cells.
“We have developed a mixed-carbazole-based SAM strategy for wide-bandgap perovskite solar cells, targeting both surface wettability and suppression of non-radiative recombination at the buried interface. By combining different carbazole-based SAMs, we were able to tune the interfacial properties and promote improved perovskite film formation for the scalabilty of device,” corresponding author Dinesh Kabra told
pv magazine
. “The impact of the mixed-SAM interface on perovskite film formation and charge-carrier recombination was systematically investigated using morphological and optical characterization.”
The scientists explained that scaling perovskite solar cells from laboratory-scale devices of around 0.1 cm² to larger areas remains a major challenge, particularly for inverted (p-i-n) architectures with wide-bandgap (WBG) absorbers. Although significant efficiency improvements have been achieved in small-area devices, increasing their size typically results in substantial performance losses.
With this in mind, they developed a mixed SAM combining [4-(3,6-dimethyl-9H-carbazol-9-yl)butyl]phosphonic acid (Me-4PACz) and [4-(7H-dibenzo[c,g]carbazol-7-yl)butyl]phosphonic acid (4PADCB). While Me-4PACz provides favorable energy-level alignment, low interfacial defect density, and efficient hole extraction, 4PADCB improves wettability and promotes more uniform perovskite crystallization and larger grain formation.
The team built the solar cell with a glass and indium tin oxide (ITO) substrate, a hole transport layer (HTL) based on the mixed SAM, a perovskite absorber, an aluminum oxide (AlOx) interlayer, a fullerene (C60) electron transport layer, a tin oxide (SnOx) buffer layer, and a silver (Ag) metal contact.
The researchers said the mixed-SAM approach combines the favorable electrical properties of Me-4PACz with the improved film-forming characteristics of 4PADCB, resulting in better device performance and uniformity.
In cells with an active area of 1.2 cm², the mixed-SAM configuration achieved a power conversion efficiency of 20.30% and a fill factor of 81.23%, compared with efficiencies of 18.17% and 19.30% for devices using Me-4PACz and 4PADCB alone, respectively. Surface and morphological analyses revealed improved wettability, more compact perovskite films, larger columnar grains, and fewer interfacial defects. Photoluminescence mapping and conductive atomic force microscopy also indicated more homogeneous optoelectronic properties and improved local charge transport.
When the active area was increased to 5.2 cm², the mixed-SAM cell achieved a maximum efficiency of 18.88%, compared with 17.20% and 17.96% for devices based on Me-4PACz and 4PADCB alone, respectively. The larger mixed-SAM cells also maintained an average efficiency of 17.81%, compared with 18.96% for their smaller counterparts, with limited device-to-device variation.
Further analysis showed that the efficiency losses associated with scaling were mainly attributable to increased series resistance at other interfaces and in the transparent conductive oxide electrode, rather than changes in intrinsic recombination characteristics.
Under damp-heat testing at 85 C and 65% relative humidity, the cells took more than 680 hours to fall to 75% of their initial efficiency. According to the researchers, the results demonstrate that mixed-SAM interface engineering can improve efficiency, stability, and reproducibility while limiting performance losses in large-area inverted perovskite solar cells.
“Importantly, the present study isolates interface- and area-dependent losses using a consistent spin-coating process; the solution-processable nature of the mixed-SAM strategy provides potential compatibility with scalable deposition techniques, such as blade coating, slot-die coating, and spray coating, which represent important pathways toward further scale-up and module-level fabrication,” the academics concluded.
The device was described in “
Mixed Carbazole Self-Assembled Monolayers Enable Scalable Large-Area (>5 cm2) Efficient Wide Bandgap Perovskite Solar Cells
,” published in
ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces

title: Utility solar generation reaches record highs in Australia - pv magazine Global
content:
The latest data from global energy consultancy Rystad Energy shows that Australia’s fleet of large-scale solar and wind assets generated 5.44 TWh of clean energy last month, an increase on the 4.99 TWh generated in
and up 7% from the 5.1 TWh recorded in September 2025.
Rystad senior analyst David Dixon said Victoria was the biggest contributor to the monthly total with the state’s utility-scale solar assets generating a record 276 GWh of clean energy while its wind assets produced 1,250 GWh – a total of 1,526 GWh.
Dixon said utility PV generation also reached record highs in New South Wales (NSW) and Queensland, totalling 841 GWh and 645 GWh respectively.
Curtailment of solar dropped year-on-year with 22% of available generation in the National Electricity Market (NEM) curtailed last month, compared to 26% in September 2025.
Acen Australia’s 400 MW Stubbo Solar Farm, in central west NSW, was ranked Australia’s top-performing PV facility for the month with an average AC capacity factor (AC CF) of 35%.
The 162 MW Columboola Solar Farm, owned by South Korea’s Hana Financial Investment, and the 204 MW Edenvale Solar Park, co-owned by Japanese companies Eneos and Sojitz, also notched 35% AC CF.
The performance of the Stubbo Solar Farm, which commenced full commercial operations in late 2025, coincided with the recent arrival of a mob of 250 sheep at the site as part of Acen’s
shared land use approach
that supports grazing, land management, and bushfire preparedness alongside renewable energy generation.
“Agriculture and renewable energy don’t need to compete for land,” the developer said. “At Stubbo Solar, we’re proud to demonstrate how farming and clean energy generation can work hand in hand, supporting local agricultural practices while delivering renewable energy into Australia’s electricity network.”
Acen said the integration of sheep grazing helps keep the land productive while providing practical benefits for site management.
“It’s a simple but effective example of how renewable energy projects can continue to support agricultural activity and create shared value for regional communities,” the company said.
While solar generation continued to reach record high, wind generation in September 2026 was flat or down relative to the same time last year in all states except Queensland.
Wind generation for September 2026 was down about 86 GWh compared to September 2025 while about 13% of available generation in the NEM was curtailed.
The top-performing wind assets for the month were the Flat Rocks facility in Western Australia with a 55% CF, followed by the Cattle Hill and Graville Harbor wind farms in Tasmania, with 49% and 48% CF respectively.

title: AI May Seem Human-Like, but That Doesn’t Mean People Think It’s Conscious
content:
Technology
Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly, with newer systems becoming better at reasoning, generating content, interpreting images, and interacting with people in more natural ways. Credit: Shutterstock
A new study suggests that people do not equate human-like AI behavior with human-like consciousness.
Artificial intelligence can respond to sounds, recognize emotions, adapt to its surroundings, and behave in ways that closely resemble human reactions. Yet people still hesitate to believe that such behavior reflects consciousness.
A new study from LMU finds that even when an AI system and a human behave in exactly the same way under identical circumstances, people judge the AI as less conscious. The distinction was much smaller when participants were asked about “awareness,” suggesting that the language used to describe artificial agents strongly influences how their mental abilities are perceived.
Human Behavior Does Not Equal Human Consciousness
The study, published in
Cognition
, was led by Dr. Louis Longin from LMU’s Chair of Philosophy of Mind together with Dr. Bahador Bahrami, Professor Ophelia Deroy, and other collaborators. The researchers wanted to separate judgments about behavior from judgments about consciousness.
“Whereas previous studies have typically asked general questions about whether AI actually has mental states, our study is the first to directly compare how people attribute the same mental states to AI and humans behaving in exactly the same way, under identical circumstances,” says Longin.
The team recruited nearly 1,100 participants. Some read short scenarios involving artificial agents that varied in how strongly they responded to events around them, such as sounds or the emotional states of other individuals. Another group read the same scenarios with human protagonists. Participants then rated how conscious or aware they believed each protagonist was of its surroundings.
Responsiveness Raised Ratings, but a Gap Remained
For both humans and AI, greater responsiveness led to higher ratings of consciousness and awareness. An agent that reacted more strongly to its surroundings was generally judged as having a richer mental state.
But the pattern changed sharply when participants were asked specifically about consciousness. Even the most responsive AI was rated as less conscious than the least responsive human. Ratings of awareness showed a much smaller divide, with artificial and human agents judged far more similarly.
“There is a growing worry in public discussion that people will see AI behaving in a human-like way and start treating these systems as if they had human-like mental states,” says Longin, lead author of the study. “We found something much more nuanced: People are quite willing to say that an AI notices things and is aware of its surroundings. But they clearly draw a line when it comes to the term ‘consciousness’. People consistently attribute less consciousness to AI than humans – even when their behavior is identical.”
Why the Word “Awareness” Changes the Picture
The difference may reflect how people interpret the terms themselves. “Awareness” can describe an agent detecting and responding to information in its environment, while “consciousness” often carries a stronger implication of subjective experience.
“We may be using mental terms to refer to AI, but this may only be because we lack better words,” says Ophelia Deroy, philosopher and a senior author of the study. “After all, AI is trained to act and speak like a human, so these descriptions seem natural.”
The results suggest that people judge AI differently depending on whether they are considering observable awareness or subjective consciousness.
Language Could Shape How AI Is Perceived
That distinction matters because terms like “aware,” “conscious,” or “intentional” can imply very different things about an AI system’s mental state.
“Our study teaches us lessons for how we communicate about AI,” says Bahador Bahrami, who is also a senior author of the study and an expert in social neuroscience. “Companies and journalists often reach for hyped descriptions of AI models, and credit them with intentions, plans, or even moral conscience and hesitation. What our study shows is that everyday judgments are much more discriminating: People do not simply put AI and humans on the same mental scale. But the boundary also depends on which terms we use. For more neutral descriptors such as ‘awareness’, the distinction can largely disappear. That makes our choice of language important.”
Reference: “AI is not as conscious as humans: Essentialism in mental state attributions to artificial systems” by Louis Longin, Jurgis Karpus, Nadine Meertens, Bahador Bahrami and Ophelia Deroy, 1 October 2026,
Cognition
DOI: 10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106733

title: Could Vitamin C Help Stop Leukemia Before It Starts?
content:
A clinical trial found that restoring vitamin C levels in people with certain precancerous blood disorders was linked to changes in inflammation and a potential survival signal. Credit: Shutterstock
Researchers are investigating whether restoring vitamin C levels can influence the biology of early blood disorders before leukemia develops.
A clinical trial suggests that correcting vitamin C deficiency may benefit people with certain blood disorders that can precede leukemia.
Results from the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 EVITA trial found that participants who took 1,000 mg of oral vitamin C daily for one year experienced fewer adverse events during the study and follow-up period than those given a placebo.
The study, led by the Van Andel Institute-Stand Up To Cancer Epigenetics Dream Team, included 109 people with clonal cytopenia of undetermined significance (CCUS) or myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), both of which can progress to acute myeloid leukemia (AML).
A possible survival signal
The findings, published in the American Cancer Society journal CANCER, also showed that vitamin C changed levels of cytokines, molecules involved in inflammation and immune signaling. The changes were associated with more favorable outcomes and may indicate that vitamin C affects pathways involved in abnormal blood cell growth.
Researchers did not find a significant difference between the vitamin C and placebo groups in the expansion of abnormal blood cell clones, a measure used to track progression toward leukemia.
However, an exploratory analysis found that after about three years of follow-up, participants who received vitamin C were significantly more likely to be alive than those given a placebo. Because this result came from an exploratory analysis in a relatively small phase 2 trial, it needs to be confirmed in a larger phase 3 study.
“We are tremendously excited and cautiously optimistic that our results could one day translate into a simple way to improve care and outcomes for people with pre-leukemia disorders,” said Peter A. Jones, Ph.D., D.Sc. (hon), a distinguished professor at Van Andel Institute, co-corresponding author of the study and co-leader of the VAI–SU2C Epigenetics Dream Team. “Our approach reflects a growing emphasis on cancer interception — intervening before cancer becomes established. We are working to build on the trial findings by exploring how exactly vitamin C interacts with pre-cancerous cells, including the idea that it may help restore normal epigenetic function in blood cells at risk of becoming leukemia.”
Why vitamin C may matter
More than half of the participants were vitamin C deficient when the trial began. Blood testing showed that vitamin C levels normalized in those assigned to supplementation.
Vitamin C has roles beyond immune function and wound healing. It also supports enzymes involved in epigenetic regulation, which controls gene activity without changing the underlying DNA sequence.
One important enzyme is TET2. Mutations in TET2 are common in leukemia and related blood disorders and can give abnormal blood-forming cells a growth advantage. Laboratory and animal studies have suggested that vitamin C can support remaining TET activity and may limit some cancer-related cellular changes.
Earlier studies often tested intravenous vitamin C, which produces much higher blood concentrations than oral supplements. EVITA instead examined whether a daily oral dose could correct vitamin C deficiency and affect early disease biology.
An option for patients with few preventive treatments
There is currently no approved therapy specifically designed to prevent CCUS from progressing to leukemia. MDS can sometimes be treated with stem cell transplantation, but age and other health conditions may make the procedure unsuitable for many patients.
“The standard approach for patients with pre-cancer blood disorders is to monitor their blood cell counts over time. This is, understandably, very frustrating — no one wants to hear that they have a condition that increases leukemia risk, but there’s nothing that can be done other than watch and wait,” said Casey O’Connell, M.D., FACP, the Lawrence and Jane Kelly Chair in Hematology at the University of Southern California and lead clinician for USC’s trial site. “The EVITA trial took on this challenge by exploring vitamin C’s potential to address the underlying factors that drive leukemia development.”
The international study was led by Kirsten Grønbæk, M.D., Ph.D., a hematologist, member of the VAI–SU2C Epigenetics Dream Team, and professor at the University of Copenhagen.
“These exciting preliminary findings lay the groundwork for a larger clinical trial to explore vitamin C as a possible way to improve patient outcomes,” said Grønbæk. “It is too early to make definitive recommendations based on our results, but we are hopeful that a more expansive study will provide further insights.”
Researchers are continuing to analyze the trial data, including biological mechanisms that may help explain the survival difference between the groups.
Reference: “Oral vitamin C supplementation in patients with clonal cytopenia of undetermined significance or lower-risk myeloid malignancies: Results from EVITA, a phase 2 randomized, placebo-controlled trial” by Stine Ulrik Mikkelsen, Ali Al-Mousawi, Amalie Bach Puglisi, Anders Pommer Vallentin, Astrid Østergaard Mortensen, Zachary Madaj, Toshinori Hinoue, Heidi Naomi Ottesen, Jakob Schmidt Jespersen, Linn Gillberg, Morten Tulstrup, Niels Richard Hansen, Jakob Werner Hansen, Mette Klarskov Andersen, Stacey Lyn Thomas, Christine Isaguirre, Ryan Sheldon, Marie Adams, Ryan Burgos, Stephen Baylin, Bo Kok Mortensen, Casey Lee O’Connell, Marianne Tang Severinsen, Peter William Laird, Jens Lykkesfeldt, Peter Jones and Kirsten Grønbæk, 21 September 2026,
DOI: 10.1002/cncr.70549

title: Don’t Miss: Saturn, Halley’s Comet Meteors and the Seven Sisters Light Up October
content:
October brings a packed lineup for skywatchers, including Saturn at opposition, the Orionid meteor shower, and a close Moon-Pleiades encounter. Credit: SciTechDaily.com
October brings several notable skywatching events, including Saturn at opposition, the Orionid meteor shower, and a close pairing of the Moon with the Pleiades, also known as the Seven Sisters.
Skywatching Highlights
October 4: Saturn reaches opposition, making the ringed planet visible for much of the night
October 6: A thin crescent Moon appears close to bright Jupiter before sunrise
October 21–22: The Orionid meteor shower peaks; moonlight may interfere, so look before dawn after moonset
October 27–28: The Moon passes near the Pleiades star cluster, also known as the Seven Sisters
Saturn will be one of October’s main attractions, while meteors from Halley’s Comet streak across the sky later in the month. The Moon will also make a close pass by the Seven Sisters. That’s What’s Up for October.
Saturn Reaches Opposition
On October 4
, Saturn reaches opposition, creating one of the best viewing opportunities of the year for the ringed planet.
Opposition occurs when Earth moves between the Sun and Saturn. From our perspective, Saturn then appears on the opposite side of the sky from the Sun. As a result, the planet rises around sunset and remains visible for much of the night.
A sky chart showing Saturn above the eastern horizon on October 4, 2026, around 9 p.m. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech
Saturn is also drawing scientific attention for activity in its atmosphere. Astronomers have known for years about the giant hexagon-shaped jet stream around the planet’s north pole, which stretches nearly 20,000 miles across.
Just last month, however,
NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope
detected a
ten-sided atmospheric wave surrounding Saturn’s south pole
. The feature in the southern hemisphere appears to be growing stronger, giving researchers an unusual chance to observe a massive atmospheric pattern as it develops.
A sky chart illustrating where to view the Orionid meteor shower. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech
Orionid Meteor Shower Peaks
The Orionid meteor shower reaches its peak from the night of October 21
into the morning of October 22
The Orionids come from small pieces of debris shed by Halley’s Comet. Although the meteors appear to originate near the constellation Orion, they can flash across any part of the night sky.
Meteors streak across the sky during the 2017 Orionid meteor shower, with the Milky Way visible overhead. Credit: Ben Goldstein via Flickr_CC BY-NC-SA
Viewing conditions will not be perfect this year because a bright waxing gibbous Moon will make some of the dimmer meteors harder to see. The best opportunity may come during the final few hours before sunrise, after the Moon has set.
For the best view, head somewhere dark, allow your eyes time to adjust, and scan as much of the sky as possible.
A sky chart showing the Moon next to the Pleiades on October 27, 2026, looking east at around 11 p.m. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech
The Moon Meets the Seven Sisters
On the night of October 27
into the 28
, the Moon will pass close to the Pleiades, one of the most recognizable star clusters in the night sky.
The Pleiades are also known as the Seven Sisters. The cluster has inspired stories in many ancient cultures, in part because it can be seen from nearly every region of the world.
To find the pairing, look toward the east during the evening as the Moon and the Pleiades rise higher in the sky. To the naked eye, the Pleiades look like a faint, slightly fuzzy cluster of 6 to 7 stars.
The cluster is easy to see without optical equipment, but binoculars or a telescope can reveal far more detail and make the view even more striking.
Here are the phases of the Moon for October.
A chart showing the phases of Earth’s Moon in October 2026. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech
