title: AEA Ammonia Certification System Pilot welcomes Woodside Energy’s Beaumont New Ammonia Facility
content:
AEA Ammonia Certification System Pilot welcomes Woodside Energy’s Beaumont New Ammonia Facility
(WASHINGTON D.C., October 06, 2026) The Ammonia Energy Association (AEA) is pleased to announce that Woodside Energy’s Beaumont New Ammonia (BNA) facility has joined the AEA Ammonia Certification System, a global certification system designed to facilitate the transparent, trusted international trade of low-emission ammonia.
BNA is located in Beaumont, Texas and has a production capacity of 1.1 million tons of ammonia per annum. The facility is designed to support growing demand for ammonia and lower-carbon ammonia. Ammonia production at BNA commenced in December 2025 and production of lower-carbon ammonia is targeted for 2027.
As the global adoption of clean ammonia scales up, the AEA Ammonia Certification System aims to support alignment across multiple regions and sectors. During the pilot phase, this voluntary system is open to all entities in the ammonia value chain, allowing producers, traders, and consumers to demonstrate key environmental attributes – namely carbon footprint and origin – using independently verified data.
Kellyanne Lochan, Woodside Vice President Beaumont New Ammonia, said “We are pleased to support the AEA Ammonia Certification System pilot and efforts to build transparency and confidence as the lower-carbon ammonia market matures.”
Trevor Brown, Executive Director of the AEA, said “we are delighted to welcome Beaumont New Ammonia into the AEA Ammonia Certification System pilot. BNA’s participation demonstrates the speed and scale at which ammonia certification needs to operate, enabling million ton-per-year registry operations with ease and integrity. It also shows that low-emission ammonia is not a theoretical future – these molecules and their certificates are available today.”
The AEA Ammonia Registry, built and operated by MiQ, provides pilot participants with a digital infrastructure that enables secure data transfer, transparency, and traceability across the ammonia supply chain, from certificate generation, through trading, to retirement. The AEA Ammonia Certification System supports three distinct chain of custody models — Segregated, Mass Balance, and Book & Claim.
For more information on the AEA Ammonia Certification System or to learn how to join the pilot, please visit ammoniaenergy.org/certification. For learn more about Beaumont New Ammonia, view the AEA’s January 2025 webinar, Woodside Energy: Early-mover advantage in the growing lower-carbon ammonia market.
About Woodside Energy:
Woodside is a global energy company. It provides energy the world needs to heat homes, keep the lights on and support industry. Woodside operates across three continents managing a resilient and diversified portfolio of oil, gas and new energy projects.
About the Ammonia Energy Association (AEA):
The AEA was founded in 2004 with a mission to accelerate the responsible adoption of clean ammonia by promoting cross-sectoral collaboration, knowledge sharing, global standards, and supportive policies. This mission supports both the decarbonization of ammonia production and the use of low-emission ammonia as a fuel and energy carrier. The AEA is a global trade association whose 200+ members represent the full value chain of ammonia across multiple sectors. For more information visit https://ammoniaenergy.org/.
______________________________________________
Note to editors:
Ammonia is one of the most abundant molecules on earth and is both naturally occurring and man-made. It is a vital product, already applied as a nitrogen fertilizer and leveraged in various industrial and consumer applications. It is quickly emerging as a zero-carbon fuel and energy carrier.
To support the adoption of ammonia in energy applications, the AEA has been working since 2021 to develop the AEA Ammonia Certification System, which aims to enable differentiation in the marketplace for low-emission ammonia, enhance credibility throughout the supply chain, facilitate cross-border trade, and support alignment between multiple certification schemes, standards, and regulations.
The key design principles of the AEA Ammonia Certification System include:
- Technology neutral, inclusive of all production pathways (fossil, renewable, bio, etc.).
- Absolute GHG emissions, site-specific, measured not modelled.
- Well-to-gate boundary, including upstream emissions.
- Tradeable, facilitating transfers of low-emission ammonia certificates.
- Regular audits by independent, accredited certification bodies provide assurance.

title: carbmee Applies AI-Native Data Foundation to the EU Digital Battery Passport Challenge - Batteries News
content:
carbmee Applies AI-Native Data Foundation to the EU Digital Battery Passport Challenge
As manufacturers face roughly 80 required data fields per battery across fragmented systems, carbmee positions AI-powered data modelling as the path to passport readiness at scale ahead of the 18 February 2027 deadline.
Carbmee, the environmental intelligence company, is applying its AI-native data foundation to one of the hardest problems in the
EU Digital Battery Passport
: assembling verified, product-level data at scale from information scattered across ERP, PLM, MES, supplier portals, spreadsheets, LCA tools, and battery management systems.
Under Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, from 18 February 2027, EV, light transport, and industrial batteries above 2 kWh require a Digital Battery Passport covering six data categories: general battery and manufacturer information, material composition and sourcing, performance and durability, sustainability and environmental impact, safety, and end-of-life and recycling. Each passport rests on roughly 80 data fields that must be verified, access-tiered, and kept current as a battery moves through use, repair, repurposing, and recycling.
Carbmee’s approach begins with the transactional data a company already holds, then uses AI to connect and model it into a single foundation rather than requiring complete supplier data before any passport can be built. Where primary data is missing, the platform helps teams identify gaps, engage the right suppliers, and validate inputs, so companies can avoid defaulting to high proxy values and the higher assumed emissions that follow.
Because battery passport data is dynamic, updating as service events, state of health, and end-of-life status change, Carbmee’s model is built to maintain lifecycle records over time rather than produce a one-time snapshot. The company argues this is the difference between a claim a manufacturer can defend once and one it can defend continuously.
Carbmee is clear that no software makes a claim lawful and that legal sign-off remains with a company’s counsel. What an AI-native data foundation provides is the verified, auditable, continuously updated data that every passport depends on.
About Carbmee
Carbmee helps enterprise manufacturers reduce cost, risk, and carbon by embedding real-time environmental intelligence into core business systems. The carbmee EIS™ platform manages 5.8 Gt CO2e and delivers, for its customers, an average 345% operational ROI with break-even in four months.

title: Bosch Sees Multi-Powertrain Future for Trucks
content:
Automotive & Mobility
Design & Manufacturing
Bosch abandons bridge metaphor for multi-lane highway, embracing combustion, hybrid & electric truck configurations.
October 6, 2026
At a Glance
Bosch rejects the assumption that the commercial vehicle market will converge on one powertrain.
The company describes powertrain diversity as a multi-lane highway rather than a transitional bridge.
Software and sensors define the truck of the future as much as propulsion systems do, Bosch says.
Bosch Mobility Americas
president and CEO Paul Thomas addressed the press at the company's Mobility Experience Days event at its Flat Rock, MI proving grounds.
The company has previously exhibited technologies like its
Powernet Guardian
at this event.
He discussed the company's support for the expected variety of powertrain options for future
pickup truck
buyers in his presentation:
"I like to call it the truck of the future. And the truck of the future isn't only defined by what's under the hood. It's defined by how you interact with the vehicle and how the vehicle interacts with the market that it operates in.
And it really depends on what it can do for the people that's driving it. And it's made possible by not only the powertrain or the propulsion, but by the software and the sensors that are included in the vehicle and the way they interact with the vehicle itself and with the environment that it operates in.
So let me walk you through, at least in my mind, what that looks like in practice. The old assumption was that the market moves in one direction towards a dominant powertrain, and that really doesn't match what we're seeing in the market today, or what the customers are buying, and what we see in our data. So our answer from Bosch is that there is no single winning powertrain.
Over the past couple of years, I've always said this: that we want to have a focus on all technologies, whether it be internal combustion engines, whether it be hybrids, or whether it be electrified mobility, we believe that there is a multi-lane highway. We used to describe it as a bridge from one technology to another, but we thought that was too myopic.
The fact that it's not a bridge. This is a multi-lane highway having multiple choices of powertrain will be there for a while, and there'll be all different types of configurations based upon what each customer wants."

title: Honda Introduces In-Motion Charging Technology for Commercial EVs
content:
Charging
EV Batteries
Automotive & Mobility
Battery Applications
Discover how Honda's wireless charging roads for EVs highlight the power of collaboration and real-world testing to advance sustainable mobility solutions.
October 7, 2026
3 Min Read
Receiver unit compatible with high power density such as large commercial EVs.
Wireless power transfer (WPT) is helping drive the transition to electric vehicles (EVs). By enabling vehicles to charge without physical connections, WPT systems can address key challenges in EV adoption, including charging convenience,
charging infrastructure limitations
, and operational efficiency. For large commercial vehicles that require significant power and often operate tight schedules, in-motion
wireless charging
could be particularly impactful, reducing downtime and improving the productivity of commercial EV fleets.
Honda R&D Co., Ltd., in partnership with Taisei Corporation and Taisei Rotec Corporation, has developed a wireless power transfer (WPT) road system designed to enable in-motion charging of electric vehicles (EVs). This initiative, which focuses on large commercial vehicles, aims to address key challenges in EV adoption while preparing for real-world implementation through extensive testing and collaboration.
Related:
EV Charging Demand Outpaces Infrastructure Growth, Signaling Market Shift for Charge Station Operators
Addressing the needs of large commercial vehicles
Unlike many wireless charging systems that primarily target passenger EVs, Honda’s WPT road system is specifically designed to meet the demands of large commercial vehicles. The companies' collaboration has developed the underlying technology for a magnetic-coupling wireless power transfer road system (“WPT road system”). Commercial vehicles, which can weigh up to 20 tons, require robust infrastructure that can handle high power loads and ensure long-term durability.
Key roles of the three companies in this joint research. Courtesy of Honda.
The system combines proprietary technology from each company: a Honda high-power-density power receiver/transmitter unit compatible with DC power distribution; a Taisei high-response DC power supply system; and Taisei Rotec technology for embedding equipment in roads.
This focus on commercial applications is particularly significant for the logistics and transportation sectors, where operational efficiency is critical. Frequent charging stops can disrupt schedules and increase costs. Honda’s in-motion charging system aims to reduce the need for stationary charging, allowing vehicles to operate more efficiently. As noted in Honda’s press release, “DWPT technology is expected to enhance the convenience of EVs by supplying power to vehicles while they are in motion, thereby reducing the frequency of charging needed at home or at charging stations.”
DC distribution-based GA system, easily embedded in roads. Courtesy of Honda.
Real-world testing and practical implementation
Starting in Japan’s 2027 fiscal year, the three companies plan to conduct demonstration testing of the WPT road system on public roads. This follows extensive validation testing at Taisei Group’s Future Technology Field (T-FIELD/SATTE), where the system’s durability and performance were evaluated under conditions simulating heavy commercial vehicle traffic.
Related:
These 10 Countries have the Most Charging Power per EV
The public road testing will focus on verifying the system’s ability to deliver high-power wireless charging at speeds suitable for large commercial vehicles. Honda aims to achieve power output levels of up to 150 kW, ensuring the system can meet the demands of high-speed logistics operations. The testing will also evaluate long-term durability, electromagnetic field leakage, and the reliability of power transfer performance. Honda emphasized, “Through these tests, the three companies will strive to ensure both power transfer performance and the safety of the ground assembly (GA) units as structures embedded in the roadway.”
A step toward sustainable mobility
Honda’s focus on large commercial vehicles and its dedication to practical testing reflect its broader vision for sustainable mobility. By addressing the unique challenges of the logistics and transportation sectors, this technology aims to enhance the convenience and efficiency of EVs.
Related:
Could AI Help In-Flight Drone Recharging Take Off?
As Honda stated, “Striving to realize a sustainable mobility society where people can enjoy freedom of mobility well into the future, Honda will continue to pursue co-creation with a diverse range of partners beyond the automotive industry, including road infrastructure-related businesses, government agencies, and energy-related businesses.” This initiative represents a step forward in developing EV infrastructure, with the potential to support the widespread adoption of EVs in both commercial and passenger applications. Once again, it has been demonstrated that collaboration is key to technology innovation.

title: AI Power Spikes Demand Chip-to-Grid Design Changes
content:
AI data center developers and operators are being forced to confront not only how much power their facilities draw, but how quickly that demand can surge and collapse, creating frequency excursions that can ripple across the grid. Panelists at the recent Data Center World Power conference in Dallas (Sept. 21-23, 2026) warned that extreme events, such as a sudden drop of hundreds of megawatts in AI power draw, could trigger wide-area disturbances if not mitigated.
The modern grid was designed for predictability and stability. Morning and evening peaks are forecastable, giving grid operators time to bring additional generation online and then ramp it down. Some turbines that provide the extra power can synchronize within minutes, while others require 30 minutes or more. That cadence is not compatible with AI workloads, which can spike and subside in seconds or even milliseconds. The panelists emphasized that no single company can solve this challenge; it will take a coordinated effort among chip providers, data center operators, utilities, and infrastructure providers.
Related:
Google’s Grid-Interactive AI Data Centers: From Backup to Grid Partner
Nvidia: Managing Rack-Level Load Swings
Nvidia’s rising rack power density has upstream consequences, said Sai Somayajula, principal electrical design engineer at Nvidia. A few years ago, a conventional data center rack typically used 5-10 kW. With Nvidia’s H100 era, that climbed to about 40 kW per rack. Blackwell-class systems pushed it to roughly 150 kW, and the
Vera Rubin generation
targets around 240 kW per rack.
“We are projecting up to 1 MW per rack when 800-volt DC distribution appears in the future,” Somayajula noted. “Power density within the rack is increasing with every generation as AI evolves and solves more complex tasks.”
To blunt the impact of rapid load swings, Somayajula said Nvidia has added rack-level storage and controls to smooth fast excursions within the rack and keep the AC input within grid requirements.
According to the panel, grid operators are increasingly asking data centers to provide
ride-through performance
– remaining connected through short-duration voltage disturbances – and to buffer the grid from volatile AI workloads.
Earlier this year, Nvidia introduced its
DSX architecture
, which combines chip, thermal, system, and software technologies to maximize AI factory throughput. It includes high-speed telemetry and advanced analytics to characterize and mitigate oscillations, allocates unused power headroom to GPUs, and reduces cooling power via warmer-water liquid cooling.
Related:
Can Supercapacitors Smooth AI’s Power Swings?
However, Somayajula stressed that Nvidia cannot solve all these problems alone. “AI workloads, rack density, and power dynamics require a rethink of how we have been designing the data center,” he said. “That is why we partner with the industry, openly share information, and co-design all the way from rack to the grid instead of designing in silos.”
“AI workloads, rack density, and power dynamics require a rethink of how we have been designing the data center.” – Sai Somayajula, principal electrical design engineer, Nvidia
Oracle’s Abilene Stargate: Right-Sizing On-Site Generation for AI
Some of these ideas are being implemented at Oracle’s AI facilities in Abilene, Texas, said Rajesh Gopanath, core infrastructure engineering architect at Oracle Cloud. Oracle’s Stargate data center complex is 60% to 70% operational, with campuses planned at a gigawatt scale, he said. As compute demand outpaces grid build-out, Oracle has been compelled to bring more energy and power-generation expertise in-house.
“Compute was needed yesterday, but infrastructure is delayed due to substation, transmission, or grid unavailability,” Gopanath said. “We can’t get enough turbines, reciprocating engines, or natural gas.”
Gopanath argued that supporting a 1 GW campus with a handful of 200 MW turbines creates
single points of failure
. Smaller building blocks improve resilience without making operations unmanageable. “Maybe 30 MW would be a good size. But you have to work out the best size of each data center building: ‘Should we build 100 MW buildings, 300 MW buildings, or 500 MW buildings?’” he said. “We have to find the sweet spot to make sure that we have the right level of availability down to the rack level.”
Related:
The UPS Is Uninterruptible by Design. Its Future Is Not.
Subsynchronous Oscillations and Ride-Through Requirements
Gopanath warned about subsynchronous oscillations, which are frequencies below the US grid’s 60 Hz operating frequency. These oscillations, if excited by AI data centers’ behavior, can induce mechanical resonance that leads to catastrophic failure, including damage to turbine shafts.
“That kind of catastrophic failure is possible, so we must make sure that it does not happen,” Gopanath said. “All these problems cannot be solved by one technology; you might need capacitors, batteries, uninterruptible power supplies, low-voltage ride-through, power smoothing, and fast-responding generation.”
Mitsubishi Electric: A Layered, Grid-to-Chip Approach to Reliability
David Roop, who leads the power systems engineering division at Mitsubishi Electric Power Products, said supporting AI workloads requires coordinated investments at the substation and grid levels. Success depends on a chip-to-grid approach that accounts for short- and long-duration energy storage, harmonic performance, power quality, and local grid characteristics.
“Data centers are going to play a much larger part in terms of grid reliability by understanding utility requirements, control needs, and the architecture criteria required for a layered approach that will deliver faster projects with reduced project risk,” Roop said. “New guidelines, new standards, and new compliance criteria are being introduced so we can deal with instability much faster.”

title: Data Center Power Demand to Grow 24% Annually by 2030: McKinsey
content:
Data center electricity demand could grow at a compound annual rate of 24% through 2030, but the availability of power infrastructure will determine how much computing capacity developers can bring online, according to McKinsey’s Global Energy Perspective 2026.
The projection places data centers among the most consequential sources of new electricity demand while highlighting uncertainty over how that demand will evolve beyond the decade.
For developers, the immediate challenge is
securing sufficient power
to meet computing requirements. Longer-term investment decisions must also account for improvements in AI efficiency and the possibility that demand develops differently than anticipated.
“From now to 2030, our most likely scenarios all have power supply lower than IT compute demand,” Sam DeFabrizio, a partner at McKinsey, told
Data Center Knowledge
Power Supply Sets the Pace
McKinsey’s projections
combine monthly tracking of CPU and GPU purchase commitments and hyperscaler capital spending announcements with assessments of how quickly power infrastructure can be delivered.
On the supply side, the model considers interconnection approvals, permitting, moratoriums, transformer lead times, and the availability of turbines, reciprocating engines, and fuel cells. Engineering, procurement, and
construction capacity
is another limiting factor.
Faster expansion would require improvements across those constraints, rather than a stronger demand for computing alone. DeFabrizio said greater construction and turbine manufacturing capacity, alongside faster interconnection approvals and permitting, could allow power supply to grow more quickly than expected.
Conversely, limited construction capacity or stronger-than-expected efficiency gains could pull electricity demand below the baseline. Those gains could come from AI models, data center buildings, or greater flexibility in when computing workloads consume power.
The report’s broader conclusion is that inexpensive generation cannot support electrification unless transmission, storage, and reliable capacity are ready to deliver it.
On-Site Generation Adds Speed and New Bottlenecks
Developers seeking faster access to power are turning to gas engines and turbines, fuel cells, and
battery storage
. Those options can reduce dependence on utility construction schedules, but they introduce infrastructure requirements of their own.
“Natural gas is often viewed as the fastest path to adding firm power capacity and generation, but competition for pipeline infrastructure could cause delays in building gas-powered generation,” DeFabrizio said.
That applies to both generation supplying the grid and
facilities operating behind the meter
. Projects requiring redundant pipeline connections to meet reliability requirements face additional complexity.
Locating closer to gas-producing basins can reduce the need for new pipeline infrastructure, DeFabrizio said. Securing rights-of-way for pipeline construction can otherwise be difficult within the short development schedules that operators are targeting.
Battery storage offers another way to manage electricity costs and improve flexibility. However, DeFabrizio cautioned that storage introduces reliability trade-offs when not paired with generation.
Grid Connections Still Matter
On-site power does not necessarily mean a permanent departure from the grid. DeFabrizio said more than 60% of operators now view their strategy as combining on-site generation with grid access.
“Eventually, many data centers that build on-site generation will retain it post-grid connection, becoming flexible grid assets,” he said.
Under that approach, generation initially installed to power a facility could later provide backup and occasional support once utility service becomes available. Running those assets less frequently could
reduce local emissions
while preserving reliability.
DeFabrizio said he also expects a more diverse supply mix beyond 2030. Growing demand and additional grid connections could support expanded solar and wind development, sometimes paired with batteries or other storage technologies.
Integrating data center loads into the wider system, he argued, provides opportunities to spread the benefits of investment beyond individual campuses.
Planning Beyond the Current Boom
For data center developers and utilities, an approach considering multiple energy futures will become particularly important after 2030, when the demand pipeline is less certain.
DeFabrizio suggested developers align capital deployment with indicators of market evolution, negotiate contractual protections with creditworthy customers, and maintain a portfolio of power solutions that can support the grid.
He noted
community engagement
also belongs in that planning process, emphasizing the need to ensure local benefits outweigh potential burdens, alongside managing construction, contractual, and demand risks.
“The leaders across the value chain will likely be those who combine early access to scarce power resources with thoughtful risk management,” he said.

title: EMEA Data Center Expansion Faces a Delivery Test
content:
Power constraints are pushing data center development beyond Europe’s established hubs, but emerging markets now face the challenge of turning ambitious project announcements into operating facilities. Grid connections,
construction capacity
, and community support will determine how much of the next wave gets built.
These were among the key takeaways from DC Byte’s
latest EMEA analysis
, which tracks 93 GW of IT capacity across operating facilities, construction, committed projects, and early-stage developments. Nearly a quarter of that total sits in Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris, and Dublin – the FLAP-D markets – although land and power constraints are encouraging expansion elsewhere.
The figures describe a development landscape rather than available supply. Oscar Gomez Comellas, research manager for EMEA at DC Byte, said roughly 60% of the region’s pipeline remains at an early stage.
Related:
Grid Constraints Steer Dutch Data Centers Beyond Amsterdam
“There are a number of things that need to take place before we consider it ‘realistic’,” he told
Data Center Knowledge
, noting that power availability is the principal obstacle to delivery.
Beyond FLAP-D: Nordics Lead; Milan and Madrid Catch Up
The Nordics are currently bringing capacity online fastest because development began earlier than in markets such as Milan and Madrid, Gomez Comellas said. He added that this lead could narrow over the next 12 months as projects in Milan and Madrid become ready for service.
Michael Winterson, secretary general of the European Data Centre Association (EUDCA), said he expects Europe’s roster of markets with more than 1 GW installed to expand from five to between 12 and 14.
“This is due to … increasing national demand married with lower risks of new deployments,” Winterson told
Data Center Knowledge
. “This is further driven by energy issues and other planning issues, driving development to markets with capacity.”
Nevertheless, the established hubs retain advantages in connectivity and customer demand. New markets must demonstrate that their infrastructure can support successive projects, not just an initial campus.
Winterson said EUDCA forecasts roughly 15% compound annual growth over seven years, taking deployed commercial capacity above 30 GW. Supply chain limitations and shortages of skilled design and construction workers constrain an industry seeking growth above 20%. That European commercial-capacity forecast is distinct from DC Byte’s broader EMEA tally, which includes projects at multiple development stages.
AI Rewrites Site Selection
AI training is giving developers greater freedom to choose sites based on the availability of electricity.
Related:
Power Bottlenecks Push Data Centers Beyond Traditional Hubs
“The majority of AI projects we see today are driven by AI training workloads, which require large amounts of power and don’t necessarily need to be near population centers or connectivity hubs, freeing developers and operators to be more flexible with location,” Gomez Comellas said.
That flexibility could diminish as demand shifts toward inference, where models deliver responses to users. Gomez Comellas said he expects inference to become the main growth driver in the medium term,
increasing demand near population centers
and well-connected metropolitan markets.
Operators, therefore, need to consider how a location’s appeal might change as customers’ workloads change. A power-rich site suited to training may offer a different proposition for services sensitive to latency.
Grid Access and Local Opposition Make or Break Projects
National grids are adding generation and transmission capacity, Gomez Comellas said, but whether those additions can keep pace remains uncertain.
“The question is whether this increase, along with the already existing capacity in the new hubs, will be enough to satisfy accelerating demand,” he explained.
Electricity is only part of the development challenge. Gomez Comellas identified expanding regulation and
local opposition
as factors that can undermine announced projects.
Related:
UAE Data Centers: Powering the Middle East’s AI and Cloud Revolution
“There is increasing awareness of data center projects among local communities, which can come with pushback, sometimes resulting in projects being abandoned,” he said.
Winterson pointed to the Climate Neutral Data Centre Pact and the EU Energy Efficiency Directive’s reporting and labeling framework as benchmarks for environmental performance. He said the industry’s commitments increasingly extend beyond facility efficiency.
“On top of water and energy efficiency, we are now measuring and targeting net new renewables, grid support, heat reuse, and biodiversity initiatives,” Winterson said.

title: HPE’s Gen13 Signals Enterprise AI Shift to CPU-GPU Balance
content:
HPE today (Oct. 7) announced the first batch of next-generation, AMD-powered servers designed to enable enterprises to run AI inference and agentic AI, as well as traditional enterprise workloads such as analytics and virtualization.
The company unveiled its first four ProLiant Gen13 servers, all powered by AMD’s sixth-generation
Epyc 9006 SP7-series CPUs
– code-named “Venice” – featuring new automated security and expanded management capabilities.
The new high-end ProLiant DL585a Gen13 server, which features up to eight GPUs and two AMD Venice processors, is designed for demanding enterprise workloads such as
AI inference
, agentic AI, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) model fine-tuning, and analytics, the company said. The server, available in March 2027, will support GPUs from Nvidia, AMD, and Intel, said John Carter, HPE’s vice president of server product management, quality, and technical pursuit.
Related:
HPE Interview: Why Data Center Efficiency Is Now Core to IT Decisions
“These are not the big [Nvidia Vera Rubin] NVL72 or AMD Helios scale-up type systems. This is for your enterprise-grade customer,” Carter said in an interview with
Data Center Knowledge
. “This is the first time we’ve done this kind of enterprise-grade AI system with an AMD head node. There is a lot of great performance improvements there, utilizing the larger memory bandwidth, higher-performance CPU.”
HPE also introduced three CPU-focused servers. The compact ProLiant DL525 server, available in November 2026, is a 1U, single-socket system featuring one AMD Venice chip with up to 256 cores, designed for AI inference and traditional enterprise workloads, such as virtualization, fraud detection, market data processing, modeling, and simulations, the company said.
The other two new servers, available in 2027, are CPU-based, rack-scale systems that offer high-density compute for very large enterprises or service providers, such as specialist cloud providers (often called
neoclouds
) that have data-intensive AI or HPC workloads, Carter said. The ProLiant XD245 is a four-node, liquid-cooled system, while the ProLiant XD285 is a two-node, air-cooled system.
Analysts: Epyc-Powered ProLiants Aim at Enterprise AI
HPE’s server announcement signals that the company sees enterprise AI adoption on the horizon and wants to be aggressive in meeting enterprise needs, said analyst Matt Kimball of Moor Insights & Strategy. AMD’s sixth-generation Epyc chip is a strong processor for AI because of its high core count, memory capacity, and bandwidth, he added.
IDC research vice president Kuba Stolarski agreed, saying HPE’s four new servers provide organizations with a good mix of hardware for their workload needs.
Related:
HPE Targets GPU Utilization With New AI Networking Portfolio
“Every enterprise is going to have a variety of different AI use cases. So you can’t have a one-size-fits-all from an infrastructure perspective,” Stolarski told
Data Center Knowledge
. “You can’t just put up the largest, most expensive GPU cluster and expect that’s going to be the best solution for every enterprise.”
How ProLiant Gen13 Systems Support Agentic AI Workflows
HPE executives and analysts said the three new CPU-focused ProLiant Gen13 servers can work alongside GPU-based servers for agentic AI workflows. For example, the CPU-focused servers can serve as a CPU head node in an agentic AI system, handling orchestration, tool calls, and retrieval, while GPU systems handle inference.
“You need a whole lot more CPUs to drive orchestration because these agents are making calls, and subagents are making calls. It’s just an ongoing traffic frenzy, and that’s what makes AMD’s Venice so interesting,” Kimball said. “That high core count and high single-threaded performance do a very good job of supporting orchestration for agentic AI.”
Security and Management: iLO 8 Automation and PQC Readiness
Chris Bradley, director of mainstream compute customer advocacy and technical enablement at HPE, said the ProLiant Gen13 systems will feature new automated security features as part of HPE Integrated Lights-Out 8, including support for self-encrypting drives and expanded post-quantum cryptography readiness.
Related:
Discover 2026: HPE Bets on Hybrid Quantum-Supercomputing Architectures
New features in HPE Compute Ops Management software include low-touch onboarding and near-real-time power capacity insights, he said.

title: France’s largest operational BESS reaches 240 MW/480 MWh - Energy Storage
content: TagEnergy has inaugurated a 240 MW/480 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) at Cernay-lès-Reims in northeastern France, making it the country’s largest operational battery storage project. The project, inaugurated on Oct. 1 after four months of operation, is TagEnergy’s first operational storage asset in France. Since its founding in 2019, the Portuguese group has built a portfolio of more than 10 GW of solar, wind and battery storage capacity across the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Japan and Australia, with more than 2 GW currently operational. Connected to transmission system operator RTE’s grid at 225 kV, the project comprises 140 Tesla Megapack battery containers spread across just over 3 hectares. It entered operation after completing the simulations, tests and certifications required to provide frequency containment and automatic frequency restoration reserve services, as well as voltage regulation, supporting grid stability. In addition to Tesla, the project involved French construction and engineering group Eiffage for civil and electrical works. Alsace-based photovoltaic and high-voltage electrical engineering firm Tewa Solar provided project management assistance from development through commissioning. TagEnergy CEO Franck Woitiez said the Cernay-lès-Reims project demonstrates that large-scale electricity storage has become an industrial reality in France. The company said the site fed 70.5 GWh back into the grid during its first four months of operation and completed 145 full cycles over 125 days. Financing for the Cernay-lès-Reims BESS was provided by a banking consortium comprising ABN AMRO, NORD/LB and Caisse d’Épargne CEPAC. The project is jointly owned by TagEnergy and Banque des Territoires, which acquired a stake in 2025. Banque des Territoires holds 49%, leaving TagEnergy as the majority shareholder. It is the first joint investment under a three-year partnership intended to finance several large-scale battery projects in France. Banque des Territoires has been active in electricity storage since 2021 and currently has more than 250 MW of batteries in operation, 150 MW under construction and several hundred megawatts in development. The institution said it plans to increase its involvement in the sector, which is expected to play a role in France’s decarbonized energy mix but still faces challenges in securing bank financing because of the relative maturity of its business model. title: Galileo secures consent for eight-hour and four-hour BESS in Italy - Energy Storage
content: Zurich-based developer Galileo has secured consent for 250 MW of battery energy storage projects in Italy and expects consent for about 100 MW more in the coming weeks. The two projects are each rated at 125 MW. One has 1,000 MWh of storage, giving eight hours of duration, and the other has 500 MWh, or four hours. They are in Italy’s North and Centre-South market zones, Galileo said, without saying which project is in which zone. The company said its Italian team developed both projects in-house, from site selection through authorization, and agreed compensation measures with local municipalities. Galileo has a pipeline of more than 3 GW in Italy across solar, storage, and onshore and offshore wind, and more than 17 GW across Europe. It sold a 98 MW battery project in southern Italy last year. Duration choice Francesco Dolzani, Galileo’s managing director for Italy, told ESS News that the company sizes battery duration country by country rather than applying one design across Europe. “In Italy, we generally develop longer-duration projects. The rationale is optionality, as a longer-duration asset keeps a wider range of offtake and business models open, so we can pursue the most attractive route to market as each project matures,” he said. Dolzani said this matters because the key parameters of Italy’s regulated mechanisms can shift significantly between auctions. These include MACSE, the 15-year storage procurement run by grid operator Terna, and the capacity market . “For example, under the current rules, longer-duration projects tend to be more competitive in MACSE while medium-duration systems may be better suited to a private offtake agreement combined with the Capacity Market,” he said. Lender appetite Dolzani said project finance is becoming a more important lever, as lenders grow more sophisticated in their understanding of battery revenue models. “Beyond long-term contracted schemes such as MACSE, they are becoming more comfortable financing structures that combine contracted and merchant revenues,” he said. Galileo said it has secured consents for more than 650 MW of solar and storage in Italy over the past 18 months. Co-founder and Chief Executive Ingmar Wilhelm said the company plans to begin operating as an independent power producer in Italy with a selection of its projects “in the near future.” Galileo is backed by four institutional investors with combined assets under management of more than €100 billion ($111.9 billion). Terna’s first MACSE auction in September 2025 awarded about 10 GWh for 2028 delivery at a weighted average of €12,959/MWh per year. The second auction , for 2029 delivery, is scheduled for Nov. 24 with a 16 GWh target, after energy regulator ARERA raised the premium cap to €27,000/MWh per year last month. Italian authorities approved 3.25 GW of battery projects in September alone. Outside MACSE, Aer Soléir closed financing in January for its 250 MW/1,000 MWh Rondissone project in Piedmont, which pairs a 15-year capacity market contract with a seven-year toll, the kind of blended structure Dolzani describes. title: Mexico approves 15 MW/150 MWh BESS for Solarig solar project - Energy Storage
content: Mexico’s Environment and Natural Resources Secretariat (Semarnat) has conditionally approved the PV Moquel Solar project in environmental impact terms. Developed by Solarig Mexico, the project will be located in Champotón, Campeche. According to the resolution issued by Semarnat’s General Directorate of Environmental Impact and Risk (DGIRA) on Sept. 10, the project is considered environmentally viable. The plant will have a maximum installed capacity of 104 MW in direct current (MWdc) and a nominal capacity of 75 MW in alternating current (MWac). It will be divided into 14 areas and comprise 162,342 monofacial Canadian Solar C57N-650MS-1500 V modules, each rated at 650 W and using monocrystalline silicon cells. Conversion from direct to alternating current will be carried out using 215 kVA SUN2000-215KTL-H0 string inverters and 14 transformer stations. Electricity will be carried through about 6.56 km of underground medium-voltage infrastructure to a substation that will increase voltage from 34.5 kV to 115 kV for injection into Mexico’s national electricity system. The substation will have a projected capacity of 102.94 MVA. The project will also include an energy storage system comprising 10 battery containers and five transformer stations. DGIRA assigns the BESS a nominal power rating of 15 MW and 10 hours of discharge duration, equivalent to 150 MWh of storage capacity. The resolution itself gives the energy figure as “150 MW/h.” PV Moquel Solar will be located in Moquel, about 4 kilometers southeast of the urban area of Champotón. The project area covers about 273.7 hectares, including 269.93 hectares for the plant site and 3.76 hectares for access roads. Infrastructure will occupy about 138.73 hectares. The project documentation provides for the removal of forest vegetation across 53.323 hectares. It also designates four no-impact zones covering 117.7942 hectares, some associated with the Champotón River and areas containing white and buttonwood mangroves. A further 17.1461 hectares of designated “white areas” will not be used for permanent or temporary works. The environmental approval is valid for 24 months for site preparation, construction and installation, starting the day after the resolution is received, and for 30 years for operation and maintenance. The resolution does not replace other permits. Before intervening in forested areas, Solarig must obtain authorization for land-use change on forest land covering the planned 53.323 hectares. Solarig must also demonstrate compliance with social impact requirements. The company said it submitted a Social Impact Assessment to Mexico’s Energy Secretariat (Sener) in May 2023, but Sener must determine whether that filing remains valid under the current regulatory framework or whether Solarig must submit a new Energy Sector Social Impact Statement. The document issued by Sener must be submitted before any construction work begins. PV Moquel Solar entered the environmental assessment process in June 2024. At that time, the project was reported to have a nominal capacity of 75 MW, maximum capacity of 104 MW and battery storage. The latest resolution does not specify the project’s investment amount, expected employment or estimated annual electricity generation. title: Quick roundup: 265 MWh comes online in Netherlands, Lithuania - Energy Storage
content: New large-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS) have come online this week with a combined capacity of 125 MW / 265 MWh entering operation in the Netherlands and Lithuania. Netherlands 100 MW European independent energy storage provider Return announced that its 100 MW / 200 MWh Antares standalone BESS in Waddinxveen, Netherlands, in the west of country, has entered commercial operation. Return said the project entered commercial operation ahead of schedule and is directly connected to transmission system operator TenneT’s 150 kV high-voltage grid. The company said the project completed construction, grid connection, testing and commissioning before entering commercial operation. Return credited TenneT, energy storage system integrator Alfen and engineering and technical services company SPIE Nederland, among others, for helping bring the Antares project into operation. “A big thank you to all our partners who contributed to bringing Antares from construction to commercial operation. Reaching this milestone ahead of schedule has been a true team effort,” Return said on LinkedIn. Hybrid park in Lithuania comes online Meanwhile, Danish renewable energy developer European Energy has opened its first battery storage project in the Baltics. Located at its renewable energy park in Anykščiai, Lithuania, the 25 MW / 65 MWh BESS is co-located with a 78.5 MW solar farm, forming a hybrid solar-plus-storage facility. The site is located towards the east of the country, some 100 km north of the capital Vilinius. “With the opening of our first battery project in the Baltics, we are adding flexibility to our activities in Lithuania and demonstrating how solar generation and battery storage can work together,” said Tadeušas Konkovskis, vice president and head of the Baltic region at European Energy. European Energy stated that the Anykščiai battery was connected to Lithuania’s electricity transmission grid in Q2 2026 . The company said it expects the approximately 120-hectare site to generate around 80,000 MWh of renewable electricity annually. European Energy currently operates more than 400 MW of renewable energy capacity in Lithuania, while its portfolio of solar, wind and energy storage projects under development in the country is approximately 800 MW. The company is also expanding its storage portfolio beyond Europe. In August 2026, European Energy commenced construction of a 40 MW / 80 MWh BESS alongside its existing 58 MW Mokoan solar farm near Winton, Victoria, Australia. title: e-Storage to deliver 100 MW/200 MWh BESS for OX2 in Australia - Energy Storage
content: e-Storage, the energy storage-focused subsidiary of PV giant Canadian Solar, has announced it will deliver a 100 MW / 200 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) to developer OX2 for its Muswellbrook solar-plus-storage project in New South Wales (NSW). Construction has already commenced on the solar and battery project being built by Swedish-headquartered renewables developer OX2 in partnership with the Australian arm of Japanese resources and energy company Idemitsu. The project, being constructed at the site of a former Muswellbrook coal mine in the Hunter Valley, will comprise a 135 MW solar farm and 100 MW / 200 MWh BESS. e-Storage has signed an agreement to supply and commission the battery system that will utilise its SolBank 3.0 battery containers. SolBank is the lithium-iron phosphate chemistry-based battery designed and manufactured by e-Storage for utility-scale applications. The Canadian company said it will deliver an integrated solution featuring SolBank 3.0 containers paired with power conversion systems (PCS), plant controls, and the company’s proprietary EQ-S Energy Management System (EMS). e-Storage said once operational, the system will support the long-term hybrid power purchase agreement (PPA) OX2 has signed with web giant Amazon for the project, converting variable solar output into firm, contracted supply. The 135 MW solar farm and 100 MW / 200 MWh BESS is one of nine Australian renewables projects Amazon signed PPAs with earlier this year as part of a part of a 430 MW deal . Amazon has contracted 94.5 MW of solar and 70 MW of battery capacity from the Muswellbrook project. OX2 Australia Vice President Steve Symons said the BESS is a key element of the project, helping to strengthen grid reliability in a region transitioning away from coal. “This battery storage system is what turns Muswellbrook into a true hybrid facility, pairing solar generation with storage so we can capture energy when the sun is shining and deliver it when the grid needs it most,” he said. “It’s a key step in providing firm, reliable renewable power to the Hunter region.” e‑Storage said shipments are scheduled to begin in Q3 2027, with commercial operation targeted for Q3 2028. In addition to supplying the BESS, e‑Storage is also responsible for the grid connection studies, supplying the hybrid power plant controller that coordinates the battery with the co-located solar farm, and leading the overall integration and commissioning of the hybrid project. The company will also be responsible for maintenance of the Muswellbrook BESS under a 20-year long-term service agreement (LTSA). The Muswellbrook project is being delivered as a joint venture between Bouygues Construction Australia and Equans Solar & Storage with Idemitsu Australia as co-development partner. title: E-bikes are causing a surprising new problem in Europe
content:
Micah Toll
| Oct 7 2026 - 7:36 am PT
Europe has spent years encouraging people to ditch cars and get around on bicycles and e-bikes instead. And in many places, it’s working. But all of those increasingly sophisticated electric bicycles have created an unexpected new problem: there aren’t nearly enough people to fix them.
Europe could need to recruit a staggering 105,000 additional bicycle mechanics by 2032, according to a new report on the continent’s cycling industry.
The NextGen Mechanics report, presented at the inaugural European Cycling Industries (ECI) summit in Brussels, estimates that Europe currently has around 175,000 bicycle mechanics. But
Bike Europe
says the industry is already short around 45,000 workers, and growing adoption of e-bikes, cargo bikes, bike leasing, and commercial cycling fleets is expected to make that shortage significantly worse.
And e-bikes are a big part of the reason why.
Modern electric bicycles increasingly require more than the traditional assortment of hex keys that can solve most issues on a good-old-fashioned ten-speed. E-bikes can require electrical troubleshooting, firmware diagnostics, motor servicing, battery expertise, and specialized training that varies between manufacturers.
Cargo bikes add another layer of complexity (especially since nearly all cargo bikes sold in Europe
are now equipped with electric motors
), while growing fleets of rental, delivery, and leased e-bikes mean many bikes are accumulating mileage much faster than the average privately owned bicycle.
The result is that workshops simply can’t keep up.
According to Shimano’s State of the Nation 2026 survey, 212 million Europeans experience some type of barrier when trying to maintain their bicycles. The report says 121 million people consequently ride less often, while 7.6 million have stopped cycling altogether due to service delays.
That last figure is particularly troubling. After all, an e-bike doesn’t do much
to replace a car
if it’s sitting in a garage for six weeks waiting for someone to diagnose a motor error.
The problem isn’t simply a lack of people interested in working on bikes, either. The report points toward relatively low wages, poor career prospects, and fragmented training systems as major contributors.
Low pay and low social status were cited by 72% of respondents as factors behind the shortage. In Germany, for example, bicycle mechanics earn an average of around €30,000 per year compared to a national average salary of €43,000. In Italy and Spain, average mechanic salaries are reportedly just €16,000 per year.
Meanwhile, training varies wildly between European countries. Germany, Austria, and Switzerland have established apprenticeship systems, while other countries rely on vocational programs, dealer training, or largely informal pathways into the industry.
ECI is now proposing a standardized pan-European entry-level qualification that would include mechanical skills as well as electrical diagnostics and safety training, with manufacturer-specific education layered on top.
Electrek’s Take
I’m going to go out on a limb here and call this one of the better problems for the cycling industry to have.
The rapid growth of e-bikes has created an entire new category of skilled technical jobs, and now the biggest issue is figuring out how to train enough people and pay them well enough to stick around. At lot of us – myself included – can talk in the past tense about the time we spent working in a bike shop. For many of us, it was a temporary job as a springboard to something else, and the number of folks who stick around is seriously lacking. The industry needs more qualified bike mechanics and it needs them yesterday.
We shouldn’t underestimate how serious the problem can become, as it directly impacts bikes’ ability to continue improving cities. As e-bikes increasingly replace cars for commuting, school runs, deliveries, and other daily transportation, reliable service becomes much more important. If your recreational mountain bike spends two weeks in the shop, that’s really annoying. If your cargo e-bike that you use to take two kids to school every morning spends two weeks in the shop, you’ve suddenly got a transportation problem.
And the increasing technical complexity of e-bikes means the old model of simply hiring someone who is good with bikes isn’t necessarily enough anymore. These are becoming increasingly sophisticated vehicles, and the people maintaining them need the training – and compensation – that reflects that.
Perhaps the biggest takeaway here isn’t that Europe somehow has “too many e-bikes.” It’s that the rest of the cycling ecosystem hasn’t grown fast enough to support them.

title: E-quipment highlight: AMT's hot-swapping battery electric rail excavator
content:
Commercial EVs
Electric Heavy Machinery
Jo Borrás
| Oct 7 2026 - 5:42 am PT
Rarely seen by the general public,
rail road excavators are a critical piece of the infrastructure puzzle
– one that can travel directly on the tracks while digging, lifting, and clearing obstacles from the track, working on everything from track maintenance and renewal to utility and civil construction projects. This one’s electric.
Co-developed by Dutch equipment brand AMT and construction firm Royal BAM, the TW series of electric rail road excavators (available in 150, 160, and 180 sizes, representing 18-24 metric tonne classes) are all-electric machines packing a 600V electrical system managing a water-cooled, permanent-magnet electric motor putting out 121 kW (~160 hp).
The motor draws power from a set of four 90 kWh battery packs (360 kWh total) good for 8-16 hours of continuous operation. The interesting bit, though, is not only that the batteries are swappable to help the excavator keep on keepin’ on – they’re hot swappable, meaning it can keep working on two or three batteries while a second machine plucks one out and pops in another one,
so the crew can keep riding the rails
What’s more, the same modular 90 kWh battery packs can be shared across a number of AMT machines, which keeps energy from being stranded in idle assets and reduces the job’s total investment in batteries and machinery in the same way – and for the same reasons – that similar systems work for
Craftsman
Milwaukee
Hot swap, won’t stop
The clever battery-swap trick doesn’t mean AMT treated charging as an afterthought, though. The excavator’s onboard charger can charge the batteries at up to 120 kW, which the company claims can bring the full 260 kW pack from a 20–80% SOC in under two hours – so you won’t need three or four machines to make the battery pack investment make sense.
You can check out some of the AMT electric rail excavator’s specs
in the company’s online brochure
, then let us know what you think of the machine’s hot-swap battery trick in the comments.

title: Hyundai shelves IONIQ 3 launch in Australia as cheaper Chinese EVs take over
content:
Peter Johnson
| Oct 7 2026 - 6:50 am PT
has scrapped plans to launch the IONIQ 3 in Australia. Importing the electric hatch would be too costly to compete with low-priced Chinese EVs.
Hyundai cancels the IONIQ 3 for Australia
The IONIQ 3 will not go on sale in Australia as Hyundai initially planned. Hyundai announced the electric hatch would arrive in Australia in early 2027, following its launch in Europe and the UK.
That will no longer happen. Hyundai quietly removed the IONIQ 3 landing page from its Australian website.
A company spokesperson confirmed to
that bringing the IONIQ 3 to Australia, which is built in Turkey, would be “too difficult” and costly.
“The cost of importation is high, and the car will be fighting in a very price-sensitive segment. The numbers just don’t work for us given the competition,” Hyundai’s spokesperson explained.
The IONIQ 3 was expected to go on sale in Australia priced from around AUD$40,000, before on-road costs. Unlike other Hyundai and Kia models, Hyundai produces the IONIQ 3 at its Izmit plant in Turkey, which would make it too expensive to compete with lower-priced Chinese EVs.
Hyundai IONIQ 3 N-Line (Source: Hyundai UK)
According to
The Driven
, the top 10 best-selling electric vehicles in Australia through September include the Tesla Model Y (35,930), BYD Sealion 7 (19,964), Geely EX5 (12,745), Zeekr 7X (10,800), Omoda Jaecoo J5 (10,664), BYD Atto 2 (8,673), Tesla Model 3 (5,775), Kia EV5 (4,722), Kia EV3 (4,541), and BYD Atto 1 (4,471).
The IONIQ 3 would have competed against others in the segment, such as BYD’s Dolphin, which starts at as low as AUD$28,888.
Hyundai IONIQ 3 (Source: Hyundai UK)
In the UK, the IONIQ 3 is
now on sale
, starting at just £18,495 ($25,000) OTR, including the £3,750 Electric Car Grant. In Europe, it costs around €28,950 ($33,000).
Hyundai’s electric hatch is available with 42 kWh and 61 kWh battery packs. The base IONIQ 3 Advance trim with the 42 kWh battery offers up to 213 miles of WLTP range. The IONIQ 3 Advance with the 61 kWh battery starts at £21,995 ($29,000) and offers a “class-leading” WLTP range of up to 308 miles.
Hyundai IONIQ 3 interior with Pleos Connect infotainment system (Source: Hyundai)
The IONIQ 3 is also Hyundai’s first vehicle in Europe equipped with its new Pleos Connect infotainment system.
Measuring 4,155 mm (163.5″) long, 1,800 mm (70.9″) wide, and 1,505 mm (59.3″) high, with a 2,680 mm (105.5″) wheelbase, the IONIQ 3 is slightly smaller than the Kia EV3.
Electrek’s Take
Because the IONIQ 3 is built in Europe, Hyundai can undercut much of the competition, including BYD’s new “Super Hybrid” Dolphin G DM-i (£23,990). That would not be the case in Australia.
While Hyundai has no plans to bring the IONIQ 3 to the US, Hyundai Motor CEO Jose Munoz
warned last month
that without barriers, the US could be next in line for a wave of low-cost Chinese vehicles.
“All ⁠the top sellers are Chinese because there are no barriers,” Munoz told
, referring to the UK.
The UK “was a very profitable, very strong market,” Munoz said, but now it “has become like China” with brands like BYD quickly gaining market share.

title: Rivian R2 gets live Pet Cam in update, AI assistant, and more
content:
Rivian R2
Fred Lambert
| Oct 7 2026 - 8:25 am PT
Rivian is rolling out Pet Cam, a new feature in software update 2026.36 that lets R2 owners check on a pet left in the vehicle through a live video feed in the Rivian app.
It’s exclusive to the R2. R1T and R1S owners get new remote Pet Mode controls instead, and the same update brings the Rivian Assistant to the R2, four months after the SUV launched.
How Pet Cam works on the R2
Rivian announced the feature today
. Pet Cam uses the R2’s interior cabin camera, which the company describes as a “high-definition RGB” unit, to send a full-color view of the cabin to your phone.
The Rivian R2. Pet Cam relies on its color cabin camera. Source: Rivian
There are two ways to use it. You can open a live stream from the Gear Guard section of the Rivian app, with a badge on the video showing the current cabin temperature. Or you can skip the stream entirely, because the app dashboard and your phone’s lock screen get fresh still images of the cabin on a regular basis.
Pet Cam sits in the Gear Guard tile of the Rivian app. Source: Rivian
Most of the time, you don’t want to watch your dog sleep for five minutes. You want a two-second look to confirm everything is fine, and a lock screen snapshot with the temperature on it does that without opening anything.
Rivian also built in an off switch. Anyone sitting in the vehicle can end the live stream with one tap on the center display.
The automaker says more than 60% of its owners travel with a dog, which explains why this got done four months into the R2’s life.
Rivian says more than 60% of its owners travel with a dog. Source: Rivian
R1T and R1S get app controls, no camera
R1 owners aren’t getting Pet Cam. Rivian ties the feature to the R2’s cabin camera and didn’t announce a version for its flagship truck and SUV.
What Gen 1 and Gen 2 R1 owners do get is remote control of Pet Mode, which the R2 gets too. Until now, you had to turn Pet Mode on before you left the vehicle. With 2026.36, you can switch it on from the Rivian app after you’ve walked away, and switch it off by tapping the paw icon in the app’s climate controls.
Either way, the app asks you to confirm first. That’s there so you don’t shut off the climate control by accident, or leave it running for hours.
Pet Mode on the R2’s center display. Source: Rivian
The catch is Connect+
Rivian’s announcement doesn’t mention pricing. But there’s a catch.
Rivian’s own Connect+ page lists “remote camera livestreaming” as a paid feature, not a standard one. Connect+ costs $14.99 a month or $149.99 a year.
The fine print on that page also caps Gear Guard Live Cam at one hour of streaming per day. It says interior viewing only works with Pet Mode enabled and “is not to be used for people.”
Tesla owners will find all of this familiar.
Tesla launched Dog Mode in 2019
, and its owner’s manual says you can view the cabin from the Tesla app while the mode is on, with periodic cabin snapshots on newer iPhones. Tesla’s
remote live camera view launched as a Premium Connectivity feature
, and that plan costs $9.99 a month.
Rivian Assistant reaches the R2
Update 2026.36 also brings Rivian’s AI voice assistant to the R2. It can adjust climate, media and navigation, answer general questions, pull up the weather at your destination, and identify the song that’s playing.
You call it up by pressing the right Haptic Halo Wheel on the steering wheel, tapping an icon on the display, or saying “Hey, Rivian.”
Rivian Assistant on the R2’s center display. Source: Rivian
R1 owners have had it since May. When
Rivian launched the “Hey Rivian” assistant
, we reported that it would be on the R2 when customer deliveries started. The
R2 launched on June 9
, so buyers waited four months for a feature that was supposed to be there on day one. And it needs Connect+ too.

title: This e-bike fits seven riders, and that’s not even the craziest thing about it
content:
Micah Toll
| Oct 7 2026 - 8:26 am PT
If you’ve ever looked at a cargo e-bike and thought, “Sure, but where am I supposed to put the other six people?”, SixThreeZero may finally have the answer.
The company’s latest addition to its growing e-bike and e-trike lineup, the
Long Range Luxury Rickshaw
, is already a fairly ridiculous machine in its standard form. It combines three wheels, dual motors, rear passenger seating bench, and enough battery capacity to make many electric motorcycles jealous. But start adding its optional passenger trailers, and you can essentially build yourself a seven-person electric bicycle train.
And somehow, that’s still not the craziest number on the spec sheet.
The rickshaw packs a whopping 7,300 Wh of battery capacity. That’s not a typo. We didn’t move a decimal. It’s literally got 10x the battery capacity of most e-bikes.
The setup includes two 48V 20Ah batteries integrated into the frame, plus an enormous 48V 112Ah battery mounted beneath the rear passenger seat. Combined, that works out to 7,296 Wh of capacity.
For comparison, a typical commuter e-bike might have a 500-750 Wh battery.
The company claims up to 120 miles (193 km) of range, though as always, actual range will depend heavily on speed, terrain, assist level, and – perhaps more than with most e-bikes – how many friends you’ve talked into joining your bicycle conga line.
But with that mileage figure working out to an efficiency of around 60 Wh/mi (36 Wh/km), that spec sheet range number might actually be a fairly realistic rating. There are a lot of e-bike companies trying to claim 100-mile ranges with a 720 Wh battery, though they admittedly don’t have the rolling resistance of this e-trike locomotive.
Power comes from a pair of 750W motors. Riders can select single or dual-motor operation, with the latter offering 1,500W of combined nominal power for hills and heavy loads. Top speed is listed at 20 mph (32 km/h), available through either pedal assist or throttle.
The base rickshaw seats the rider plus two rear passengers and starts at
a rather hefty $7,495
. But that’s where things get interesting.
SixThreeZero offers $999 rear “sub-frames” that attach behind the trike, with options for passenger seating or cargo baskets. Up to two can apparently be connected, creating the seven-person configuration pictured above.
There are even powered versions of those sub-frames with their own motor and battery, controlled from the cockpit of the main bike. At that point, we’re getting dangerously close to building a Mad Max electric road train one bicycle component at a time.
Other equipment includes hydraulic disc brakes on all three wheels, a torque sensor, 20 x 4-inch fat tires, suspension fork, ergonomic handlebars, headlights with high and low beams, turn signals, mirrors, brake lights, a rear differential, and a front cargo basket.
Oh, and a captain’s chair that looks significantly better than the seats in my first car.
Electrek’s Take
Is a $7,495 three-wheeled e-bike with more than 7 kWh of batteries and a pair of passenger trailers excessive? Absolutely.
But I’m also having trouble pretending I don’t want to load six friends aboard and find out just how far this wonderfully absurd contraption can actually go.
And having
personally tested SixThreeZero Rickshaws in the past
, including putting at least six people on one (pictured below), I know they make these things well.
Lord help the first guy who ever tries to back one of these e-bike trains up, though.
Definitely don’t try this at home. But if you do, follow my lead and use borrowed kids from around the neighborhood

title: Dodge Charger Daytona EV Sales Crater: Less Than 800 Deliveries This Year
content:
Dodge Charger Daytona EV Sales Crater: Less Than 800 Deliveries This Year
Sales of the world’s first and only electric muscle car dropped nearly 90% compared to last year.
- The Dodge Charger Daytona electric muscle car is looking like a sales flop this year.
- Dodge sold fewer than 800 units so far this year, a steep drop compared to last year.
- Meanwhile, the recently introduced gas version is picking up the slack.
The Dodge Charger Daytona EV is gearing up for a disastrous year. The battery-powered Charger sold just 767 units from January through September, a massive 89% drop compared to the same period last year, when the American automaker managed to find 7,057 new customers for the world’s first and only electric muscle car.
To make matters worse, Dodge moved just 233 electric Chargers in the third quarter, revealing that customers have pretty much had enough of the admittedly cool-looking EV. Since debuting in late 2024, the dual-motor Charger racked up 8,242 cumulative sales in the United States. Last year, the EV had its best year, selling 7,421 units.
It’s a bleak picture for what was supposed to be a headline-making machine, but one that ultimately ended up causing headaches for customers and dealers alike. Software gremlins took center stage when we tested the Daytona EV, and when contributor Andrew Lambrecht decided to lease a 2025 Charger EV for a great price, he didn’t see much of his car after paying the first round of invoices.
The car didn’t move an inch for over two months while it was undergoing repairs, and Dodge eventually bought the car back from Andrew six months after he signed the lease documents. Not a great look.
On paper, the Dodge Charger Daytona looks pretty good. It’s powered by a dual-motor setup that’s good for 630 horsepower, with an additional 40 hp that can be added for 10 seconds when the PowerShot feature is enabled. It looks good and has the unique Fratzonic Chambered Exhaust, which makes it sound like it has a big, stomping V-8 engine under the hood. That may or may not be up everyone’s alley, but it’s a cool take on the external sound systems that all the other EV makers have been trying to figure out in the last couple of years.
The 2027 model comes with a NACS charging port from the factory, but the 94-kilowatt-hour (usable) battery pack is the same as before. Charging from 20% to 80% takes roughly 24 minutes, and the estimated driving range with a full battery is 267 miles. These aren’t record-setting numbers by any stretch of the imagination, but they’re adequate. However, with the 2027 model, Dodge upped the pricing significantly, adding $12,500 on top of last year’s already hard-to-digest $61,990, bringing the total to $74,490 (including destination charges).
Meanwhile, the entry-level gas Dodge Charger, which is powered by a 3.0-liter inline-six gas engine, starts at $51,990. More expensive versions are also available, but they still cost less than the EV, though it’s worth noting that the Daytona remains the most powerful of the lineup.
All this being said, it’s no surprise that the gas-powered model handily outsold the EV in the third quarter, with 8,023 units reaching new customers in the U.S.

title: Even Russia Is Beating The U.S. In EV and PHEV Market Share
content:
Gasoline shortages are pushing Russian buyers toward electric cars and plug-in hybrids. Most of them come from China.
Photo by:
Andrei Nedelea
12:47pm ET
EVs and PHEVs have captured a larger share of the Russian market as the country reels from a fuel crisis.
Gasoline shortages following Ukrainian refinery strikes are pushing Russian buyers toward Chinese plug-in cars.
Russia's EV and PHEV market share is now higher than the U.S.'s
Russia is an unlikely place for an electric car sales breakthrough. It has enormous oil resources, long driving distances, middling infrastructure, and winters that wreak havoc on EV range. Yet it now has a higher share of plug-in car sales than the United States, according to new research from Autostat, as cited by
The New York Times
. There's a clear reason why
Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have disrupted fuel supplies, leaving motorists searching for gasoline or waiting hours at stations, as the
has reported. So while the country has plenty of oil, refining it and delivering it to customers has been a major challenge in 2026. That has given some buyers a pressing reason to choose a car that can run without it.
Citing Russian automotive research agency Autostat, the
reports that electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids reached a combined 11.5% of Russia’s new car market at the end of September, up from about 5% at the beginning of the year. That share is slightly higher than America’s.
The statistic includes plug-in hybrids, so it doesn't establish that Russia has overtaken the U.S. in fully electric cars alone.
Autostat chief Sergei Tselikov recounts what determined him to make the switch. After visiting five nearby gas stations, none of which had gasoline, he bought a GWM Ora 03 GT electric hatchback in July. He notes that the model’s price rose by roughly $2,000 within days as demand increased.
Stay informed with our newsletter every weekday
Reuters reported that Russian sales of new pure electric cars and plug-in hybrids reached 26,543 during the months of June through August, more than double the 12,187 sold in the same period a year earlier. It linked the increase to fuel shortages and said suppliers had been caught off guard by demand. Separately, NEWS.ru cited Tselikov reporting 2,216 new electric-car sales in August, up 105%, with the main growth coming from models priced at 2 million–3 million rubles ($23,500–$35,300).
America, meanwhile, faces a different disruption. EV sales spiked just before September 30, 2025, when the federal tax credit ended, then
immediately slumped
, although they have shown some
signs of recovering
Cox Automotive estimates that Americans bought 78,895 new battery-electric vehicles this August, accounting for 5.7% of new-vehicle sales. Volume rose 2.5% from July but fell 46.9% against the unusually strong August 2025 comparison. That is a BEV-only figure, so it should not be compared directly with Russia’s combined 11.5%.
Energy Information Administration
, citing Omdia, says BEVs represented 6% of new light-duty sales in the second quarter, with PHEVs adding 1.4%. It covers an earlier period than Russia’s reported September share, but shows how low plug-in interest remains among Americans, although conventional hybrids reached 16%.
More On This
The European Union is much further along.
reports 1.64 million BEV registrations during January through August, representing 21.7% of new cars. Another 758,082 PHEVs brought the combined plug-in share to 31.7%. In Europe, more model choice and lower prices are helping buyers switch, with
fuel prices providing a clear nudge
China operates on another scale again. According to CPCA figures, August retail sales included 698,000 BEVs and 307,000 plug-in hybrids (including
range extenders
). That is roughly 1 million plug-in cars capturing over 65% of the country’s passenger car market. Fully electric models alone accounted for approximately 45.3%.
The numbers aren’t perfectly apples-to-apples. But in a world of rising gas prices and growing EV demand, America looks further and further behind the pack.

title: Honda Will Test Wireless EV Chargers On The Highway In 2027
content:
Honda Will Test Wireless EV Chargers On The Highway In 2027
Next year, Honda will begin testing out a wireless charger baked into a stretch of highway near Tokyo.
- Honda will begin testing wireless charging on a Japanese highway next year.
- It envisions commercial use at first and sees it as a path to cheaper, lighter EVs with smaller batteries.
- The path to real-world viability is bigger than just one car company.
Car companies have discovered quite a few ways to improve EV range over the years. There's the efficiency route, which produces a 500-mile EV like the Lucid Air. There's aerodynamics and, of course, stuffing a big ol' battery into something like the Chevy Silverado EV.
Some automakers are looking outside the vehicle too. This week, Honda announced that it has developed wireless-charging technology and that it aims to start testing it on public roads next year. We're not just talking about any wireless charging—Tesla and Porsche have that covered.
This is wireless charging that powers up a car while it's in motion. Hardware embedded in the road will wirelessly beam up to 150 kilowatts of power to vehicles traveling at 75 mph. Honda's R&D subsidiary developed the technology alongside a Japanese company called Taisei.
Before you get your hopes up, this isn't a massive rollout. Honda calls the first stage "demonstration testing." The manufacturer has targeted a small stretch of highway in the Chiba prefecture outside of Tokyo spanning just over an eighth of a mile (300 meters) where it will work to install the necessary infrastructure and deploy it commercially.
This particular test is aimed at validating the initial tech for use in commercial vehicles. Think large trucks or big people movers that do a lot of commuting and require continuous uptime. But on the flip side, if there's viability in big trucks, there's certainly the possibility that the tech could eventually make its way into passenger cars as well. Honda notes that the tech works in both passenger cars and big trucks.
Honda's chief engineer of R&D, Taku Ueda, told Nikkei Asia that this type of charging could even reduce the number of battery cells installed in future EVs. That's a huge deal because not only are batteries a major contributor to the cost of new electric cars, but the weight also plays into range inefficiencies and road wear. So while the total range might be reduced on paper, sipping on electrons while in motion could actually translate into traveling just as far thanks to wireless charging. He also said the technology could relieve some of the Japanese public's charging anxiety.
Honda isn't the first automaker to research this type of charging. Other companies and governments have tried this before with varying levels of success over the years. Electreon is the big player, and it installed a short stretch of wireless-charging road in Detroit.
Some companies are looking to charge EVs at lightning speed while others swap batteries. Meanwhile, Honda apparently sees a future where wireless charging and more efficient cars roam the roads. Maybe the answer is all three.
