The Battery Show North America 2026: Arkema highlights Material Solutions for production of EV and ESS batteries
Arkema, a global leader in Specialty Materials, will showcase its unique portfolio of solutions and innovations for battery electric vehicles (BEV) and energy storage systems (BESS) at the upcoming
US Battery Show 2026 in Detroit, Michigan (US), October 12-15, Booth # 2714.
EV batteries need range, safety and compact design, while stationary storage demands low cost, long life and large-scale reliability. Arkema will present solutions specifically designed for both markets, including materials for use both inside and outside the cell.
Meet our team at the Booth #2714
While ESS production has increased significantly in the past year, we continue to see healthy demand across all segments of the battery market. We are actively looking at the needs of all battery segments to offer solutions that meet both existing and emerging technology needs.
Nicolas Champagne, Global Market manager for Batteries and Datacenter applications
EV Batteries
– Material Solutions to improve range, safety and compact design
Arkema is working closely with battery manufacturers to improve upon both existing and new materials for use in EV battery applications. Efforts include solutions that significantly increase energy density, including recently introduced
Incellion
acrylic binders designed for silicon-based anodes, and
PVDF products
used as a cathode binder and separator coating in lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries. These solutions are designed to support higher active-material loading and the development of higher-energy-density battery cells.
The group also provides a wide range of materials that improve thermal management and other safety-related needs outside the battery pack, including Rilsan
Polyamide 11, Reafree
coating resins, Zenimid
Polyimide, Rilsamid
Polyamide 12, Sartomer
UV-curable materials, Bostik adhesives and other materials.
ESS Batteries
– Solutions to improve value, lifecycle and scalability
ESS battery applications require a different balance of cost, safety and scalability. Arkema is working with manufacturers to offer unique solutions across those products. The group offers both
Incellion
binders for use in LFP systems, the primary chemistry in stationary energy storage.
Additionally, the group introduced new
Incellion
binders for primer coatings and ceramic-based separator layers that complement existing
Flex PVDF
coating products already in use.
To address the industrialization of new battery technologies, Arkema recently introduced advanced research and production capabilities notably  with the successfully completion of a 15% PVDF capacity expansion at its Calvert City, Kentucky plant in June 2026.

Manufacturing by Informa’s annual event features speakers covering North American battery competitiveness, AI, commercialization and the future of electrification
DETROIT, Oct. 08, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) —
The Battery Show and Electric & Hybrid Vehicle Technology Expo North America
, returning to
Huntington Place
Detroit, Michigan
October 12-15
has announced five keynotes
exploring the challenges and opportunities shaping the battery industry—from building a competitive North American supply chain to scaling manufacturing and commercializing energy storage technologies. The event will bring together industry leaders to discuss practical pathways toward resilient supply chains, reliable production and long-term industry growth.
Tuesday, October 13
The Next Chapter of Battery Materials: Building a Competitive and Resilient North American Graphite Supply Chain: Venkatesh Vasudevan, Vice President, Graphite Materials, ExxonMobil Product Solutions
Vasudevan will examine the evolving battery materials landscape and what it will take to build a resilient and globally competitive North American graphite supply chain. The discussion will include the challenges of scaling domestic production, navigating global supply dependencies, meeting cell manufacturer and OEM requirements, and creating the industrial infrastructure needed to support long-term battery growth.
Looking toward 2030 and beyond, the keynote frames a critical question for the industry: Can North America build a battery materials supply chain that is not only resilient, but globally competitive?
The Future of Battery Manufacturing: Risks and Opportunities in the Age of AI and Cold War Two: Jason Schenker, Economist and President, Prestige Economics
Economist, futurist, and author Jason Schenker will examine how AI, reshoring, geopolitical tensions, critical minerals, tariffs, and supply chain risks are reshaping battery manufacturing and investment.
Attendees will leave with practical insights on where the greatest opportunities and risks are likely to emerge over the next decade.
Wednesday, October 14
Powering the AI Economy: From Energy to Compute: Paul Charles, Principal, Charles and Associates
Inventor and infrastructure strategist Paul Charles will address how AI training and inference affect power requirements, where batteries fit from the server rack to the site, and why cooling and electrical design must keep pace with increasing computing density. The session will explore approaches to faster deployment, the challenges of integrating power and compute, and the opportunities for battery and energy storage suppliers in the growing AI economy.
Miller will offer keen insights on the challenge of global battery electric vehicle demand not reaching anticipated levels while interest in electrified vehicles including hybrids, plug-in hybrids, and extended range electric vehicles has continued. In parallel, there has been an unprecedented increase in renewable energy generation and AI data center development. The net result is an increase in energy storage demand.
Whether grid support requires Li-Ion technology akin to that found in electrified vehicles, sodium ion, flow batteries, or other sources of energy storage, advancing the technology from a laboratory concept to a commercial product requires thoughtful scale up and validation. This talk will look into the path forward to bridging the gap.

Looking Back, Moving Forward: The Evolution of the Battery Industry: Robert Galyen Senior Strategic Consultant & Advisor – Retired Chief Technical Officer of CATL at Galyen Energy,
Dr. John Warner, Chief Industry Relations Officer, American Battery Solutions
Industry veterans Galyen and Warner will connect for a closing fireside chat reflecting on the evolution of the battery industry and looking ahead to what comes next. The conversation will include lessons learned, emerging opportunities, and the future of battery innovation and leadership.

Vice President, Manufacturing by Informa, says:

title: XBM USA and SiCAM Technologies Collaborate to Advance Next-Generation Silicon-Sulfur Battery Technology - Batteries News

XBM USA and SiCAM Technologies Collaborate to Advance Next-Generation Silicon-Sulfur Battery Technology
Collaboration pairs SiCAM’s low-cost silicon-carbon anode material with XBM’s sulfur cathode and cell technologies, to offer US battery OEMs an integrated silicon-sulfur (Si-S) battery platform.
LOS ANGELES, Oct. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — XBM USA LLC (“XBM”) and SiCAM Technologies, Inc. (“SiCAM”) today announced a technology collaboration to develop a Silicon-Sulfur (Si-S) very high-energy-density battery materials platform by coupling SiCAM’s silicon-carbon (Si-C) anode material with XBM’s lithium-sulfur (Li-S) cathode materials and advanced cell technologies.
Silicon-sulfur is amongst one of the most promising next-generation battery cathode and anode chemistry platforms, with substantially higher theoretical energy density than conventional li-ion batteries (LIBs). Silicon is the second-most-abundant element in the Earth’s crust, sulfur is a U.S. petroleum-refining byproduct, and XBM’s Li-S cathode is derived from lignin, an abundant U.S. paper pulping byproduct.
Asia, predominantly China, currently controls ~80–95% of the global battery cell and materials supply chain. U.S. battery manufacturers are seeking better, lower-cost, domestically sourced chemistries that reduce reliance on foreign materials. This shift creates opportunities for U.S. OEMs to leapfrog legacy technologies.
Jon Shan,
Chief Technology Officer of XBM USA, said,
Our near-term objective is to optimize our high-capacity Li-S cathode and SiCAM’s Si-C anode in a first-of-its-kind silicon-sulfur battery platform, initially targeting high-energy-density, lightweight eMobility battery applications such as eVTOLs and drones.
SiCAM’s proprietary silicon anode material and process are unique amongst all other Si-C anode products made today. Most other Si-C anode material developers use silane (silicon) in a CVD process to make their Si-C anode products. SiCAM uses chlorosilane (TCS) silicon in a fluidized-bed chemical vapor deposition (FB-CVD) process. This novel approach creates a true bonded silicon-composite primary structure, helping to reduce the 300% silicon swelling problems experienced during battery charge and discharge cycles.
On the cathode side, XBM’s high-capacity Li-sulfur cathode targets improved sulfur utilization, cycle life and cell-level energy density using abundant industrial byproducts, such as sulfur and lignin.
Phillip Roberts,
co-founder of SiCAM Technologies and XBM USA, said:
This silicon-sulfur cell technology collaboration is the natural evolution of our company’s US centric “Sustainable Battery” vision avoiding longstanding battery chemistries that are mined, more expensive, and foreign sourced and controlled

title: EV Charging Design Becomes Business Advantage
content:
Automotive & Mobility
Charging
Market Analysis
Interviews
As adoption accelerates and affordable models arrive, intuitive charging systems become essential infrastructure for communities.
October 9, 2026
4 Min Read
ABB E-mobility's X1600 commercial charger.
ABB E-mobility
At a Glance
User-centric design transforms charging from unreliable technology into trusted infrastructure.
Modular platform thinking reduces costs while improving serviceability and manufacturing efficiency.
Design excellence directly impacts business growth, operator scalability, and driver adoption rates.
In the early days of the EV charging industry, calling design an afterthought was extremely generous. The products felt like they had more in common with a fax machine than an iPhone.
Chargers were difficult to use, creating frustrating experiences and failed sessions for drivers, and lost revenue for operators. They required complex, bespoke engineering that made the logistics behind manufacturing, service, and maintenance expensive and prone to bottlenecks.
Ask the person waiting in line at your coffee shop why they don’t drive an EV, and the answer is likely some combination of the unreliability or lack of charging.
A 2026 survey from JD Power
showed that public charging consistently remains the top reason new-vehicle shoppers reject EVs.
Even so,
consumer interest in EVs is accelerating,
and new, more affordable models are hitting the marketplace. So, how can we prevent the EV charging failures of our past from derailing adoption?
Related:
7 Battery-Electric Semi Trucks Hauling Freight in 2026
The answer emerged when our design team endeavored to answer two simple questions. Who are we designing for, and what do they need? As EV charging matures, success depends less on adding new technology and more on designing systems that work naturally for the people who use them, the businesses that operate them, and the communities in which they exist.
Raising the Standard
Great user experience and great product design are everywhere. It's on your wrist, it's in your pocket, it’s parked in your driveway. We are perceptive judges of good design because we interact with it continuously. So when people used chargers in their earliest form it didn’t take long to recognize they weren’t going to meet their expectations.
Complex, confusing, and unreliable, it felt like UFO architecture, just dropped in without consideration. Then, it seemed like the industry was lagging or that no one had the time, people, or expertise to consider design.
Now, it’s at the heart of product and commercial decisions, and we’ve collectively recognized the need to design with sympathy and consideration for users and the environment in which these chargers will occupy for a decade or more.
Looking to Civic Infrastructure
EV charging is public infrastructure and part of the fabric of our future cities. As new drivers who aren’t early adopters begin to plug in, the urgency to make charging more intuitive and seamless while earning its place in the public domain is rising.
Meeting those twin demands meant looking to design that solves similar problems. Insight into wayfinding and guiding the user journey emerged from Schiphol Airport, where structured iconography and typography deliver the right information at the right time to simplify navigation.
Related:
Jaguar Type 01 EV Delivers 1,015 HP and 400-Mile Range With Breakthrough Battery Engineering
In Anthony Gormley’s sculptures, we found the presence and posture for human scale, and in Zurich’s street furniture, the empathy and permeance that simple forms can create.
The Airplane Galley Principle
Historically, the EV charging industry built point products. Today, the opportunity is in building platforms, modules, and experiences that work together as a coherent system.
Imagine, for a moment, an airplane galley. It's an example of a mature design system where a relatively small number of components create an extraordinary amount of flexibility. Everything has a place, everything has a purpose, and the whole thing is designed to be robust, serviceable, and adaptable over time.
It's about defining the minimum number of components for the maximum amount of utility. That's the way we've approached our charging portfolio.
ABB E-mobility product designs. ABB E-MOBILITY
Take, for example, the charge posts of our recently announced
OM system
. The extruded aluminum structural module becomes the foundation of an adaptable system. Using that same architecture, we can create a single-connector or dual-connector configuration, with or without a screen, while maintaining a consistent design language and shared components across the portfolio.
Related:
Bosch Envisions Multi-Lane Highway for Truck Powertrains as Market Rejects Single Solution
That has obvious benefits for customers because it gives them flexibility while maximizing the applicable use cases: It simplifies manufacturing, increases component reuse, reduces complexity in the supply chain, and makes servicing products in the field much more efficient.
Service technicians encounter familiar systems regardless of configuration, which reduces training time, simplifies spare parts management, and speeds maintenance. In the end, good system thinking isn't just a design exercise. It's a way of creating better experiences while improving the economics of the entire product lifecycle.
Design as a Business Lever
Ultimately, that's why rethinking design is so important. As EV charging moves from emerging to essential infrastructure, success will depend on more than power output, port counts, or charging speeds.
The companies that succeed will be the ones that create experiences people trust, systems operators can scale, and products service teams can maintain efficiently. Good design makes charging easier to use, easier to manufacture, easier to service, and more sympathetic to communities where it will live for decades.
The proximity of design to the success of the business and the EV industry is very, very close. It is a business tool, a growth driver, and increasingly a competitive advantage.
About the Author
Rhys Newman
Global Head of Design, ABB E-mobility
Rhys Newman is Global Head of Design at ABB E-mobility, where he leads industrial design and user experience across the company's charging portfolio. Over a 30-year career spanning Nokia, Google X, Everyday Robots, Casper, and co-founding OMATA, he has built high-performing design organizations that use design as a strategic driver of innovation, customer experience, and business growth.

title: Jaguar Type 01 EV Engineering Breakthroughs
content:
Automotive & Mobility
Design & Manufacturing
EV Batteries
The automaker's first all-electric sedan combines dramatic styling with innovative powertrain tech & advanced thermal management systems.
October 9, 2026
At a Glance
Engineers relocated 32 battery cells ahead of the firewall to provide rear legroom while adding 70 miles of range & 148 hp.
The 118-kWh battery uses side-mounted bus bars instead of top-mounted ones, trimming height from 150 mm to 120 mm.
Silicon carbide inverters switch at variable frequencies from 2 to 20 kHz, optimizing efficiency based on driving conditions.
is taking a step into a new future that frees the company of the baggage of a glorious past that has, in recent years, served to weigh the company down.
The new Type 01 EV (pronounced Type Zero One) boasts an impressive 1,015 horsepower and 1,007 lb.-ft. of torque driving through all four wheels to produce 3.1-second 0-60 mph acceleration.
The low-slung four-door sedan packs a 118-kilowatt-hour 850-volt (effectively 800v) battery that is good for 400 miles on the typical government test cycle and 320 miles when hammering down the highway at 75 mph, the company reports.
Using 350-kW
DC fast charging
, the Type 01 can add 200 miles of driving range in 13 minutes. In the 10% to 80% state of charge benchmark, the Type 01 takes 22 minutes, which is especially impressive considering the battery’s size and the corresponding amount of electricity needed to accomplish that.
Polarizing design
The car features noteworthy engineering throughout, with more than 360 patent applications for its various innovations. This technology risks being overshadowed by the Type 01’s dramatic styling, whose crisp industrial lines are a clean break from Jaguar’s historically voluptuous bodywork.
Related:
7 Battery-Electric Semi Trucks Hauling Freight in 2026
Public reaction to the car’s styling has been polarized, but a fresh design is crucial for Jaguar to engage a new generation of customers. And the styling prompted the engineering department to up its game in several areas in a bid to deliver the dramatic sheetmetal envisioned to showrooms.
The Type 01's long hood is meant to evoke classic designs without relying on tired design cues. JAGUAR
This is necessary because Jaguar sales have slumped as its customer base has aged. The Baby Boom exploded the US car market as it began driving in the mid-1960s, and automakers delivered models catering to them.
Ford sold 560,000
Mustangs
in 1965 and another 607,000 of them the next year. Rival carmakers rushed their versions of Pony cars to market, bringing nameplates like Camaro, Firebird, Cougar, ‘Cuda, and Challenger.
Now, these cars are all gone, and last year Ford’s original model sold fewer than a tenth as many cars as its forebear did 60 years ago. Jaguar is in a similar spot, with the group who appreciated the brand’s virtues buying fewer cars in their golden years. The break with tradition needed to be dramatic, and Jaguar’s styling department delivered. That put the onus on the engineering department to find ways to bring the eye-catching design to showrooms.
Design enabled by technology
The significant design attributes are the car’s low roof, its long hood, and its large wheels, creating a silhouette worthy of Cruella De Ville’s car in “101 Dalmatians.” Engineers can’t just decide to build a car that looks like this. It takes work to produce parts like the hood itself, which is formed from a single stamping that is bonded to an innovative subframe for support.
Related:
Why EV Charging Design Is Now a Competitive Advantage for Operators & Manufacturers Alike
The car’s long front end stretches the bodywork out ahead of the passenger compartment, which, in EVs, is usually the space where the battery cells are contained. The Type 01 has a battery case beneath the floor of the passenger compartment in standard fashion. However, because of the low roofline, engineers carved out a section in the rear-seat footwell where there are no battery modules beneath the floor, providing the legroom necessary for rear-seat comfort.
They moved those batteries ahead of the firewall, outside the protection of the car’s passenger cell. That provides space for 32 more of the Type 01’s nickel-manganese-cobalt prismatic cells, boosting the car’s driving range by 70 miles and its power output by 148 hp compared to only using the batteries that are under the floor.
This is possible due to a pair of large, complex aluminum die castings that Jaguar calls Tri-Apex Nodes. These protect the cells in the event of a crash, along with the battery management system, which is also located there.
Related:
Bosch Envisions Multi-Lane Highway for Truck Powertrains as Market Rejects Single Solution
Jaguar's Tri-Apex Node die casting. JAGUAR
The car’s North American Charging Standard-spec charge ports are on both sides of the car behind the front wheels, and the Tri-Apex Nodes are cast with a large passage in the center for the charge port wiring to go through. In the US, the driver’s side port is AC-only, while the passenger’s curbside port supports both AC Level 2 charging and DC fast charging.
Unorthodox battery configuration
The Type 01’s prismatic cells are 120 mm high, so to minimize their height beneath the car’s floor, engineers located their bus bars on the sides, rather than putting them on top in conventional fashion. That would have produced batteries that were 150 mmm. This means that 80% of the battery’s height contains energy, compared to only 62% when the bus bars are top-mounted, according to propulsion manager Andrew Ellis.
The Type 01's battery pack shows a gap between the last module on the left and the next one, where the rear seat footwell dips into that space for additional legroom. JAGUAR
The pack is split into two 400-volt sub-packs, in recognition that 800-volt charging infrastructure is not the norm, he added during his remarks at the press preview of the Type 01 at Jaguar’s headquarters in Gaydon, UK.
“We know that the 800-volt infrastructure around the world is not very widespread,” he said. “Four hundred volts is much more common. So, actually, our battery with its 200 cells is split into two. There are two individual streams of 100 cells inside the battery, which allows us to switch those from a series configuration at 800 volts down to the parallel configuration at 400 volts. So, we can natively charge the car still at 400 volts and still with 250 kilowatts of power, focusing on that fast charging, no matter where the customer is.”
Silicon (carbide) valley
There is also a junction box mounted ahead of the firewall that houses the car’s battery management system while also serving as a strut brace between the two front suspension towers that contributes to the Type 01’s remarkable torsional rigidity of 38,100 lbs.-ft./degree. That BMS employs silicon carbide switches for maximum efficiency.
“We take those switches, and we control them in the most efficient way possible with variable frequencies,” Ellis explained. “Depending on the driving style of the car and of the occupant, we change how we're switching the chips,” he said.
“At low-speed cruising, we can switch the chips really slowly,” Ellis continued. “That reduces our losses. Every time you switch them on and off, you get a small loss. We reduce that power by switching them on and off slowly. But when you need all of that power delivery, we can turn that up from two kilohertz all the way up to 20 kilohertz, so you can switch them on and off really fast and deliver all of the power the bus can deliver.”
The company credits the know-how for this to the
Jaguar TCS Racing Formula E
racing team’s experience in maximizing the use of energy in its race cars. Power from the inverter goes to a trio of permanent magnet motors: two 310-kW motors at the rear axle and one 260-kW motor at the front.
The car gains efficiency here by switching off the energy-consuming rear-axle motors when it is cruising at highway speeds, relying on just the front motor to pull the car along.
“We call it inverter deactivation, and it turns the car into a single-axle drive,” said Ellis, “seamlessly to the customer, and we're able to turn it back on unbelievably fast. Overall: able to save 18 miles of range for a customer on a typical drive cycle.”
Miraculous motors
The motors themselves contain more advanced engineering. “On our stators, on hot windings, rather than having the traditional oil spray end windings, we have oil-submerged end windings to allow us to extract heat from the stator as quickly as possible, making sure we can minimize stage temperatures and keep the system weight working as efficiently as possible,” Ellis said.
“In the rotor, the magnets have technology for magnet segmentation. What that's doing is breaking the eddy current losses, reducing them down and again keeping the efficiency in the mode. If I come around the rear, we've got two heat exchangers, one for each motor, which are intelligently controlled by active bypass valves underneath.”
The dual drive motors of the Type 01's rear drive unit are visible on the left and right sides. JAGUAR
That works with the Type 01’s ThermAssist system, which moves heat throughout the car so that areas that need warmth receive it without needing to use additional range-sapping electricity to provide it. “So on a cold day, we can actually warm up the motor before we focus on warming up the rest of the system. We can leave the battery cold, let the motor get nice and warm, and then shed excess heat around the car.”
Do. Or do not. There is no try.
Further engineering in service to the car’s styling includes the massive nine-foot stamped aluminum panel that stretches along the top of the door frames to the rear fender. Jaguar calls this the impossible panel because computer models said that it couldn’t be manufactured.
“The computer system says you can't do that,” recounted Jaguar Managing Director Rawdon Glover in an interview with
Design News
during the event. “It's too wide. You've got too many different angles on it. It's too complicated. We can't press that in aluminum.”
That’s where engineers would normally look for alternatives. “What many people would do is say, ‘Okay, all right, we'll make it simpler. We'll put a crease line in. Maybe we'll do something different,’” said Glover.
“But this team said ‘No, we're not going to do that. Jaguar is not about compromise. We're going to find a different way.’ So literally, we went way back to sort of artisanal principles of trial and error and craft, and basically, we found a way to make this impossible panel possible.”
According to conventional wisdom, no more than three planes with sweeping curves and no acute angles are possible on a single body panel. The impossible panel features five different planes with three feature lines converging on a single point. Jaguar uses a six-stage, 2,500-ton stamping process to achieve the result.
More sweat equity
Similarly, the team found ways to finesse the car’s edges to reduce aerodynamic drag. The Type 01’s 0.23 coefficient of drag was achieved thanks to a myriad of details that whittled away at the problem over the course of more than 7,000 wind tunnel tests.
One example is the compressed-radius hemming technique to hide the glass seals for the frameless windows in the Type 01’s doors. Another detail is how engineers shaved millimeters from the car’s front corners to imperceptibly adjust airflow without affecting styling. This contributes as much as 12 miles of additional driving range compared to the original design.
Active front shutters are an obvious drag-reduction tool, and for the Type 01, they add as much as 27 miles of driving range by only opening when the brakes or powertrain need cooling. The car’s rear spoiler is also active, with three positions that include its normal stowed location, a 7-degree position for speeds higher than 50 mph, and a final dramatic high-downforce 21-degree position that provides as much as 165 lbs. of downforce at speeds above 96 mph.
Inside, the car is spartan, in the manner of a contemporary Scandinavian car such as Polestar, with Woolblend Kvadrat DuoWeave textile fabrics and Ultrafabrics NeoGrain vegan leather in place of the expected leather, which remains an available option. The dashboard is bereft of ornamentation and is dominated by the car's OLED display screens.
Muted tones and uncluttered surfaces are the theme inside the Type 01. The black screen at the base of the windshield is the rear-view display. JAGUAR
As with the exterior styling, established expectations are for a Jaguar cabin to have the wood-and-leather atmosphere of a cigar lounge. But, just as smoking is going out of fashion, so are such traditional interior treatments. The question will be, what sets such cabin furnishings apart from those of less expensive mainstream brands.
Another Polestar-like detail is the absence of a rear window and the corresponding reliance on a rear-view camera and display screen. We found the
Polestar 4’s lack of a rear window and use of a video display
in place of its mirror less jarring than anticipated, so keep an open mind about the Type 01’s setup.
However, a key difference here is that the Jaguar team decided to buck tradition further and locate the rear camera display atop the dashboard, at the bottom of the windshield, rather than the mirror’s usual spot at the top of the windshield. However, sitting in a prototype revealed that with the driver’s seat adjusted to a low position, the center infotainment display obscures a good bit of the view to the rear-view screen.
The original Corvette mounted the rear-view mirror on the dashboard, as was often done at that time. SJO VIA GETTY IMAGES
Refinement is expected
While we did get to sit inside prototypes, there was no chance to drive the Type 01. For dynamic impressions, we have to rely on a decidedly biased but highly credible source, in the form of Matt Becker, director of driven attributes at Jaguar. Becker has tuned ride and handling at most of the storied British sports car marques, including Lotus, Aston Martin, and McLaren.
British engineers are renowned for their ability to optimize ride and handling, so that other companies have regularly consulted with companies like Lotus to fix issues with their cars. Becker, in particular, has an impeccable reputation for his work in the field, and it speaks well of Jaguar’s seriousness of intent that they have him on this project.
With torque vectoring, four-wheel steering, and active damping with two-stage air springs at his disposal, Becker had a lot of variables to consider in tuning the Type 01 with the goal of providing the cushy ride that is the signature of Jaguar sedans and the responsive handling of the company’s sports cars.
To achieve that, the Type 01 lets drivers choose between Jaguar mode and Dynamic mode. “Jaguar mode is very comfortable, very relaxed,” Becker reported in a video produced for the introduction. “The impact isolation, the comfort is incredible.”
“When you go to Dynamic, though, what we start to do is to make the car even more engaging,” he promised. “The car starts to rotate around my hips, and it really starts to talk to you if you want to drive the car in a more spirited way.”
This is where the active dampers and springs come into play, according to Becker. “On top of that, we've got dual-rate air springs, which allow us to vary the stiffness of the spring. Beyond that, we've got twin-valve dampers, which allow us a huge bandwidth of damping capability available to tune the different settings with the car: Jaguar mode and Dynamic mode.”
This is how drivers will be able to enjoy a car that is simultaneously soothing and responsive. “I really enjoy this primary control, where the car is kept equal, front to rear,” he said. “It ‘breathes’ upwards and downwards. It's got this really nice body control, which informs the driver of what the car is doing, and also it's got this lovely level of isolation to remove the unwanted impacts that you don't want to feel.”
These are the insights that lead companies to bring Becker in to sort their car’s dynamic behavior, and until we get a chance to drive the Type 01 in person, we’ll have to take his word for it.

title: Second-Life EV Batteries Cut Grid Storage Costs 50% | B2U CEO
content:
Stationary Batteries
Battery Recycling
Battery News
Interviews
The Battery Show North America panelist Freeman Hall explains how repurposed batteries are meeting surging power demands from AI and data centers while delivering equivalent performance at 50% lower cost.
October 8, 2026
5 Min Read
The Bexar Martinez project in Bexar County, TX is a 24 MWh /10.0 MW energy storage system that includes more than 700 repurposed EV batteries.
B2U Storage Solutions
At a Glance
Repurposed EV batteries deliver equivalent performance to new systems at 50% lower cost for grid-scale storage.
B2U has real-world operating data since 2020 proving reliability across thousands of additional battery cycles.
US-made systems qualify for domestic content tax credits and are ready now to serve surging data center power needs.
Freeman Hall is CEO of
B2U Storage Solutions
, a pioneering company that's redefining energy storage by giving EV batteries a second life on the grid. Rather than relying solely on new battery production, B2U repurposes batteries from electric vehicles to create cost-effective, sustainable grid-scale storage solutions—a circular economy approach that addresses both performance and environmental challenges in the energy transition.
The company has been making significant strides recently, including a major partnership with LG Energy Solution and the successful connection of its second commercial project to the ERCOT grid in Texas.
Hall will be joining the panel "
Energy Storage at an Inflection Point: Scaling for the Next Era of Power Demand
," where industry leaders will explore how to meet surging electricity needs driven by AI, data centers, and grid modernization. The discussion will examine the evolving role of different battery technologies, the challenges of scaling deployment in North America, and which innovations are positioned to move from promising concepts to solutions deployed at meaningful scale.
Related:
Report: Data Center Battery Storage Market to Reach $4.27 Billion by 2035
B2U Storage Solutions CEO Freeman Hall. Credit: B2U
I had a few questions for Hall prior to the panel, which he was kind enough to answer by email:
B2U has really carved out a unique space by using repurposed EV batteries for grid-scale storage. What are the biggest advantages you're seeing with this approach compared to deploying brand new batteries, and where do you think this model will be in five years?
B2U Storage Solutions CEO Freeman Hall:
First, there is an increasingly vast supply of batteries that are perfect candidates for repurposing in large-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS) where the residual value in the batteries can be realized. B2U's approach, enabled by our technology, experience, and business model, is uniquely able to realize that residual value. BESS using repurposed batteries can cost 50% less than BESS with new batteries with equivalent performance to new battery BESS.
Over the next 5 years, the repurposing industry will scale significantly to realize the embedded residual value in the batteries before the batteries are recycled.
Congrats on the LG Energy Solution partnership and getting your second project connected to the ERCOT grid. What do these milestones mean for B2U's growth, and how do they help you meet the increasing demands on the grid?
Thanks, our partnership with LG Energy Solution continues to strengthen as we move to deliver long-term economic returns by capturing more useful life from batteries, scaling our business which reduces unit costs and cost of capital, while driving down the cost of energy storage for market. Bringing our second site in Texas online is yet another proof-point of the bankability of our solutions.
Related:
Battery Technology’s Role in AI Growth and Innovation
Battery chemistry doesn't matter—residual value does
The panel will dig into lithium-ion versus emerging technologies like sodium-ion and long-duration storage. How do you see the competitive landscape shaking out? Where do second-life EV batteries fit into the mix?
B2U is agnostic to battery chemistry. Our technology captures the residual value of batteries no matter their chemistry. Repurposing is important to realize the highest and best use of the battery before that asset is essentially destroyed in the recycling process. The competitive landscape in large format batteries is extremely dynamic across automotive and stationary storage applications, both in lithium-ion chemistries and other emerging battery chemistries. B2U will be able to work with any chemistry to ensure batteries' full value is realized before recycling.
The SEPV Sierra project in Lancaster, CA is an 8MW/32MWh hybrid energy storage system that uses more than 1,300 repurposed EV batteries.  Credit: B2U Storage Systems
One question that often comes up about repurposed batteries is whether they can maintain performance and reliability over time. How does B2U tackle those concerns, and what's the real-world data telling you about how your systems are performing?
Related:
La Verne Battery Fire Evacuates 500—New Tech Could Stop the Next One
Great question, Michael, because you have hit on something that is truly unique to B2U. We have operating data since 2020, demonstrating the reliability and performance of our products over that timeframe. Our solutions leverage EV batteries from a variety of vehicles, and they all perform very well in the less demanding use case of energy storage, enabling the repurposed batteries to operate over thousands of additional cycles.
to serve data center demand
AI and data centers are driving massive new power demands. How is B2U positioned to serve that market, and what makes repurposed battery storage a good fit for these kinds of applications?
The good news is, B2U has capacity available now to serve data centers. Our systems are made in the US, qualify for domestic content bonus investment tax credits, and have no FEOC or PFE issues. Overall, our superior pricing further increases economic benefits for data centers while delivering equivalent performance to competing BESS systems. B2U's projects not only serve the grid but can be used to co-locate load, including data centers that need ready access to power.
Closing the gap between perceived and actual risk
As you think about scaling up in North America, what are the biggest challenges you're running into—whether it's supply chain issues, regulatory hurdles, or getting the market on board—and how are you working through them?
There's a significant gap between perceived risk of BESS using repurposed batteries and the mitigated risk profile of B2U's systems. We continue to demonstrate with an ever-expanding dataset that B2U's BESS systems are reliable and high performing, providing exceptional returns relative to the underlying risk profile. As for other challenges, there is ample room for improvement to reduce the regulatory and financing hurdles, interconnection delays and other impediments impacting the industry today.
When you look out to 2030 and beyond, where do you think the biggest investment opportunities are in energy storage? Which technologies or business models do you think will actually make the jump from "promising" to "deployed at scale"?
Demand for cost-effective energy storage will continue to grow, with a dynamic industry competing to meet this growing demand. Repurposing is an under-capitalized nascent industry segment, but where the opportunity for strong returns is high with firms that can mitigate and manage the sector's inherent risks well.
Hear more from Freeman Hall at The Battery Show North America.
He'll be joining industry leaders on the panel "
Energy Storage at an Inflection Point: Scaling for the Next Era of Power Demand
" to discuss the future of grid-scale storage, emerging battery technologies, and meeting the power demands of AI and data centers. To register for the Battery Show North America,

Michael C. Anderson
As editor-in-chief of
Battery Technology
, Michael C. Anderson leads the brand’s coverage of advancements in battery technology as well as associated materials and manufacturing techniques across industries such as automotive/EVs, e-mobility, maritime, aerospace, medtech, and consumer electronics.
Mike is also a member of

Mike and

This all followed more than a decade of teaching English, ESL, literature, and argumentation as a lecturer at Eastern Michigan University (Ypsilanti, MI) and, for five years, at Sakura no Seibo Junior College (Fukushima, Japan).

title: Permits, Not Power, Halt Google’s Finland Data Centers
content:
Finland told Google to halt major site work at two planned data centers after regulators found that substantial land clearing and other site preparation had occurred before the required environmental impact assessments were completed.
For data center operators, Google’s experience shows that securing power and grid capacity does not guarantee that construction can proceed. Google had access to significant
grid capacity
in northern Finland through the Finnish grid operator Fingrid, but the project encountered another constraint when site preparation crossed into permanent environmental alteration.
“Power was the part Google had already solved. Fingrid said the northern grid had room,” said Stephen Sopko, practice lead for semiconductor and deep tech at HyperFrame Research. “The failure was treating forest clearance as preparatory work when Finnish law treats permanent conversion above 200 hectares as the action regulators are there to judge.”
Related:
Google’s Grid-Interactive AI Data Centers: From Backup to Grid Partner
The Finnish Licensing and Supervisory Authority, known as LVV,
directed Google
s subsidiary Tuike Finland Oy to suspend work
that significantly alters the environment at planned sites in Muhos and Kajaani. The agency called for the work to stop immediately and no later than Oct. 23.
The request covers tree removal, topsoil removal, excavation, blasting, crushing, earthmoving, drainage work, and construction of site roads and storage areas. Planning, measurements, soil surveys and other limited or reversible activities can continue.
At Muhos, Tuike reported that about 330 hectares had been felled or prepared. At the Kajaani-Otanmäki site, the reported area was just under 200 hectares.
LVV said environmental impact assessment reports for the two projects are expected to be completed in 2026. The agency said allowing major site work to continue could undermine the assessment process by limiting the ability to identify environmental impacts, examine alternatives and prevent harmful effects.
Grid Capacity Wasn’t the Constraint
LVV’s intervention followed a Sept. 18 request for information from Tuike Finland, the Municipality of Muhos, the City of Kajaani and local building-control authorities. Based on the information it received, the agency determined that the preparatory activities warranted intervention under Finland’s EIA Act.
The issue is the sequencing of the work. An environmental impact assessment is intended to gather information about a project’s environmental effects before that information is used in decision-making, including identifying impacts, considering alternatives and determining measures to prevent or reduce environmental harm.
Related:
Google Says AI Growth Is Outrunning Grid Decarbonization
With major site alteration already underway, the assessment has less ability to serve that function, according to Tiina Paloniitty, associate professor of environmental and sustainability law at the University of Helsinki, in an email.
“You can often do surveys and reversible site work ahead of the permit. ... What you can’t do is clear 300 hectares and call it anticipation.” – Stephen Sopko, practice lead, HyperFrame Research
announced the €13 billion investment in September
, including new data centers in Muhos, Kajaani and Vaala and an expansion of its Hamina site.
Google selected the northern Finland sites in part because of the available grid capacity near carbon-free electricity sources. Fingrid has said Muhos, Kajaani and Vaala have significant grid capacity in an area where electricity production exceeds consumption.
For operators planning large data centers, the Finnish case shows that environmental approvals can impose separate sequencing requirements even when a site has the electricity and transmission capacity needed for a large facility.
“This is not just a data center rule. It is the rule for any major project,” Sopko said. “You can often do surveys and reversible site work ahead of the permit. You certainly can in Finland. What you can’t do is clear 300 hectares and call it anticipation.”
Related:
The Ripple Effect of Data Center Project Cancellations and Delays
Google Says It Followed Forestry Rules
Google said it acted in good faith under Finland’s Forest Act, conducted nature surveys and took measures to protect environmentally valuable areas.
“We understand the concern caused by the situation. In this case, we did not meet the high standards we set ourselves,” said Sondre Ronander, communications manager for Finland and Norway at Google, in a public statement.
Google said it is advancing landscaping and biodiversity plans, including tree planting across 130 hectares at Muhos.
Paloniitty said compliance with forestry rules does not necessarily satisfy separate environmental impact assessment requirements. The two laws serve different purposes, and complying with one does not remove obligations under the other.
“Compliance with one applicable law does not equal … compliance with other applicable laws,” Paloniitty said.
Based on publicly available information from LVV and Finnish media, Paloniitty said it appears that Google failed to comply with the Finnish EIA Act, even after the authority indicated that the projects required an environmental impact assessment.
“Good faith is not a legally relevant argument here,” she said.
Paloniitty said the environmental review cannot fully serve its intended purpose once substantial site work has already altered the area being assessed. That also limits the ability to evaluate alternatives and environmental impacts before decisions are made, she said.
Google’s plans to plant new trees do not resolve that issue, she said.
“New trees do not replace a full-grown forest,” Paloniitty said.
Intervention Is ‘Highly Unusual’
Paloniitty described LVV’s intervention as “highly unusual.” She said she could not recall a comparable intervention at this scale, although such action is not entirely without precedent.
The intervention does not cancel either data center project. It seeks to stop major site work while the environmental assessment procedures are completed.
The projects can continue through limited activities such as planning, measurements and soil surveys.
Tuike Finland has until Oct. 14 to provide LVV with a written explanation and state whether it will comply. Separately, the agency set Oct. 23 as the latest date by which the suspension of major site work must be in effect.
LVV is initially seeking voluntary compliance. If Tuike does not comply, the agency said it will consider initiating a formal enforcement procedure that could be backed by a conditional fine.

title: ThisWay Global to Convert Bankrupt RELLIS Site into 73 MW AI Hub
content:
The Texas A&M University System (TAMUS) has
explored building a data center
at its RELLIS Campus in Bryan, Texas, since 2013. A private developer began building one in 2024 but
filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection
in November 2025, leaving the project unfinished.
ThisWay Global (TWG), an Austin-based AI software company, says it acquired the project out of bankruptcy and completed the transaction on September 30, 2026. TWG plans a phased Research and AI Compute Center (RACC) totaling 73 MW on about 25 acres of TAMUS land.
TWG plans to use the location to demonstrate its Sovereign AI Blueprint, which it developed and introduced in September 2026, as a framework for documenting who controls the data, AI models, and computing resources in an environment and who can access them. The goal is to make claims of digital sovereignty verifiable.
“ThisWay saw great value in the bankrupt, languishing project, as the ideal place to demonstrate our Sovereign AI Blueprint and the meaningful outcomes that result from a mission-focused center for innovation,” TWG CEO Stephan Fabel told
Data Center Knowledge
. “The project’s location, on public land administered by TAMUS and RELLIS Campus leadership, presents the opportunity for ThisWay to not only support TAMU research but also its industry, defense, and governmental partners.”
Related:
Five Ways to Assess Your AI Infrastructure Readiness
Why the RELLIS Campus for AI/HPC?
RELLIS provides TWG with an existing building on public land inside a university research campus. “The first building will encompass about 25% of the total compute power of the innovation-focused campus,” Fabel said. “ThisWay Global, in partnership with Texas-based Centaurus Capital, Skylar Capital Management, and other investors, provided the capital to purchase the project and make creditors whole.”
TWG describes RACC as a sovereign training and innovation center for research, workforce development, and regulated industries, including defense, healthcare, and energy.
“We are also looking forward to working with the larger R1 university ecosystem to provide short-term, large-scale access to HPC-grade infrastructure,” Fabel noted.
Facility Redesign: HPC Density and Liquid Cooling
TWG plans to adjust the existing design and expand capacity. “The building was designed to have a small amount of computational power, with over half the facility planned to have typical office and classroom space,” Fabel said. “Our team spent several weeks conducting structural analysis and computational planning so that the existing design could be converted into a state-of-the-art innovation and training center.”
Related:
CoreWeave Targets Enterprises with Forge Platform
The original plan contemplated conventional colocation and air cooling. TWG says it will add a closed-loop
liquid cooling system
using a propylene glycol-water mix, enabling high-density racks and HPC workloads.
On power, TWG has not disclosed its requested capacity from Bryan Texas Utilities (BTU). “RACC is planned as a phased development, with deployment tied to confirmed power availability and the applicable utility approvals,” Fabel said.
Planned AI/HPC Workloads and Compliance Stack
TWG plans to run its Amalgamy.AI software stack on each node to enforce sovereign controls and compliance. “RACC is meant to provide desperately needed GPU access to some of the world’s most important missions: security, healthcare, energy, and research,” Fabel said. “Our mission is to bring large-scale compute to underserved industries and create an opportunity for us to leapfrog in innovation and scientific progress.”

title: Bangladesh approves eight-hour battery storage for 442 MW solar project - Energy Storage
content: Bangladesh has approved a 442 MW grid-connected solar power plant with battery storage as the country seeks to address persistent electricity shortages and increase renewable energy generation. The Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC), chaired by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, approved the project on Wednesday. The BPDB will develop the project at a total cost of BDT 25 billion, making it the country’s largest solar power plant. The facility will be built next to the 1.32 GW coal-fired Rampal Power Station in Bagerhat district, southwestern Bangladesh. Around 371.7 hectares of land previously earmarked for a second unit of the coal-fired facility will instead be used for the solar project. pv magazine reported in April that BPDB was planning the 442 MW solar facility at Rampal, with the project expected to become Bangladesh’s largest PV installation. The project is scheduled for implementation between September 2026 and March 2029. Junior Planning Minister Zonayed Abdur Rahim Saki said the facility will include eight hours of battery storage, twice the duration envisaged under the initial plan, allowing a larger volume of solar electricity to be stored for use outside daylight hours. “We want to set up the solar power plant as soon as possible to help meet the power demand,” Saki said. Planning Commission officials said the project is intended to increase the share of renewables in Bangladesh’s electricity mix while reducing dependence on fossil fuel-based generation and cutting greenhouse gas emissions. Bangladesh has stepped up its support for solar deployment in recent months as power shortages have intensified. The government’s Renewable Energy Development Policy 2026–2030 targets renewables accounting for 20% of the country’s electricity generation mix by 2030, with rooftop solar expected to play a significant role in the expansion. The government recently established a $123 million fund for rooftop solar and other renewable energy projects . It has also introduced a series of fiscal and regulatory measures to accelerate solar deployment. In September, Bangladesh cut the tax burden on solar equipment imports from 17% to 1% for 180 days . Earlier that month, the government introduced a BDT 10.50 ($0.086)/kWh tariff for surplus electricity supplied by eligible rooftop solar systems under the country’s net-metering regime. The measures follow other changes aimed at expanding the market. Bangladesh revised its net-metering rules in 2025 to broaden access to rooftop solar, while the government has also reinstated payment guarantees for renewable energy projects in an effort to improve project bankability and attract investment. Bangladesh currently has 1,871 MW of installed renewable energy capacity, including 1,492 MW of solar. title: C&I storage the 'sleeping giant waking up', says WoodMac - Energy Storage
content: The global energy storage market is entering a new phase of scale and complexity, according to Wood Mackenzie’s latest outlook. Cumulative capacity is forecast to grow to over 7 TWh by 2035. Demand growth in 2026 alone is close to 30%. But growth at that rate and capacity is no longer the most interesting part of the story. The composition is. Global energy storage outlook by segment (% of total MWh installed in 2026) Regional competition: the running order is changing faster than the totals suggest While China and the US are still the two biggest global energy storage markets, in 2026, for the first time, Europe’s annual installation overtook annual US energy storage capacity and took second place after China. In the utility segment, government-led tenders remain the main market drivers, having globally cleared over 80 GW (de-rated) capacity, with India the single largest contributor. Poland has become the global number-one emerging market, on the back of capacity-market auctions and a grid short of flexibility. In mature utility markets, the demand signals behind the forecast are also firm. Contracted offtake for storage has passed 130 GW, with utility power purchase agreements and tolling deals together accounting for more than three-quarters of all contracts signed, according to our global offtake tracker. In the residential landscape, the centre of gravity has shifted south: Australia has overtaken Germany as the world’s leading residential energy storage market , with more than half a million installations under its Cheaper Home Batteries subsidy, while the US market contracts this year as tax credits become less available. Commercial and industrial storage is the sleeping giant now waking Wood Mackenzie forecasts commercial and industrial storage capacity separately. The split shows industrial demand is materially larger in some regions. A single “utility” line no longer tells the story: standalone still leads, but some regions need pairing far more than others In the latest market outlook update, Wood Mackenzie changes how the utility energy storage market is measured. The utility segment is now reported in three parts: standalone, solar-paired and wind-paired, instead of one, because the three are growing for different reasons, at different speeds and in different places. Standalone projects still dominate and will keep doing so through 2035. But paired capacity is no longer a rounding error: close to a third of the storage expected online by 2035 will sit alongside a wind or solar plant. The new breakdown exposes how little the regions resemble one another, given their different policy and economic parameters. Europe is the most standalone-heavy market in the world, with the overwhelming majority of its utility pipeline unpaired. Yet it is also poised for the fastest growth in paired capacity, as worsening economics for standalone solar push developers towards co-location. That makes Europe the market most likely to shift quickly towards co-location as an economic solution for stranded solar projects in markets such as Spain or Germany. The Americas sit at the opposite end, where, for example, in the US, close to half of utility storage additions are solar-paired — a legacy of the ITC pairing requirement in the early days and now poor solar capture rates in key markets like CAISO. That share is expected to fall as storage spreads into lower solar-penetration states, where standalone economics work better. Data center-linked battery projects are also taking shape in the US, though not all of them are paired with wind or solar: gas-plus-storage pairings are the new co-location favorites for emerging data center projects. Asia Pacific sits in between, with solar pairing the fastest-growing utility category, driven largely by India, which has overtaken Australia as the region’s largest utility-scale market. Regulatory changes are central to this: India’s new rules will require solar and wind projects commissioned after July 2027 to include co-located storage equal to at least 10% of capacity, rising to a four-hour minimum duration from 2029. The replacement cycle and repowering appear in the energy storage market at last Aging storage assets will only start to come offline and be replaced at scale after 2030, adding 40 GWh of repowered capacity by 2035, led by the US, Japan and Germany. This is the first sign of a market old enough to need replacing, which has earned a reporting line in our latest energy storage outlook. Wood Mackenzie is hosting a global energy storage outlook webinar on 3 November to discuss which markets and segments are shaping the future of global energy storage. Anna Darmani is a research director on the Wood Mackenzie Power & Renewables team, heading the EMEA energy storage team. She previously worked at EIT InnoEnergy, developing innovation and technology roadmaps and contributing to EU research and advisory projects. title: Italy authorizes five BESS projects totaling 468 MW - Energy Storage
content: Italy’s Ministry of Environment and Energy Security (MASE) has authorized five battery energy storage system (BESS) projects totaling 468.2 MW across Piedmont, Friuli-Venezia Giulia, Puglia and Emilia-Romagna. The approvals follow a record September, when the ministry issued single authorization (AU) decrees for more than 3 GW of battery storage projects. The largest of the five projects is Engie Produzione’s 140 MW Leini BESS in Leinì, near Turin, in Piedmont. Under decree 281/2026, the project received authorization to build a system comprising modules rated at approximately 7 MW each. Construction is expected to take 24 months. Two other projects originated from applications filed by GRA BESS in 2024. Following a corporate split initiated in late 2024, the applications were transferred to separate subsidiaries. Santa Maria Srl received authorization under decree 279/2026 for a 104.4 MW BESS spanning Santa Maria La Longa and Pavia di Udine, in the province of Udine, Friuli-Venezia Giulia. Construction is scheduled to take approximately 10 months. Casei Srl received authorization under decree 280/2026 for a 100.8 MW BESS in Casei Gerola, in the province of Pavia, Lombardy. Associated grid connection works will also take place in Castelnuovo Scrivia, in the province of Alessandria. Construction is expected to take around 10 months. In Puglia, Galatina BESS 2 Srl secured authorization under decree 282/2026 for a 73 MW storage system in Galatina, in the province of Lecce. Its planned construction period of approximately nine months is the shortest among the five projects. Casetta Storage Srl received authorization under decree 283/2026 for the 50 MW Finale Emilia storage project in the province of Modena, Emilia-Romagna. Construction is expected to take 18 months. title: BYD launches pre-orders for the new Seagull, a larger version of its popular $10K EV
content:
Peter Johnson
| Oct 9 2026 - 8:58 am PT
The Seagull is
most affordable electric vehicle, starting at about $10,000 in China and sold overseas as the Dolphin Surf. BYD is preparing to introduce a new version that will likely be an even “bigger” hit.
BYD opens pre-orders for the new Seagull EV
BYD is best-known for its ultra-low-cost vehicles, but the Seagull is much cheaper than anything sold in the US.
In China, BYD’s electric hatch starts at 69,900 yuan, or around $10,000. Meanwhile, the lowest-priced vehicle in the US is the 2026 Hyundai Venue, which costs just over $20,000.
Even in markets outside China, like Europe, the Dolphin Surf, as sold, starts at just €22,900 ($25,000). In places like Brazil and Mexico, the electric hatch is rebadged and sold as the Dolphin Mini.
As one of the most affordable electric cars in many markets, the Seagull (Dolphin Surf/ Mini) has been among the world’s best-selling EVs.
According to the most recent data from
CleanTechnica
, BYD’s entry-level EV was the world’s sixth-best-selling EV through August, with over 212,000 units sold. It ranks behind only BYD’s own Yuan Up (Atto2), the Tesla Model 3, Geely Xingyuan (EX2), BYD Song (Seal U), and the Tesla Model Y.
For its second generation, BYD is upgrading the Seagull to compete with the incoming wave of entry-level electric cars hitting the market.
The new Seagull is bigger, smarter, and adds a bit more luxury over its predecessor. We caught a glimpse of the second-gen Seagull last month when Zhang Zhuo, general manager of BYD’s Ocean series,
revealed the first official images
BYD said shortly after that part of “Growing Up” means living up to expectations. As such, the new Seagull adds premium features, such as ambient lighting and massaging front seats.
It will also offer more legroom for rear passengers and a refined, immersive cockpit design. The setup includes a larger infotainment display, a new two-spoke steering wheel, and a redesigned center console for extra storage.
Instead, it will display the information on the center infotainment screen. It also gains physical buttons below the infotainment and on the steering wheel.
BYD opens blind pre-orders for the second-generation Seagull (Source: Zhang Zhou/ BYD)
Zhang announced on Weibo that blind pre-orders for the second-generation Seagull officially opened on Friday with six exterior color options.
However, he didn’t reveal prices, which is common in China when opening blind pre-orders for a new vehicle.
BYD hasn’t confirmed battery specs or any other details. Zhang said during the Chengdu Auto Show in August that the second-generation Seagull will launch as the “Great Seagull,” confirming it will go on sale by the end of 2026.
After the new model appeared in China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) regulatory filing in August, we learned a few key details.
For one, the new Seagull is 4,205 mm long, 1,810 mm wide, and 1,570 mm high, with a 2,650 mm wheelbase. That’s 425 mm longer and 150 mm longer in wheelbase than the current Seagull, which measures 3,780 mm in length.
The filing also revealed it will gain a more powerful 95 kW (127 hp) electric motor, up from the 55 kW (75 hp) the current Seagull offers.
Instead of a front-mounted motor like the current Seagull, the new model will switch to a rear-mounted electric motor.
Like many of its new vehicles, the second-generation Seagull now has a roof-mounted LiDAR. As such, it’s expected to offer an upgraded ADAS system with BYD’s God’s Eye B intelligent driving system.
We will learn more details soon, with an official launch expected by the end of 2026. While not yet confirmed, the new Seagull is expected to offer BYD’s latest Blade Batteries 2.0 and Flash Charging tech on more premium trims.
After its launch in China, BYD is expected to introduce a larger version overseas, likely as a variant of the Dolphin Surf and Dolphin Mini.

title: Geely confirms Canada entry with first cars in 2027 — but no models yet
content:
Fred Lambert
| Oct 9 2026 - 6:08 am PT
Geely is coming to Canada. The Chinese automaker’s mainstream brand announced today that it has started setting up Canadian operations and recruiting a dealer network, with its first vehicles going on sale in 2027.
What Geely isn’t saying is which vehicles. There are no models, no prices and no dealer locations, just a new website at geely.ca and a promise of more details closer to launch.
A 3-million-car automaker most Canadians have never driven
Geely Auto Group sold more than 3.02 million vehicles in 2025, including nearly 1.69 million electrified vehicles (BEVs and plug-in hybrids), according to the company. It has sold over 2.23 million so far in 2026, through September.
The group sells cars under three brands: Geely, Zeekr and Lynk & Co. Its parent, Zhejiang Geely Holding, also owns Volvo Cars, Polestar and Lotus, so Geely cars have been on Canadian roads for years. Just under Swedish and British badges.
This time it’s the Geely name itself.
Bryan Wu, managing director of Geely Auto Canada, said the brand is entering with “a long-term commitment” and added that “trust is earned over time, and we are committed to earning it here.”
The company says it’s building its retail and service network with “highly trusted and experienced partners who understand their local communities.” That reads like a traditional franchised dealer model, not Tesla-style direct sales.
As for product, Geely leads with the EX5 electric SUV (the Galaxy E5 in China) and the Starray EM-i plug-in hybrid in export markets like Australia and the UK. Those are the obvious candidates, but Geely Auto Canada won’t confirm anything yet.
Ottawa’s 6.1% quota opened the door
The timing is no coincidence. In January,
Canada broke with the US and slashed its 100% tariff on Chinese EVs
as part of a deal with Beijing that also lowered Chinese tariffs on Canadian canola.
The arrangement created a quota of 49,000 Chinese-made EVs per year at the 6.1% most-favoured-nation rate, effective March 1. Anything beyond that still gets hit with the 100% surtax.
And the quota isn’t even full. Global Affairs Canada hands out permits in two six-month periods, first-come, first-served, and only to EV makers or their Canadian agents. Demand fell short in the first period, so 8,897 unused vehicles rolled over, bringing the current period, which runs to February 28, 2027, to 33,397 vehicles.
Geely’s 2027 timeline means its first cars will most likely come in under the second quota year.
It won’t be alone.
BYD is planning 20 Canadian dealerships
, starting in Toronto. And in June, China’s ambassador to Canada said the first Lotus EVs built in China by Geely Holding would arrive under the deal in July.
Canada is Geely’s only door into North America
For US readers, this is as close as Geely’s own brand is going to get. Washington’s rule on Chinese connected-vehicle technology has already
shut Geely-owned Polestar out of the US market
, and a Chinese brand selling Chinese-built cars has no path there.
So Canada becomes the test case for how Chinese automakers do in a North American market with real dealers, real winters and real competition from GM, Ford, Toyota and Tesla.
Electrek’s Take
Announcing a market entry a year or more out with no product attached is a bit odd. But I get it. Geely needs dealers before it needs cars, and the best dealer groups in Canada are being courted by Chinese automakers right now. Getting the flag planted early matters.
I’m really curious to know which vehicles the brand will bring to Canada.
I’m heading to the Paris Motor Show with Geely next week, and you can be sure I’ll be asking everyone I meet which models are coming to Canada. I’ll report back with whatever I can get.

title: Max stupid: EU may loosen EV rules for third time in two years, aiding China
content:
During multiple historic fuel crises and a climate crisis that left tens of thousands dead across Europe this summer, the bloc is reportedly close to striking a deal to allow its automakers to produce more of the vehicles that directly caused each of those problems.
In doing so, it would only ensure that its automakers are unprepared to compete against the country that actually is providing solutions to those problems: China.
Back in 2021, Europe announced a target to phase out new gas car sales by 2035, in order to meet an overall goal of 55% emissions reductions by 2030 and full climate neutrality by 2050.
These goals are important given the climate crisis the world is currently in the throes of, and how negatively it will continue to affect all living things on Earth until humans act to solve the problem we are causing. Those effects cannot be negotiated away by governments – they are a matter of physics.
Notably, that climate crisis led to record heat waves which killed 35,000 people this summer alone in what used to be a traditionally mild continent.
This crisis has been driven largely by overuse of resources by the Western world, though Europe has made some progress at reducing the rate at which it pumps deadly emissions into the atmosphere. And the faster we solve it, the easier it will be to solve.
Cars are a major contributor to this crisis – in rich countries, transportation is the largest-emitting sector, and the majority of transportation emissions come from personal gas-powered vehicles. So this means they are also among the most important things to regulate, given their outsized effect.
But in the last two years, Europe has made several foolish moves to loosen those EV targets. And it’s looking to make another.
Europe’s targets aren’t serious if they keep changing
The first was in March 2025, where EU gave automakers “breathing room” (ironically polluting the air more, and thus giving those of us who actually breathe, humans and all other animals, less breathing room) by reducing the amount of emissions reductions they would have to do in the short term.
Europe said at the time that “the [long term] targets stay the same,” but that didn’t last long.
Just nine months later, the EU rolled back those targets, allowing automakers to continue to make polluting vehicles after 2035, and only requiring a 90% emissions reduction rather than 100%. This 90% target was further watered down by an excess of optional credits, including allowing so-called “e-fuels,” which are not a green solution.
At the time, I took a dig that Europe’s regulations mean nothing if they shift whenever automakers so much as clear their throat, suggesting:
Given Europe has shown that it can change its mind every 9 months on regulations that were supposed to last for 14 years, maybe 9 months from now it can go back to the initial regulations that should have stuck around anyway.
And here we are, ten months later, almost as if on cue, and… the automakers have reportedly whined themselves into another loosening of regulations. Just the sort of regulatory whiplash that makes every target meaningless, because companies know they can just cry a little and get it changed as always.
France and Germany want another 10% of pollution
Clean Energy Wire reported this week that France and Germany have struck a deal that would bring emissions reductions down to 80%, from the current 90%, and would weaken interim targets once again as in the “breathing room” announcement.
Previously, France had opposed Germany’s proposal to loosen car rules (at the behest of its large auto industry) and Germany had opposed France’s “Buy European” demands, but the countries have now agreed to back each other’s proposals, and will present them to the EU on October 15. Six other countries opposed watering down car rules, but with France flipping sides, the votes are likely there to pollute European air more.
The move could have repercussions outside of Europe’s borders, too. Currently, Europe is trying to strong-arm the UK into putting a tariff on Chinese EVs, as a requirement for UK to join the “Buy European” agreement and allow its products the same preferred treatment in the EU market.
Heretofore the UK has not had tariffs on Chinese EVs, which has led to EVs being cheaper than gas cars in the country and BEVs being the most popular powertrain there. If UK is brought into the fold, EU could encourage it to slow down its own EV targets, something the UK government is already considering.
“Market conditions” suggest targets should be strengthened, not rolled back
Previous iterations of these rollbacks have used the excuse that they’re simply trying to match “market conditions,” suggesting that EV sales were not rising as quickly as expected.
But not only were EV sales on target then, Europe is leading the world in EV sales growth now.
So what’s the excuse now? If you change your mind every 9 months, and market conditions have proven your last rollback to be the wrong move, how is the current answer another rollback, rather than a more reasonable answer of returning to the original rules in the first place?
Besides, “market conditions” are not the reason for these targets. They were set 14 years in advance not because anyone knew what market conditions would look like in 2035, but because it’s government’s job to get everyone on the same page about the big, long-term questions society faces.
Cutting oil use, solving climate change, and maintaining high-tech domestic manufacturing are the priorities for government, not reacting to your quarterly reports.
It’s absurd that we’re talking about this during multiple oil wars
And if we do consider current “market conditions,” EVs are a perfect match for the market conditions of multiple (self-inflicted) crises facing global oil markets.
One of those crises is a continued war of aggression in Europe, perpetrated by Russia, and financed by oil, the country’s major export (well, until Ukraine started blowing up oil refineries). Given oil is a global market, every oil-burning vehicle sold in Europe buoys the price of oil and funds the war within its borders.
Due to all those oil crises, the price of oil is quite high right now. Seems like a good time to learn the lesson that it’s a bad idea to rely on this resource that everyone has known for decades that we need to stop relying on.
Which, incidentally, is both a short-term and a long-term consideration at the moment, so it’s ripe for everyone to coalesce around a solution that involves less oil, not more, as Germany and France are planning to propose.
China is taking advantage of all of this
And what actually is rising in popularity in European markets right now? It’s not European EVs, as automakers bungle their way into canceling models and cutting EV investments. It’s Chinese EVs, which are gaining share rapidly.
(Okay, that’s not entirely true, European EVs are also popular. So why are companies cutting models and asking for lower targets?)
Top comment by Axel Foerderreuther
Chinese electric vehicles aren't just cheaper because of the strategic long term regulation in place in China. That argument is too short and simplistic. What should be mentioned as well: Lower prices of raw materials, lower interest rates for investments, electricity costs that are a fraction of western Europe, much less regulation, no legacy manufacturing infrastructure, lower wages and cost of personnel (Unions? what unions?), longer working hours per person, much faster development cycles etc. All those together lead to cost advantages that are impossible to compensate on the product side. Without import tariffs Chinese OEMs could sell for 50-60% of equivalent European-made models and still earn money. So we will need import tariffs otherwise we can kiss our industry goodbye. But giving our OEMs slack in electrification isn't going to help anybody - not the consumers and not the industry in the long run. If we wanted to help our industry to compete we have to eliminate the disadvantages.
Chinese EVs are gaining share because the Chinese auto industry isn’t going though all this nonsense of whining about having to make electric cars, it’s just making them. As a result, it’s making them cheaper and better than Europeans.
This has led sales of Chinese EVs to continue to skyrocket in Europe and around the globe – China is bringing in tons of money on these exports, and the rest of the world’s auto industries seem content to let them have it.
And if Europe shows that it will once again loosen targets at the tiniest hint of whining from its automakers, its automakers will continue down the same path they’re lumbering down, refusing to recognize the reality of the world around them, refusing to offer the products needed to reduce today’s problems, and will end up falling even further behind the ascendant Chinese rivals that are currently eating their lunch. Tariffs won’t help, only waking up will. So knock it off with these stupid rollbacks.
