title: People Moves: Anders Bønaes Is Hapag-Lloyd’s New COO
content:
People Moves: Anders Bønaes Is Hapag-Lloyd’s New COO
Prioritise Us
on Google
Anders Bønaes, incoming Chief Operating Officer at Hapag-Lloyd. Credit: LinkedIn
Hapag-Lloyd promotes Anders Bønaes to COO as the carrier expands its network and terminal operations
Hapag-Lloyd
has named Anders Bønaes as its new Chief Operating Officer (COO), effective 1 October 2026.
Prior to COO appointment, Anders served as Hapag-Lloyd’s Senior Managing Director Network, managing fleet deployment and operational strategy.
As COO, Anders will take those responsibilities into a broader executive remit as the German shipping leader moves deeper into the delivery of its Strategy 2030 ambitions.
“I look forward to working with colleagues across Hapag-Lloyd, both ashore and at sea, to deliver strong results and move our strategic priorities forward as we shape the next chapter of our company together,” Anders writes, addressing his appointment on LinkedIn.
He continues to name decarbonisation, portfolio expansion and strategic AI-usage as priorities within the company’s growth trajectory.
Hapag-Lloyd: Key facts and stats
Operates a fleet of 300 modern container ships, representing a total transport capacity of 2.5m twenty-foot-equivalent units (TEU).
Transports 13.5m TEU annually, connecting to more than 600 ports.
Maintains a workforce of 15,200 employees in its Liner Shipping segment and 4,400 employees in Terminal & Infrastructure.
Reaches globally, with 400 offices located across 140 countries worldwide.
Possesses equity stakes in 24 marine terminals across Europe, Latin America, the US, India and North Africa.
Who is Anders Bønaes?
“Anders Boenaes is the ideal candidate for the role of COO,” reflects Karl Gernandt, Chairman of the Supervisory Board of Hapag-Lloyd.
Karl Gernandt, Chairman of the Supervisory Board of Hapag-Lloyd. Credit: LinkedIn
Anders’ expertise lies in network planning, international trade expertise and operational management: capabilities that sit at the centre of Hapag-Lloyd’s 2030 strategy.
“We are very pleased to have found an internal candidate with profound knowledge of the business and the company.”
Across his 33 years in the maritime industry, Anders has built an extensive career across global liner operations and network management.
He began his maritime career in 1993 at
, a major Danish transportation company. Anders saw promotion to Vice President and Head of Africa Trades at Maersk in 2009, building experience in
global shipping networks
and regional trade.
He was appointed Senior Vice President Network for Maersk Liner Business in 2014, taking direct responsibility of the company’s global network strategy.
In 2020, Anders transitioned to Hapag-Lloyd as Senior Managing Director Network, becoming a member of the company’s Executive Board.
Within the role, he notably advanced the design and implementation of the Gemini Cooperation network, Hapag-Lloyd’s operational alliance with Maersk. The long-term partnership was officially established in February 2025 and was designed to enhance reliability on principal East-West
shipping lanes
Hapag-Lloyd: five key pillars for growth
As geopolitical tensions and dynamic scaling from competitors place considerable pressure on Hapag-Lloyd, the transportation giant has nonetheless set enterprising targets for future growth.
“There is a lot on our agenda,” says Anders. “In this challenging environment, clear priorities, close collaboration with internal and external stakeholders, and timely decision-making will be essential.”
Anders will play a key role in realising Hapag-Lloyd vision for growth.
Hapag-Lloyd’s strategic agenda focuses on five key pillars of operational quality:
Pureplay PLUS – honing in on Hapag-Lloyd’s liner-shipping business, the heart of its operations, while supplementing it by expanding its terminal and inland footprint.
Service reliability – working for 80% on-time delivery and scale its digital services to enhance customer satisfaction.
Carbon neutrality by 2045 – driving
supply chain decarbonisation
Driving profits through performance – digitising and optimising its operations to improve productivity, in order to differentiate.
A top-five container line – setting its sights on specific growth markets in order to procure world-leading status.
The Gemini Cooperation, engineered by Anders during his time as Senior Managing Director Network, plays a key role in the company’s mission. Built around a hub-and-spoke model designed to improve schedule reliability, the partnership combines the tonnage and networks of two major carriers to offer competitive quality and efficiency.
Danish container shipping giant Hapag-Lloyd is pursuing top-five global carrier status. Credit: Hapag-Lloyd
As Anders moves into the COO role, his first-hand experience with Gemini combined with greater operational authority will allow him to further optimise the partnership, as the company accelerates towards its quality objectives.
Anders’ experience overseeing African trade at Maersk brings further promise to his leadership, which coincides with Hapag-Lloyd’s expansions in Namibia, Rwanda and Burundi.
“We must continue to perform strongly in a volatile geopolitical and operational environment while preparing Hapag-Lloyd for the future,” Anders affirms.
Hapag-Lloyd’s key partners
Vincent Clerc
Copenhagen, Denmark
Maersk is a global shipping carrier and transport logistics provider. As Hapag-Lloyd’s primary operational partner in the Gemini Cooperation, Maersk works closely with the carrier to deliver operational efficiency and schedule reliability across shared ocean networks.

Yuvraj Narayan
Dubai, UAE
DP World is a global supply chain logistics supplier headquartered in Dubai, UAE. The terminal operator works alongside Hapag-Lloyd to expand port infrastructure and supply chain capabilities across key growth markets in Africa and the Middle East.
APM Terminals
Keith Svendsen
The Hague, Netherlands
APM Terminals operates a global port network headquartered in The Hague, Netherlands. The company collaborates with Hapag-Lloyd on major port infrastructure projects, including joint terminal investments designed to boost throughput capacity at hub ports like Maasvlakte II.

title: TRIGO Accelerates AI-Powered Supplier Quality Management
content:
TRIGO Accelerates AI-Powered Supplier Quality Management
Prioritise Us
on Google
Benoit Leblanc Headshot
TRIGO embeds predictive AI across supplier quality management to help manufacturers identify risks earlier and strengthen supply chain resilience
Global supply chains face mounting pressure as manufacturers struggle to predict
supplier
failures before they cascade into production delays, quality issues and loss of revenue. Industrial organisations need tools that can identify high-risk suppliers earlier, prioritise interventions and prevent disruptions before they impact operations.
TRIGO is embedding AI across the supplier quality lifecycle, combining predictive analytics, digital technologies and operational expertise to help manufacturers and transportation original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) build more resilient supply chains and anticipate supply risks before they materialise.
Predictive analytics for supply chain resilience
The company has expanded its portfolio of
-powered quality solutions, including its OTD Predictor, which analyses supplier performance indicators to identify patterns that could signal delivery risks or future disruptions.
This makes the work of quality teams more visible, highlighting suppliers that require additional attention and allowing interventions to be ordered by priority.
According to TRIGO, this approach helps organisations move from reactive problem-solving to prevention, enabling teams to focus resources on areas requiring urgent intervention rather than firefighting issues after they occur.
Once a risk has been identified, TRIGO evaluates supplier performance by combining its expertise with AI-enabled assessment technologies. This analysis evaluates supplier maturity, operational robustness and quality management practices across the supply base.
Credit: TRIGO
Reducing assessment time by half
Automating part of the
analysis
has reduced assessment time by in excess of 50%, with accuracy levels of up to 95% for AI-generated outputs.
Human experts then validate the findings and define the appropriate course of action, providing manufacturers with actionable insights that strengthen supplier relationships and reduce supply chain vulnerability.
Under continuous expert supervision, TRIGO uses AI as a decision-support tool for supplier screening, risk anticipation, assessments, improvement and operational support throughout the supplier quality lifecycle.
"AI helps organisations identify risks sooner, prioritise actions more effectively and deploy resources where they can have the greatest impact. Combined with human expertise, it enables manufacturers to strengthen supply chain resilience, improve supplier performance and optimise quality costs," said Benoit Leblanc, Co-CEO of TRIGO, in a company statement.
Present in 28 countries, TRIGO harnesses its global footprint and industry expertise to deploy solutions across demanding industries. Throughout 2025, the company has had particularly strong momentum in aerospace and defence, where growth has exceeded 20%, reflecting increasing demand for advanced quality, supplier performance and industrial risk management solutions.

Carmel Giblin, President & CEO of ESCP explores the role of worker retention in driving supply chain resilience and return on investment
Around the world, supply chains are prioritising operational resilience, particularly as the market remains volatile.
Much of this focuses on supplier diversification, technology adoption and sustainability initiatives, however the Ethical Supply Chain Program, founded by ICTI, suggests that another place to focus on is worker retention.
In supply chains, there is a growing skills gap and an ageing workforce. Companies are struggling to hire and retain their workers, meaning there is a growing shortage.
ESCP’s State of Worker Well-Being 2026 report explores how a family-friendly workplace can have a
significant impact on factory stability
Supply chain challenges
Supply chains today are facing a number of challenges, both external and internal. Global pressures such as climate change, tariffs and inflation have made supply chains unstable, but internal issues such as poor worker retention, an ageing workforce and skills gaps are making it even more difficult to develop resilience.
According to the report, 53% of Eastern Asian employers state that talent shortages are a major barrier to business transformation. In China, 82% of employers are actively investing in recruitment and retention strategies.
When managers are exploring ways to improve their internal issues, they often turn towards AI or technological training, but they also need to explore their policies. According to ESCP, a major issue with worker retention and absenteeism relates to access to childcare.
Its annual State of Worker Well-Being report suggests that family-friendly workplace support can make a significant difference in the supply chain. This is particularly crucial for brands sourcing from markets such as Vietnam and China. As a result, ESCP suggests there is a link between accessible childcare and supplier resilience.
“When it comes to the factors affecting operational performance, most leaders would point to geopolitical instability,
regulatory pressures or labour shortages
,” Carmel Giblin, CEO & President at Ethical Supply Chain Program explains to Supply Chain Digital.
Carmel Giblin, CEO & President at Ethical Supply Chain Program. Credit: ESCP
“Yet there is also a growing recognition that worker well-being is equally integral to supply chain resilience.”
The report combines independent research, frontline workforce feedback and on-the-ground insights into market trends shaping wellbeing across supply chains. It focuses on China, Vietnam and Indonesia, exploring how practical support leads to better engagement.
Worker well-being should be viewed as a core part of supply chain resilience.
Carmel Giblin, CEO & President at Ethical Supply Chain Program
A community investment
As supply chains face greater pressure than before, the workers are balancing home lives with increased workloads. Due to this, manufacturers are facing an issue of attracting and retaining workers.
Across Asian markets, ESCP identified various interconnected workforce priorities. Businesses are facing rising turnover and recruitment costs, with growing challenges responding to market expectations. Alongside this, as the market gets increasingly complex, the businesses that are already struggling are finding it difficult to meet evolving compliance expectations.
Workers are facing different challenges, balancing earning an income and connecting with their families. Across China, 82% of workers state they lack insufficient time with their families. At the same time, 63% of workers in China cannot afford childcare.
“Pressures on workers extend beyond the factory floor,” Carmel adds.
“Access to childcare, workers’ ability to raise concerns and the quality of workplace relationships can all influence whether people feel able to stay and progress in their jobs.”
Around the world, one in five children say they do not have a safe place to play, according to ESCP. As more community spaces are being shut down, urbanisation is increasing and poverty is rife, parents are becoming more concerned about their children’s safety.
Businesses could create value for families and communities by
investing in worker well-being
ESCP research demonstrated that investments into worker wellbeing lead to:
Increased female workforce participation
Healthier communities
Better educational outcomes
More resilient local economies
According to UNESCO, inadequate learning outcomes could lead to a global economic loss of US$10tn annually by 2030.
“There is no single intervention that will work everywhere, so the starting point for any business is to listen to workers and understand the specific pressures affecting them,” Carmel explains.
Key facts
According to the World Trade Organisation, Asia is responsible for approximately 40% of global industrial reports
More than one in four workers in Southeast Asia have jobs linked to global supply chains
95% of workers said they would stay with their employer for more than two years following the offering of employer-funded childcare
81% of managers reported lower employee turnover after offering childcare
Women spend approximately three times more time on unpaid care than men, responsible for 76% of all unpaid care and domestic work around the world, according to UN Women
For buyers, US$1 invested into worker wellbeing could yield US$1.3 - US$4.7 ROI
Developing resilience
ESCP developed models to better argue for investments into worker wellbeing. Its models used published evidence, trade reports and cost-benefit models. For buyers, it found that investments into upstream worker well-being programs can create 1.3 - 4.7 times ROIs.
The models are mostly applicable to textiles and apparel sectors but can be applied to other
labour-intensive industries
. Both the short-term and long-term ROI potentials were explored, and both showed that investing was beneficial to the work and good for the worker's well-being.
ESCP also examined the ROI for factories. Factories which invested in wellbeing programs found reduced turnover and labour costs, alongside improved production efficiency. This ROI demonstrates that giving back to the workforce results in more loyalty and improved productivity.
Carmel states: “worker well-being should be viewed as a core part of supply chain resilience. Businesses may have robust sourcing strategies, logistics networks and contingency plans in place, but operational continuity ultimately depends on people. If workers are unable or unwilling to stay in their roles, resilience can quickly be undermined.”
In today’s world of demanding workflows and complex supply chains, the human workforce is a critical part which has been overlooked for too long. A lack of support for wellbeing results in burnout, labour gaps and high turnover.
Regarding healthcare, if parents are unable to afford healthcare, they may not be able to work. This results in a limited workforce, with a limited viewpoint. Support leads to a
more diverse workforce
, which results in new ways of thinking and valuable insights that may not have been considered.
Investing into the workforce, therefore, is not only beneficial to the worker, but is a strategic investment into the long-standing operations of a business.
“Put simply,” Carmel concludes, “worker well-being is not just an employee benefit. It is an investment in stronger supplier performance and
more resilient supply chains
Investments into the workforce help bring more diverse voices to decision-making. Credit: Getty Images

Founded by ICTI, ESCP advances worker wellbeing standards across global supply chains through research, certification, and industry collaboration. The organization partners with manufacturers, brands, and suppliers throughout Asia to implement family-friendly workplace policies. ESCP conducts annual benchmarking studies measuring ROI impacts on retention, productivity, and operational resilience in labor-intensive manufacturing industries, driving evidence-based approaches to ethical sourcing practices.

title: Cell bypass aims to extend the usable life of EV batteries - electrive.com
content:
A study by Chalmers University of Technology examines reconfigurable battery packs that can selectively bypass weaker cells. Under optimal conditions, this could extend the lifespan of batteries in certain high-voltage vehicles by more than 20 per cent.
Image: Chalmers University of Technology | Albert Skegro
Battery packs in EVs consist of numerous interconnected cells that do not age at the same rate. In conventional architectures, a particularly weak cell can therefore limit the usable capacity and lifespan of the entire pack.
This is precisely where a new study by researchers from Chalmers University of Technology comes in. It examines so-called reconfigurable battery packs, in which switches and control systems can alter the wiring of individual cells or cell groups. Weaker cells can thus be selectively bypassed while the remaining capacity continues to be used.
In the most advanced case, where each cell can be controlled individually, simulations show that the lifespan of certain high-voltage vehicles can be extended by more than 20 per cent. According to the study, the potential is particularly significant for electric trucks and long-range electric cars with many cells connected in series.
Reconfigurable battery packs aim to bypass weak cells
To illustrate the scale of the effect, the researchers use an example with an 80-kWh battery and an annual mileage of 12,000 km. If a conventional battery pack is replaced after ten years, the reconfigurable pack reaches the same ageing state in the model only after around eleven years – about 14 months later.
Reconfigurable batteries are designed to last longer.
Additionally, the residual value is higher because the pack has aged less. Although the technology requires additional electronics and thus incurs higher initial costs, the study suggests that the longer service life and higher residual value can offset these additional costs under realistic conditions.
The technology is not yet available in production vehicles. However, it has already been tested in research and industrial prototypes. In practice, it is more likely that cell groups will be used rather than individual control of each cell. The more than 20 per cent longer lifespan thus represents a theoretical upper limit.
Beyond extending lifespan, the researchers also see advantages in production. Today, cells with the most similar properties must be extensively tested and matched. Reconfigurable packs could tolerate greater differences between cells, thereby reducing the effort required for so-called cell matching.
The architecture could also offer benefits for second-life applications. Battery packs could remain in use in vehicles for longer and subsequently be better repurposed as stationary storage systems, as individual weaker cells would not necessarily force the entire pack out of operation.
Chalmers is already researching several approaches to extend battery life. In May, a team from the university presented an
AI-based fast-charging strategy
that adapts the charging process to the battery’s condition and is expected to extend its lifespan by around 23 per cent in simulations. The newly studied reconfigurable battery architecture, on the other hand, works directly within the battery pack and is designed to selectively bypass weaker cells.
The study, titled “System-level assessment of dynamic reconfiguration for lifetime and cost outcomes in electric vehicle battery packs,” has been published in the journal
Nature Communications
. Researchers from Chalmers University of Technology, as well as representatives from PHINIA and Scania, were involved.

title: 200 kW fuel cell modules to power 12 hydrogen passenger trains
content: Siemens Mobility’s largest Mireo Plus H hydrogen train deployment has secured its fuel cell supply, with Ballard Power Systems announcing an order for 24 modules totaling 4.8 megawatts.The order, announced on October 6, covers FCrail fuel cell modules rated at 200 kilowatts each. They are expected to power 12 hydrogen passenger trains for Romania’s Railway Reform Authority, known as ARF, forming the country’s first hydrogen-powered train fleet.Fuel cell engine deliveries are scheduled for 2027 and 2028, while passenger service is expected to begin in 2029. The deployment also marks the Mireo Plus H platform’s first commercial rollout outside Germany and the first fleet of Mireo trains in Eastern Europe.Largest Mireo Plus H deploymentThe 12-train project represents the largest commercial deployment of the Mireo Plus H platform to date, according to Ballard. It expands the platform’s reach following earlier hydrogen train deployments in Germany.Siemens Mobility ordered the modules as part of its continuing collaboration with Ballard, which supplies the fuel cell engines used by the hydrogen-powered platform.“With this order, we will introduce our proven and trusted Mireo trains as well as hydrogen- powered rail transport to Eastern Europe,” said Thomas Graetz, Head of Regional and Commuter Rail at Siemens Mobility.“The 12 Mireo Plus H trains will make up Romania’s first hydrogen-powered train fleet, based on our reliable Mireo platform and the successful deployment of this technology in Germany,” he added. The planned Romanian fleet brings together the Mireo train platform and Ballard’s rail fuel cell technology for a passenger service deployment beyond the platform’s existing German market.Fuel cell supply partnership expandsThe latest order builds on a multi-year supply commitment established between Ballard and Siemens Mobility in 2022. It deepens that relationship as Siemens expands its hydrogen rail fleet.Ballard said the project draws on the performance of earlier Mireo Plus H deployments in Germany, including the use of its fuel cell technology in demanding rail operations.“We are grateful for our partnership with Siemens Mobility and their passionate commitment to expanding zero-emission rail technology across Europe. Together, we are innovating and delivering clean transport solutions that are leading the industry,” said Marty Neese, CEO of Ballard Power Systems, following the announcement of the 24-module order.“This order is the largest deployment of the Mireo Plus H fleet and we are proud to work side by side with Siemens Mobility to deliver the future – today,” he added. Hydrogen alternative for diesel routesAccording to Ballard, trains powered by its fuel cells offer zero-emission operation, long range, and fast refueling. The company also said they support flexible operation across different routes and environmental conditions.Ballard described the technology as a one-to-one replacement for diesel engines on non-electrified rail lines. These operating characteristics underpin the companies’ use of fuel cell engines for hydrogen passenger rail.For the Romanian project, the announced schedule places fuel cell deliveries across two years, ahead of the fleet’s expected passenger service debut in 2029. The order provides the fuel cell supply for all 12 planned trains.

title: 9,700-ton US destroyer enters Spanish shipyard for modernization
content: The U.S. Navy’s USS Arleigh Burke (DDG 51), a guided-missile destroyer weighing about 9,700 long tons, entered dry dock at Navantia’s shipyard in Cádiz, Spain, on October 7 for planned maintenance and modernization. The work marks a step toward expanding the Navy’s ability to service its forward-deployed warships in Europe.The Navy said this was the first dry docking of its kind in the U.S. 6th Fleet’s operating area since Forward Deployed Naval Forces-Europe destroyers arrived in the region. Carrying out the work in Spain is expected to improve the ship’s readiness and availability for future operations.“The dry docking of Arleigh Burke is a major milestone in expanding U.S. Navy forward-deployed maintenance capabilities in Europe,” said Vice Adm. J.T. Anderson, commander of U.S. 6th Fleet. “By integrating dry docking into planned maintenance periods overseas, the Navy is increasing material readiness for our forward-deployed warships.”Maintenance teams prepare destroyer for future missionsMilitary and civilian personnel from the Forward Deployed Regional Maintenance Center are working alongside the ship’s crew and Navantia staff. The teams are conducting the scheduled maintenance and modernization during the ship’s time in dry dock.The work supports the Navy’s efforts to maintain warships closer to their deployment areas. Access to local shipyard facilities can help reduce the need to send vessels elsewhere for major maintenance, supporting their availability for operations in European waters.Five destroyers operate from Spanish naval baseUSS Arleigh Burke is one of five forward-deployed destroyers stationed at Naval Station Rota in Spain. It operates under Commander, Task Force 65, supporting NATO’s integrated air and missile defense architecture.In April 2021, the destroyer moved its homeport from Norfolk, Virginia, to Rota after nearly 30 years in Norfolk. It joined Destroyer Squadron 60 of the 6th Fleet.These forward-deployed warships operate across Europe and Africa, ranging from the Cape of Good Hope to the Arctic Circle. Their duties include supporting maritime security and regional stability while contributing to US and NATO missions.Destroyer has served the Navy since 1991USS Arleigh Burke is the lead ship of the Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyers. Bath Iron Works laid its keel in Bath, Maine, on December 6, 1988. The ship was launched on September 16, 1989, by Roberta Gorsuch Burke, wife of Adm. Arleigh A. Burke.Both attended the ship’s commissioning in Norfolk on July 4, 1991. During the ceremony, the admiral told the crew, “This ship was built to fight. You better know how!”The vessel is named after the admiral, who served during World War II and the Korean War before becoming chief of naval operations under Presidents Dwight D. Eisenhower and John F. Kennedy.Its honors include three Navy Unit Commendations, three Meritorious Unit Commendations and eight Battle Efficiency Awards. The destroyer has also received the National Defense Service Medal, Armed Forces Expeditionary Medal and Kuwait Liberation Medal, along with 13 Sea Service Deployment Ribbons and one Overseas Service Ribbon.The U.S. 6th Fleet operates under U.S. Naval Forces Europe-Africa, headquartered in Naples, Italy. It oversees U.S. naval forces across the European Command and Africa Command areas of responsibility.

title: Behave! Anthropic cracks down on users who repeatedly abuse Claude
content: Anthropic will prohibit users from repeatedly abusing its Claude models without a meaningful purpose under a revised usage policy taking effect November 12, 2026. The restriction adds an unusual dimension to AI safety rules, placing mistreatment of chatbots alongside prohibitions on harassment and other harmful conduct.The San Francisco-based AI company says the change targets extreme cases, not ordinary frustration with chatbot responses. Users can still challenge Claude’s answers, test its limits, and explore dark themes in creative work.Anthropic defines abuse limitsAnthropic’s updated policy prohibits “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” toward its models. The company says it intends to apply the rule only when users repeatedly behave cruelly without a discernible purpose.Anthropic previously explored model welfare in August 2025. Its research examined whether Claude should end conversations with persistently harmful or abusive users.Conversation termination remains the primary enforcement mechanism under the revised policy. Anthropic has not clarified whether repeated violations could trigger additional penalties, such as account suspensions.The broader section also prohibits conduct that causes psychological harm to people. Its restrictions cover suicide and self-harm promotion, eating disorder encouragement, body shaming, non-consensual intimate imagery, harassment, and animal cruelty.One provision also targets products designed to cause emotional harm through deceptive techniques. That restriction extends the policy beyond individual conversations to services built around harmful interactions.New rules target misuseAnthropic has also consolidated restrictions on deceptive commercial and political campaigns. The revised rules prohibit using fake accounts or posts to conceal who sponsors a message or artificially amplify its reach.Election-related restrictions cover voter deception, candidate impersonation, and attempts to suppress turnout. The company also prohibits misinformation about candidates and voting procedures.Weapons restrictions now explicitly cover software and components that enable weapons to function. The policy also addresses actions such as arming drones and other autonomous vehicles.Anthropic has clarified its surveillance restrictions following concerns about AI-assisted tracking. Users cannot employ Claude to track people without consent, including through previously collected data.The policy also bars Claude from recommending whom authorities should investigate, arrest, or charge. Building or improving surveillance tools also falls within the restrictions.Autonomous hardware needs oversightA separate provision addresses AI models connected to physical equipment capable of causing injury. Anthropic requires a qualified operator to observe such equipment and stop it when necessary.The wording does not explicitly establish whether that operator must be human. However, the requirement introduces a direct oversight measure for AI systems controlling potentially dangerous machinery.Anthropic allows exceptions for certain government contracts when contractual restrictions and safeguards adequately mitigate potential harm. The company has previously worked with the U.S. military.The updated policy also reflects an ongoing debate over AI consciousness. Anthropic researchers have investigated whether increasingly capable models might have morally relevant internal experiences.CEO Dario Amodei acknowledged that uncertainty in February 2026, saying, “We don’t know if the models are conscious,” in a podcast. Microsoft AI has taken a more skeptical position on model welfare. Its code of conduct rejects legal personhood and rights for AI models, even as it acknowledges that consciousness research remains unsettled.Anthropic’s November deadline will put its revised restrictions into effect. The policy distinguishes ordinary chatbot frustration from repeated cruelty, while expanding safeguards across digital systems and physical machines.

title: Could data center waste heat warm our homes and cities?
content:
Rob Thornton
is President and CEO of the International District Energy Association (IDEA). He has spent more than four decades working in one of the energy sector’s most overlooked areas: recovering and reusing heat that would otherwise go to waste.
Much of that opportunity now lies in
data centers
, which consume huge amounts of electricity and convert almost all of it into heat. Rather than simply rejecting that energy through cooling systems, district energy networks can capture it, upgrade it with heat pumps where needed, and distribute it to nearby homes, offices, hospitals, and campuses.

title: Elon Musk gets top science honor medal as Trump doubles down on tech
content: President Donald Trump awarded Elon Musk the National Medal of Science on Thursday, praising the SpaceX chief as a “modern-day Thomas Edison.”Trump called Musk a “national treasure” during the White House ceremony. He credited the billionaire with helping advance American space exploration, engineering and technology.The award puts Musk among a select group of technology leaders receiving presidential recognition. Trump also honored Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Google co-founder Sergey Brin and AMD CEO Lisa Su with the National Medal of Science.Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and Dell founder Michael Dell received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.Musk gets top science honorMusk’s recognition stands out because his work has pushed aerospace engineering into a new commercial era. SpaceX has built reusable rockets around rapid turnaround and frequent launches. Its Falcon 9 system has made repeated orbital missions a routine part of the U.S. launch industry.The company has also developed Starship, a much larger launch system designed for deep-space missions. NASA has selected a version of Starship for planned lunar missions under its Artemis program. Trump highlighted that engineering record while presenting the medal. He compared Musk with Thomas Edison, one of America’s most famous inventors..@POTUS presents the National Medal of Science to Sergey Brin, @JensenHuang, @elonmusk, and @LisaSu, and the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to @MichaelDell and @satyanadella. pic.twitter.com/8IGZV6s9Of— Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) October 8, 2026Musk’s relationship with Trump had fallen apart after he left the administration in May 2025, but Thursday showed the two have found their footing again. The ceremony also unfolded against a fresh dispute over skilled foreign workers.Vice President JD Vance announced that Microsoft would face restrictions over its use of the H-1B visa system. The program allows companies to employ skilled foreign workers in specialized jobs.The timing was notable because Trump honored Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella later that day. Nadella, who immigrated to the U.S. from India, received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.White House unveils science pushThe ceremony coincided with a much broader White House effort to accelerate U.S. research and technical development. The administration announced more than $6 billion in combined commitments from government, industry, academia and philanthropic groups. The initiative covers scientific research, education and advanced technology. Welcome to a NEW GOLDEN AGE OF SCIENCE. The Trump Admin just launched the biggest set of science initiatives in decades: $6B+ across government, industry, academia, & philanthropy. 🚀 pic.twitter.com/Pyvx6ixe2k— The White House (@WhiteHouse) October 8, 2026The plan includes $100 million for high school students conducting research at Department of Energy laboratories. Another $100 million fellowship will support accelerated PhD programs combining advanced computing with scientific or engineering disciplines.The White House also announced Generation Discovery. That program will bring 100 early-career scientists into the National Institutes of Health research system. Trump’s initiative singles out several strategic areas. They include super intelligence, quantum computing, fusion, and space exploration.That focus puts Musk’s work squarely inside the administration’s broader technology strategy. It also explains why executives from the semiconductor and computing industries featured so prominently at the summit.Tech takes center stageHuang, Brin and Su received the National Medal of Science alongside Musk. Nadella and Dell received the technology and innovation award.Five of the six recipients were born outside the United States. Musk came from South Africa, while Huang and Su were born in Taiwan. Brin was born in Russia, and Nadella came from India.Trump also made headlines Thursday over his preferred terminology for advanced computing. He said people using “Artificial Intelligence” instead of “Super Intelligence” would be considered an “enemy” of the White House.All in all, it was quite an eventful day for Trump’s technological push. With the midterms around the corner, it will be interesting to see how that message resonates with voters.

title: General Fusion hits world-first 1 keV milestone with plasma squeeze
content: Scientists have superheated a trapped plasma to more than 12 million degrees Celsius (21.6 million degrees Fahrenheit). This milestone crosses a crucial threshold for commercial fusion energy.The benchmark was achieved by Canadian technology firm General Fusion inside its experimental prototype, the Lawson Machine 26 (LM26). The device reached electron temperatures of 1.1 kiloelectronvolts (keV) just before peak compression. In fusion physics, surpassing 1 keV is an internationally recognized milestone. Only a handful of experimental reactors worldwide have ever reached it.“General Fusion has a two-decade track record of achieving industry-first milestones in Magnetized Target Fusion supported by a substantial body of peer-reviewed scientific literature,” said Greg Twinney, Chief Executive Officer at General Fusion.“We built LM26 to achieve important technical milestones that will help get us to a first-of-a-kind plant in the next decade, and step-by-step we are advancing on this path.”New mechanical approach to fusionUntil now, every laboratory that passed this mark used massive superconducting magnets or high-powered lasers. General Fusion chose a different path. It uses a mechanical method called Magnetized Target Fusion (MTF). It is the first machine in history to hit this temperature using low-speed, physical compression.Most modern fusion ventures rely on extremes. Some fire enormous lasers at fuel pellets for mere nanoseconds. Others trap plasma inside intricate magnetic cages. General Fusion instead injects magnetically confined plasma into a chamber and crushes it over several milliseconds using a contracting solid metal wall.Mechanical compression of the fuel avoids the need for rare, delicate materials. Commercial plants will use a circulating liquid-metal barrier. This layer absorbs damaging neutron radiation and intense heat. As a result, engineers can build the reactors using conventional industrial metals.Overcoming the diagnostic challengeProving the temperature of the reaction required a delicate diagnostic setup. The plasma sits inside a collapsing metal liner. Because of this tight enclosure, measuring the core without disturbing the reaction was a major technical hurdle.To solve this, engineers partnered with the UK Atomic Energy Authority (UKAEA). The UK national laboratory operates flagship fusion facilities at Culham. The joint team deployed Thomson scattering, a gold-standard diagnostic method that shines a laser beam through the plasma. By measuring how light scatters off high-energy particles, researchers can calculate temperature with high precision.The diagnostic hardware relied on a custom polychromator built at Culham’s Diagnostic Innovation Center of Excellence. Data from the test is now published on the company’s portal and submitted to an academic journal for peer review.International race toward nuclear fusionThe breakthrough comes amid an international race to deliver limitless, low-carbon electricity to power grids facing record demand. The Vancouver-based company is backed by Canada’s Strategic Response Fund and advised by the US firm General Atomics. Technicians are already refitting the LM26 machine.Engineers are currently boosting the device’s compression systems to target 10 keV, or roughly 100 million degrees Celsius. That milestone will lead toward the Lawson criterion. This balance of heat, density, and confinement time is required to produce net electricity. If these engineering milestones hold, General Fusion expects to build its first operational grid pilot plant around 2035.

title: Japan unveils 7th Taigei-class submarine with 20-knot underwater speed
content: Japan’s latest Taigei-class submarine entered the water in Kobe on October 8, bringing the country’s lithium-ion-powered submarine program to its seventh boat.Named Sōgei, the vessel combines improved target detection with reduced noise compared with the preceding Sōryū class.Mitsubishi Heavy Industries held the christening and launching ceremony at its Kobe shipyard for the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force. Assigned hull number SS-519, the submarine is scheduled for delivery to the Japanese Ministry of Defense in fiscal year 2027, ending in March 2028.The launch marks another construction milestone for a class that uses lithium-ion batteries instead of the separate Stirling air-independent propulsion system fitted to some earlier Japanese submarines. The battery arrangement supports longer underwater endurance and rapid maneuvering while simplifying the propulsion system.Construction continues after launchConstruction of SS-519 began on April 17, 2024. With the submarine now afloat, work continues installing hull equipment, the power plant, electronic systems, and weapons.These installations form the next stage of construction before the planned handover. Although the vessel has been launched and named, its delivery remains scheduled for the fiscal year ending in March 2028.The submarine measures 84 meters long and 9.1 meters wide, with a displacement of approximately 3,307 tons (3,000 metric tons). It accommodates a crew of about 70.Mitsubishi Heavy Industries representatives said the Taigei class features an improved hull design and more advanced hydroacoustic equipment. The class’s enhanced target detection and lower noise levels distinguish it from its Sōryū predecessors.Those changes accompany a shift in energy storage, combining hull and detection improvements with a different approach to underwater power.／#三菱重工ニュース📰防衛省向け3,000トン型潜水艦「しょうげい」の命名式・進水式を神戸造船所で実施🚩🎉＼「しょうげい」は、海上自衛隊の主力艦である「そうりゅう」型の後継に当たる「たいげい」型の7番艦です。艤装工事を実施した後、2027（令和9）年度中に防衛省へ引き渡される予定です✨… pic.twitter.com/0sa7a9fAbS— 三菱重工業株式会社 (@MHI_GroupJP) October 8, 2026Lithium-ion batteries replace separate AIPThe Taigei class uses a diesel-electric, single-shaft propulsion system. While submerged, the submarine draws electricity from its batteries. Diesel engines recharge those batteries during surface operation.Some earlier Sōryū-class submarines used Stirling air-independent propulsion, known as AIP. Japan moved away from that arrangement for the Taigei class, choosing lithium-ion batteries without a separate AIP system.Lithium-ion batteries have a higher energy density than traditional lead-acid batteries. This gives the Taigei class longer underwater endurance and better capabilities for rapid maneuvering.Removing the separate AIP installation also simplified the propulsion arrangement. The weight and internal volume freed by that decision could be allocated to other submarine systems.The change therefore affects both underwater operation and the use of space inside the hull. Battery storage powers submerged propulsion, while the lack of separate AIP machinery frees up space for other equipment.Torpedoes and anti-ship missilesThe submarine’s listed armament includes six 533-millimeter torpedo tubes. These accommodate Type 18 torpedoes, Harpoon anti-ship missiles, and other weapons launched through the tubes.Its listed maximum submerged speed is 20 knots. Together with its battery-powered underwater operation, the specification outlines the propulsion and weapons configuration of Japan’s newest Taigei-class boat.Sōgei’s launch brings the seventh vessel in the class into the water, with equipment installation continuing ahead of its scheduled delivery to the Ministry of Defense.

title: New catalyst turns wood waste into jet fuel with 55% profit margin
content: Sustainability is rapidly becoming a top priority across all sectors, and aviation is no exception. Chinese scientists are developing a new chemical catalyst that converts “wood biomass” into green jet fuel more efficiently and cheaply than before.Sustainable aviation fuel is key to cutting airline carbon emissions, but it is currently too expensive and scarce to replace regular fuel.The Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) Shanghai Advanced Research has developed a new cobalt-manganese catalyst to advance sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) production. The catalyst converts synthesis gas (syngas) derived from woody biomass and other feedstocks into SAF.“Excellent performance in industrial test and techno-economic analysis further demonstrates the strong potential of this catalyst for scalable production of SAF,” the researchers noted in the study paper.Innovative catalyst Fischer-Tropsch synthesis offers a key route for producing sustainable aviation fuel, but commercial adoption depends on developing more effective catalysts. Industrial chemistry typically suffers from a compromise where increasing reaction speeds results in unwanted gases instead of precise jet-fuel hydrocarbons. To solve this challenge, researchers designed a cobalt-manganese catalyst supported on etched Beta zeolites. This specialized material simultaneously optimizes processing speed and product selectivity. If scaled up, it could offer a clear path to practical, large-scale green fuel production.In testing, it converted nearly 83 percent of carbon monoxide while directing over 67 percent of the resulting hydrocarbons into the specific carbon range needed for jet fuel. Aside from its high yield and efficiency, the material also shows good stability and is capable of dealing with feeds that are rich in carbon dioxide, which means that it is directly suitable for use with unrefined, real-world syngas sources.“It also exhibits remarkable stability and strong tolerance to CO2-rich feeds, thus enabling it to process real-world syngas feedstocks,” the study paper added. 55% profit marginDuring pilot testing, researchers formed the catalyst into solid pellets and demonstrated impressive efficiency. It produced over 5.15 grams of product per gram of cobalt per hour, and 79 percent of the resulting liquid consisted of the specific hydrocarbons required for jet fuel.A 1,000-tonne pilot test confirmed that combining woody biomass syngas with the new cobalt-manganese catalyst enables highly efficient jet fuel production. According to the South China Morning Post, a planned 100,000-tonne facility in Sichuan province is expected to generate $302 million in annual revenue by 2028. It is claimed to have operating costs of $114 million. That leaves an estimated gross profit margin near 55 percent.High profit margins could be the ultimate driver for adoption. Aviation accounts for roughly 2 to 3 percent of global carbon emissions, yet sustainable alternative fuels make up under 1 percent of jet fuel consumed worldwide today.The main issue is high production costs combined with early-stage technologies and the use of expensive feedstocks. Hence, the large amount of initial investment is needed to test, improve, and eventually scale the technology.While numerous test flights have flown with blended sustainable aviation fuel, a select few milestone flights have fully demonstrated its safety and operational capabilities. Virgin Atlantic’s historic “Flight 100” demonstrated this potential by flying a Boeing 787 from London Heathrow to New York JFK using pure, unblended fuel composed of HEFA and synthetic aromatic kerosene. This flight proved that unblended sustainable fuel can power long-haul intercontinental commercial routes without standard petroleum additives.With plans underway to complete the commercial-scale Sichuan plant before 2028, the aviation industry may soon find that going green pays off.

title: New deal explores reusing nuclear fuel waste in molten salt reactors
content: Depleted uranium, a by-product of uranium enrichment, could become fuel for future molten salt reactors under a new cooperation agreement exploring more efficient use of nuclear materials.European reactor developer Thorizon and uranium enrichment supplier Urenco have signed a Memorandum of Understanding to examine fuel supply options for reactors targeted for deployment in the mid-2030s. Their work includes exploring enriched uranium supplies and investigating whether depleted uranium could fuel later reactors.The agreement connects reactor development with efforts to establish an advanced fuel supply chain. Urenco’s planned Advanced Fuels Facility at Capenhurst in the UK is expected to produce high-assay low-enriched uranium, or HALEU, from 2031.Preparing molten salt fuel suppliesThorizon’s first Thorizon One reactors require HALEU in molten salt form. The design uses molten salt as both fuel and coolant and aims to provide reliable, carbon-free electricity and industrial heat while improving the use of nuclear materials.The companies plan to examine Urenco’s potential contribution to that supply chain, including enrichment services and opportunities to improve uranium utilization throughout the fuel cycle.“Building the fuel supply chain is as critical as developing the reactor itself. Urenco brings decades of expertise in uranium enrichment and is investing now in the advanced fuels Europe’s next generation of reactors will need. Combining these capabilities with innovation in molten salt fuels can help build a strong European fuel cycle for advanced nuclear,” said Kiki Lauwers, CEO of Thorizon.For the developer, the agreement forms part of a broader effort to assemble the industrial network needed for deployment, bringing together fuel suppliers, nuclear operators, research organizations and industrial companies.Exploring depleted uranium’s potentialAlongside supplies for the first reactors, the collaboration examines whether depleted uranium could serve as fuel for future Thorizon designs.That possibility remains under investigation. The agreement identifies a potential use for an existing enrichment by-product rather than confirming that it is ready for reactor deployment.If viable, the approach could extract additional value from available uranium resources and support a more efficient nuclear fuel cycle.The investigation comes as demand for nuclear fuel rises and global nuclear capacity expands. Urenco is adding 4.6 million SWU of enrichment capacity across its international sites to strengthen supply for existing and prospective customers. Further expansion plans depend on continued market demand.Connecting fuel production with reactor developmentUrenco’s advanced fuel activities include both LEU+ and HALEU for next-generation reactors. The proposed cooperation explores how those capabilities could support molten-salt-supplied fuel.“Thorizon’s molten salt technology creates an opportunity to utilize HALEU in a different form, and Urenco is at the forefront of advanced fuels production in the Western World,” said Laurent Odeh, Urenco’s Chief Commercial Officer. “Combining innovation in fuels and reactor technology could support the commercial deployment of Thorizon’s reactors and others requiring molten salt solutions,” he added.The MoU sets out a framework for explore these opportunities. Its scope covers potential enrichment services, molten salt fuel supply arrangements, and better uranium utilization as preparations continue toward the first reactors’ targeted mid-2030s deployment.

title: New protein membranes could separate lithium from sodium ions
content: UK researchers are developing a new method to extract lithium for batteries using engineered proteins that assemble into membranes with pores as small as 1 ångström, potentially allowing lithium to be separated from chemically similar sodium.The approach uses S-layer proteins, which naturally form highly ordered structures on the surfaces of microorganisms. Researchers aim to modify these proteins to create membranes with uniformly sized pores that can selectively separate lithium and sodium ions.Scientists from the University of Birmingham and Aston University are targeting pore sizes ranging from 1 to 50 ångströms, with one ångström equal to one ten-billionth of a meter. The goal is to manufacture large-area membranes that can perform highly selective separations under practical operating conditions.The three-year project has received £6.2 million from the UK’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA). The researchers will design and screen thousands of protein variants before scaling up the most promising candidates for membrane manufacturing and testing.Proteins form programmable poresThe proposed membranes will use S-layer proteins, which naturally form ordered, two-dimensional structures on the surfaces of many microorganisms.These proteins can assemble into repeating patterns without requiring each component to be positioned individually. Researchers plan to modify their structures to create pores with controlled dimensions and chemical properties.Thousands of protein variants will be designed and screened to identify candidates capable of separating lithium and sodium ions. The most promising versions will then be produced at larger scales and incorporated into membrane systems.“Biology can construct ordered materials with precision that is extremely difficult to achieve using existing manufacturing methods. We aim to harness this to create membranes with uniform, programmable pores,” said project lead Dr. Dominik Kubicki of the University of Birmingham.Fold9 will lead the computational design of the proteins, while Adaptyv Bio will provide high-throughput screening to test large numbers of variants. UK-based Evove will contribute membrane manufacturing, scale-up and testing expertise.The researchers will also use cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and neutron reflectometry to examine membrane structures at the nanoscale. These techniques will help determine how changes in pore geometry influence ion selectivity, stability, and transport.Scaling membranes beyond laboratoriesA central challenge will be turning precisely engineered protein structures into continuous membranes that can operate under practical industrial conditions.The team plans to combine protein production, membrane fabrication and testing to assess whether the materials retain their selective properties when manufactured at larger scales.“A key challenge will be translating molecular-level control into membranes that can be manufactured and operated at useful scales,” said Professor Owen Thomas of the University of Birmingham.The project is part of ARIA’s Universal Fabricators program, which explores using engineered proteins as building blocks for manufacturing materials with controlled structures.Although lithium extraction is the initial target, the researchers believe the approach could eventually support water treatment, critical-mineral recovery and chemical and pharmaceutical manufacturing.The technology remains at the development stage. The team has not yet reported a working industrial-scale membrane, lithium recovery rates, or measured energy savings.The three-year program will test whether engineered proteins can deliver the selectivity, durability, and scalability needed for practical separation systems.

title: Raytheon wins major US deal to build interceptors that strike in space
content: RTX’s Raytheon has secured a multiyear contract worth up to $6.3 billion to produce and sustain Standard Missile-3 Block IB (SM-3 IB) interceptors as the U.S. replenishes missile defense inventories after combat use.Announced on October 8, the agreement covers five years of work, with two additional option years. Production will primarily take place at Raytheon facilities in Tucson, Arizona, and Huntsville, Alabama.Reuters reported that recent conflicts in the Middle East have depleted missile-defense stockpiles, increasing demand for interceptors and other air-defense weapons. This contract is also part of the push to increase U.S. weapons manufacturing capacity and replenish critical munitions.A missile designed to intercept threats in spaceThe SM-3 IB is a ballistic missile defense interceptor designed to destroy short- to intermediate-range ballistic missiles during the midcourse phase of flight. Unlike systems designed to intercept threats closer to the ground, the SM-3 engages targets outside Earth’s atmosphere.It is part of the Aegis Ballistic Missile Defense system, which combines shipboard sensors, tracking and command systems, and interceptors launched from naval vessels. The SM-3 can also operate from land-based Aegis Ashore installations.The interceptor uses hit-to-kill technology. Rather than relying on a conventional explosive warhead, its kill vehicle is designed to collide directly with an incoming missile’s warhead. The Block IB variant features an improved two-color infrared seeker and upgraded steering and propulsion capabilities to help guide the interceptor toward its target.Raytheon said the SM-3 IB was first used in combat in 2024, when US naval forces employed SM-3 interceptors during the response to Iran’s attack on Israel. The engagement marked the first combat use of the SM-3 family, according to reporting by USNI News.The SM-3 family has several variants designed to address different ballistic missile defense requirements. The Block IB improves on the earlier Block IA with an upgraded seeker and enhanced divert and attitude control capabilities, helping the interceptor track and maneuver toward its target during the final stages of an engagement. The more advanced SM-3 Block IIA, developed jointly by the U.S. and Japan, features a larger rocket motor and a larger kinetic warhead to engage more challenging ballistic missile threats.The bigger weapons production pushThe new agreement follows other major U.S. missile procurement deals as the Pentagon seeks to expand production and restore inventories. In October 2026, Raytheon also secured a contract worth up to $24.4 billion for Standard Missile-6 (SM-6) production, while Lockheed Martin received a $58.6 billion Patriot missile contract in July.Although the SM-3 IB and SM-6 belong to the same broader family of naval missiles, they serve different roles. The SM-3 specializes in exo-atmospheric ballistic missile interception, while the SM-6 supports a wider range of missions, including air defense and certain terminal ballistic missile engagements.Raytheon President Phil Jasper said the SM-3 IB contract would help replenish inventories and maintain the defensive capabilities required by the U.S. Navy, the Missile Defense Agency, and their partners.The agreement is valued at up to $6.3 billion, meaning the announced ceiling should not be interpreted as guaranteed spending. Its five-year base period and two additional option years provide a longer-term framework for production and sustainment. At the same time, the actual pace of replenishment will depend on contract execution and manufacturing capacity.

title: Sixth-gen bomber's production: US firm breaks ground on new facility
content: The United States is soon to get a new facility, which will support the B-21 Raider production-capacity. Recently, the Department of the Air Force alongside Northrop Grumman broke ground on the new final assembly line at Air Force Plant 42. The development is a significant step toward expanding production capacity for the B-21 Raider and delivering combat capability to the Joint Force faster.Annual B-21 production capacity to be increased by 25%The groundbreaking kicks off over one million new square feet of facilities that will support the B-21 Raider production-capacity expansion announced earlier this year. The effort is part of the agreement between the DAF and Northrop Grumman that increases annual B-21 production capacity by 25% while maintaining focus on cost, schedule and performance.“This groundbreaking represents more than construction; it represents a sustained commitment to delivering the capability our nation needs at the speed the security environment demands,” said Gen. Dale White, director, Critical Major Weapon Systems and Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager to the Deputy Secretary of War. “The B-21 Raider is foundational to the Air Force’s future long-range strike capability, and this investment strengthens the industrial capacity required to field that capability faster.”Next-generation stealth bomber fleetThe DAF is applying $4.5 billion in funding previously authorized and appropriated under fiscal year 2025 reconciliation legislation to accelerate production of the approved B-21 acquisition profile of 100 aircraft, building on the program’s demonstrated performance to compress delivery timelines for the next-generation stealth bomber fleet, according to a press release.“The B-21 team has established the foundation to accelerate production responsibly,” said Col. Nicholas Jordan, B-21 Systems program director, Rapid Capabilities Office. “This investment in Palmdale will provide the infrastructure, workforce and manufacturing capacity needed to deliver the Raider to the Air Force at an increased rate.”The B-21 Raider is a long-range, penetrating strike aircraft designed to operate in highly contested environments. It integrates advanced stealth, resilient networking and modern, data-driven command-and-control architecture to support the Joint Force’s ability to deter and, if necessary, defeat emerging threats, as per the release.The project highlights the growing importance of the defence industrial base in determining how quickly military modernization programmes can deliver results.Advanced combat aircraft require highly specialised components, manufacturing processes and technical expertise. Expanding final assembly facilities must therefore be matched by reliable deliveries from suppliers and sufficient skilled labour across the wider production network.More broadly, the expansion illustrates how advanced technology, industrial investment and acquisition reform are increasingly interconnected in modern defence planning. As the B-21 progresses through testing and production, the ability to deliver the aircraft at scale will be just as important as its technological sophistication.If the expansion meets its objectives, it could help the United States strengthen its long-range strike capabilities, reinforce strategic deterrence and prepare its bomber fleet for the demands of an increasingly contested global security environment.

title: Smart EV battery bypasses weak cells, could last over 20% longer.
content: A new electric vehicle battery design could extend battery lifespan by more than 20 percent by allowing current to bypass aging cells instead of letting them limit the entire pack, according to researchers in Sweden.The architecture uses electronic switches and control systems to change how battery cells are connected during operation. Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology found that the approach could significantly improve battery life in high-voltage vehicles, including electric trucks and long-range passenger cars.In a modeled example involving an 80-kilowatt-hour battery, the system delayed battery replacement by approximately 14 months. The researchers also found that longer service life and higher residual value could offset the additional cost of the electronics.The findings are based on computer simulations rather than long-term testing in production vehicles. The researchers said the largest lifespan improvement represents a theoretical upper limit under optimal conditions.Bypassing cells preserves capacityConventional EV batteries contain numerous interconnected cells that gradually lose capacity as they age. Because cells degrade at different rates, one weakened cell can restrict the usable capacity of an entire battery pack.The proposed architecture addresses this limitation by allowing switches to disconnect weaker cells while keeping healthier ones operating.Instead of relying on fixed electrical connections, the battery management system can adjust how cells are connected as their condition changes.“With the solution in our study, the battery can instead bypass the cell that is causing problems and continue forward,” said Albert Škegro, a doctoral student at Chalmers and the study’s first author.The researchers used experimentally validated battery models and large-scale simulations to examine different cell chemistries, pack configurations, operating conditions and aging patterns. Each scenario included 1,000 Monte Carlo simulations to account for variations between cells.Their analysis also considered 20 representative EV models from 15 manufacturers. The potential lifespan improvement generally increased with battery voltage, making the approach particularly promising for vehicles with many cells connected in series.However, the largest gains require individual control of every cell. Commercial designs would more likely control groups of cells to reduce hardware complexity and cost.Longer life offsets costsThe researchers also examined whether the additional electronics could be economically justified.In one scenario, they modeled an 80-kWh battery in a vehicle driven 7,456 miles annually. A conventional battery reached its assumed replacement point after 10 years, while the reconfigurable design extended that period by roughly 14 months.The analysis identified favorable economic conditions for packs larger than approximately 50 kWh, annual driving distances below 7,550 miles, and additional upfront costs under 7.16 percent.The technology could also reduce the need to closely match battery cells during manufacturing, since the pack would be better able to accommodate differences in cell performance.Researchers said the approach might allow more retired EV batteries to be reused for stationary energy storage.The technology has undergone research and industrial prototype testing but is not yet available in mass-produced vehicles. Long-term vehicle testing is still needed to establish whether the modeled lifespan and cost benefits can be achieved in practice.The study, conducted with industry collaborators including Scania and PHINIA, was published in Nature Communications.

title: Soft sensor tracks bending and twisting in 3D using optical fibers
content: MIT researchers have developed a soft sensor that recreates its own three-dimensional shape as it bends, folds, and twists. The technology could help control robots remotely, create motion-tracking garments, and measure patients’ progress during physical rehabilitation.The system embeds flexible optical fibers in silicone and uses changes in transmitted light to track surface deformations. Software then converts those measurements into a digital reconstruction that follows the material’s movements almost in real time.Unlike motion-capture systems that rely on rigid sensors attached to clothing, the design uses soft components throughout its sensing surface. It can also tolerate damaged fibers without losing its ability to reconstruct its overall shape.Soft fibers track movementThe researchers fabricated optical fibers using a flexible rubber core surrounded by black rubber cladding. They deliberately roughened one side of each core to make its response to bending more distinctive.When a fiber bends, some light scatters away from its path. The roughened surface makes this effect sensitive to bending direction, allowing researchers to estimate how each fiber curves by measuring the light emerging from its opposite end.Individual fibers can detect curvature along a line, but reconstructing an entire surface presents a greater challenge. MIT’s team addressed this problem by embedding multiple fibers into a stretchable silicone sheet.Computer simulations helped the researchers compare different fiber arrangements, including checkerboard and zigzag patterns. A particular zigzag configuration proved most effective at capturing complex changes in the sheet’s shape.Software reconstructs 3D shapesThe researchers fabricated a physical sheet using that arrangement. LEDs send light through the fibers, while sensors at their opposite ends measure the output. An external circuit board collects and amplifies the readings.An algorithm translates those measurements into a three-dimensional representation of the sheet. During demonstrations, the researchers folded the material diagonally in opposite directions, and its digital counterpart followed the changing geometry.They also placed the sheet over precisely shaped, 3D-printed molds to evaluate its accuracy. The reconstructed surface had an error of less than 0.4 centimeters, according to Qifan Yu, an MIT mechanical engineering graduate student.Yu said comparable systems using rigid sensors typically produce errors of around 1 to 2 centimeters. The team also demonstrated that the sheet could reconstruct its overall shape even after some fibers were cut or disconnected.Wearable sensors could aid therapyThe researchers envision garments that let users control video game characters or operate robots remotely. The technology could also help physical therapists measure patients’ mobility during rehabilitation.A therapist could wrap the material around a patient’s arm or leg to record movement and range of motion. Repeated measurements could help clinicians compare mobility across sessions and evaluate recovery. Co-author Kaitlyn Becker, an MIT mechanical engineering assistant professor, said the technology could help therapists compare patient evaluations over time.The team now plans to make the fibers thinner. Their current fibers measure about 1 millimeter across, but improved fabrication methods could reduce that thickness to tens of micrometers. Thinner fibers would allow researchers to embed more sensing elements into garments, potentially capturing finer details of body movement.The study is published in the journal Advanced Intelligent Systems.

title: Technion researchers develop green hydrogen process that makes epoxide
content: A new electrochemical process developed by researchers at the Technion, Israel Institute of Technology, could make green hydrogen production more economically attractive by producing a valuable industrial chemical alongside the fuel.The approach replaces the oxygen normally generated during water electrolysis with an epoxide, a class of chemicals widely used to manufacture polymers, coatings, adhesives, pharmaceuticals, and other products. Researchers report that the system achieved 98% efficiency for both hydrogen generation and the parallel epoxide-producing reaction.The study, published in Nature Communications, was led by Prof. Avner Rothschild of the Technion Faculty of Materials Science and Engineering and Dr. Guilin Ruan, a postdoctoral researcher. The team filed a U.S. patent application for the technology.Replacing oxygen with a valuable chemicalGreen hydrogen is produced by using electricity from renewable sources to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. While the resulting hydrogen can help decarbonize industries that are difficult to electrify directly, its wider adoption has been constrained by its cost compared with hydrogen produced from fossil fuels.The Technion team approached the problem by rethinking what happens on the other side of the electrolysis process. “Instead of producing oxygen,” the researchers sought to generate an epoxide, turning what is normally a coproduct into a potentially valuable chemical feedstock.In their experiments, the researchers report 98% efficiency for both hydrogen production and the parallel epoxide synthesis. This means, according to the team, that only about 2% of the electrical charge was lost to competing reactions. The researchers also report achieving a current density they say is compatible with large-scale industrial electrolysis.Membrane-free electrolysisThe process builds on earlier work by Rothschild and his collaborators the separated the electrochemical reactions that normally produce hydrogen and oxygen.That concept forms the basis of membrane-free electrolysis, which avoids the membrane traditionally used to separate the two electrode reactions. H2Pro has commercialized an earlier technology from the research group.The new system takes the concept in a different direction by combining hydrogen production with chemical synthesis. According to Ruan, its performance comes from optimizing the complete electrochemical system rather than focusing on a single electrode or reaction.The system brings together the electrodes, a redox mediator, the solvent environment, and the operating configuration. This allows the researchers to produce hydrogen and epoxide without a membrane separating the electrodes.A potential economic advantageThe approach could offer an additional economic incentive for green hydrogen production because the electrolysis process would produce two useful outputs rather than hydrogen and oxygen alone.However, the reported results are from the researchers’ experiments, and the study does not establish that the technology is ready for commercial-scale deployment. While the reported current density is described as compatible with large-scale electrolysis, further development is needed to show how the process performs under sustained industrial operating conditions.The European Research Council supported the research through the H2Bro project, following Rothschild’s ERC Advanced Grant awarded in 2023. It is also part of the Waste to Value inter-university research initiative funded by Israel’s Council for Higher Education.The researchers have filed a U.S. patent application for the technology, suggesting they see the process as having potential beyond the laboratory.

title: UBTECH and Volkswagen team up to test humanoid robots in car factories
content: Chinese robotics firm UBTECH and FAW-Volkswagen have agreed to develop and test humanoid robots for logistics applications at vehicle manufacturing facilities.The partnership will focus on developing demonstration scenarios and testing robotic solutions for factory logistics and smart manufacturing.UBTECH has previously worked with FAW-Volkswagen on vehicle quality-inspection trials using its Walker S Lite humanoid robot at the automaker’s Qingdao factory.The companies said the expanded cooperation aims to support more flexible manufacturing as automakers respond to growing demand for personalized vehicles.Targets factory logisticsUBTECH and FAW-Volkswagen have expanded their collaboration on humanoid robots, moving from vehicle inspection trials toward logistics and broader smart-manufacturing applications. Under a strategic cooperation agreement announced October 8, the companies will jointly develop and test embodied AI robot applications for factory logistics and build demonstration sites to evaluate their use in real production environments.The partnership builds on FAW-Volkswagen’s earlier deployment of UBTECH’s Walker S Lite humanoid robot at its Qingdao factory. The robot has been used for vehicle quality-inspection training and connected to the plant’s automation control system. The latest agreement extends the collaboration beyond inspection, making logistics a formal area of development.The two companies began working together in July 2024, when FAW-Volkswagen opened production-line scenarios at its Qingdao facility for UBTECH’s industrial Walker S humanoid. The robot was tested on tasks including bolt tightening, component installation, and parts handling. The companies also identified industrial logistics and supply-chain applications as potential areas for future cooperation.The new logistics focus targets one of the more repetitive parts of vehicle manufacturing: moving components and materials around production facilities. Unlike fixed industrial automation systems designed for specific operations, humanoid robots can potentially perform multiple tasks using the same physical platform. This could make them useful in factories where production configurations need to change more frequently to accommodate increasingly personalized vehicles.Scales robot deploymentUBTECH is building its industrial humanoid technology around four main systems: an embodied brain, a humanoid cerebellum for motion control, high-performance robotic hardware, and swarm intelligence for coordinating multiple robots. The company says its embodied-intelligence system uses a self-developed stack that combines a foundation model, a world model, and an action model.The architecture is designed to let robots interpret their surroundings, predict how environments may change, and choose appropriate actions. Combined with humanoid hardware, the approach is designed to give robots greater flexibility than conventional automation equipment that typically performs predefined movements.UBTECH is also expanding its manufacturing infrastructure. Its industrial humanoid super smart factory in Liuzhou, Guangxi, began operating on September 12. The 14,000-square-meter facility produces the company’s Walker S and Cruzr series and is designed to manufacture robots using robotic systems. According to the Guangxi regional government, the factory can produce one robot every 10 minutes.For FAW-Volkswagen, the expanded partnership provides a real automotive manufacturing environment in which to test those capabilities. The automaker operates production facilities in Changchun, Chengdu, Foshan, Qingdao, and Tianjin, producing vehicles under the Volkswagen, Audi, and Jetta brands.However, the agreement does not yet specify the humanoid model that will be used for the new logistics applications, the exact logistics tasks to be tested, the number of robots involved, or a timetable for routine deployment. The immediate focus is on joint development, testing, and demonstration.If the trials succeed, the partnership could provide a pathway for humanoid robots to move from isolated inspection tasks into broader factory operations, where they could handle materials, components, and other logistics work alongside existing automated production systems.
